#3127. AI Is The Accommodation Nobody Has To Approve

Dave Goyal | CEO, Think AI | Author | Speaker | Harvard AI Certified | 30+ yrs in Data & AI | Inc5000 Honoree.

​When I roll into a conference on my electric scooter, I see it on people’s faces: sympathy, then distance. When I reach out, some people pull back. When the room starts to mingle, I often get left out.

My first thought used to be, “I shouldn’t have this problem.” My second thought is the one that built my career: “Let me shine through with my knowledge and connect with a few people.”

Founders are expected to move city to city, state to state, country to country. Physical limits hit hardest right when you want to grow fastest.

Mindset is the bigger fight. You spend years trying to show you are not different.

Then there is money. Entrepreneurs with disabilities average about $61,000 a year in revenue, less than half the $135,000 of other entrepreneurs, according to a 2025 fact sheet from AEO based on NORC data.

Yet we choose this path more often. In 2025, 9.1% of employed people with a disability were self-employed, compared with 5.9% of everyone else, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The ones who make it have serious grit. But grit is tied to mindset, and it runs low. What keeps mine going is a life mission. Find your one superpower and a mission for life. Without them, it is very hard to survive, let alone grow.

An employee with a disability asks HR for an accommodation and waits for a yes. A founder has no HR. AI is the accommodation you can give yourself.

This summer I drove 3,200 miles: Los Angeles to Seattle to Yellowstone, back through Las Vegas and home. My car’s supervised self-driving system let me drive without my braces, using only my left leg. An AI assistant connected to a mapping service planned every day: miles between stops, where to eat and which hotels had the access I need. Not every hotel does, so I packed a folding shower chair.

Founders like me are already leaning in. Twenty-two percent of entrepreneurs with disabilities use generative AI, compared with 10% of other entrepreneurs, per the same AEO fact sheet.

Franklin D. Roosevelt had polio, like me, and founded the March of Dimes. Richard Branson and Ingvar Kamprad built Virgin and IKEA with dyslexia. Stevie Wonder, blind since infancy, has owned a Los Angeles radio station since 1979. Tony Robbins grew up poor and turned it into a lifelong mission to feed families.

Music was my own calmer. Learning to sing, write songs and play guitar built my confidence and songwriting taught me to write.

I have started nine companies, and five failed. AI helped me learn the full process of building a business, end to end, check it against what those nine taught me and turn it into a repeatable system. AI can keep the notes, so you do not have to carry it all in your head.

Preparing my first podcast episode took 24 to 30 hours: guest research, follow-ups, questions and how to bring my own thinking into the conversation. Today an automated process does that work, and I plan an entire episode, including recording, in two to three hours.

Start by tracking which tasks drain your energy for a week. Hand off the worst ones first.

I earned an MBA in international business with a finance major and studied toward the CFA, yet dyslexia meant I swapped numbers and never fully trusted them.

Now my AI works from a read-only copy of my accounting data. Nothing goes back without my approval, and client names are stored apart from the amounts, so the AI never sees who paid what. It sorts every transaction and catches my slips. It also catches the email where I meant one name and typed another. I finally trust my numbers.

I run an agentic operating system: an AI C-suite that holds daily stand-ups and works through a now, next, later task list with time for reflection. Several AI models share one knowledge base, so when something drops, it gets picked back up quickly.

Every agent has hard stops. Never delete anything. Never touch the financial system. Never send anything to clients or anyone outside the business. It all runs on a separate computer, cut off from the internet, that takes input only through a firewall.

My belief system: Practice active and reflective listening, offer solutions on the spot and never judge. Give without expecting money or work in return. If you give someone one thing in value, you get 10 times back in the long run. Just do not give because you hope for it.

To founders with disabilities: Find your superpower and get out in public. Do not worry about how you look, how you speak or what you do. Be open about your story, build in your niche and, once you succeed, give back. I have helped build tools that have reached a few thousand children with learning differences, most of them ages 6 to 13.

To technology leaders: Build communities and systems that teach people with disabilities to start and run businesses, and help them grow.

AI will not fix access to capital, health insurance costs or other people’s bias. But it can give back the energy, the hours and the confidence those barriers take.

#3126. 1 Unstoppable Cryptocurrency That Could Join Bitcoin in the $1 Trillion Club

If Solana can replace Ethereum as the top Layer-1 blockchain network, then it has a potential path to a $1 trillion valuation.

Bitcoin remains the only cryptocurrency that has ever hit a $1 trillion market cap. Today, Bitcoin has a market cap of $1.6 trillion, roughly on par with Tesla's or Meta Platforms'.

While a number of cryptocurrencies have been talked about as potential entrants to the $1 trillion club, the one I have my eye on right now is Solana (SOL -7.18%). Here's why.

Right now, Solana has a market cap of $54 billion. For the sake of argument, let's call this $50 billion. So, for Solana to become a $1 trillion digital asset, it would need to increase in value by roughly 20x. Given Solana's current price of $90, that works out to a future price of approximately $1,800.

That's obviously a stretch goal, but it's within the realm of possibility. As a smart contract platform with a highly diversified blockchain ecosystem, Solana has several pathways to a trillion-dollar market cap.

If you assume Solana hits $1 trillion in market cap, you should also expect it to eventually supplant Ethereum (ETH -8.93%) as the top Layer-1 blockchain network. That's how Solana gets to a $300 billion valuation, which is the current value of Ethereum.

From there, Solana needs to continue eating Ethereum's lunch in key areas such as decentralized finance (DeFi), and it needs to keep winning over users and developers with its faster speeds and lower costs.

Beyond that point, Solana will need to more than triple in value, rising from a $300 billion valuation to $1 trillion. This will likely require a wholesale revamp of how investors, users, and developers view Solana. It will need to transform from a blockchain primarily used for trading and speculation in digital assets into one that is part of the global financial infrastructure.

In short, Solana will need to grow up and realize its full potential. It will need banks and financial institutions to use the Solana blockchain to move money and settle transactions. And it will need to remain at the forefront of important fintech trends, including stablecoins and real-world asset tokenization.

The good news is that Solana could go much higher than $1,800 (the price needed to reach a $1 trillion market cap). Back in October 2023, investment firm VanEck outlined an ultra-bull-case scenario, in which Solana eventually hit a price of $3,211. That assumed major market share gains in DeFi, huge growth in institutional adoption, and expansion into new blockchain niches.

Just be aware: Investing in Solana is not for the faint of heart. While Solana has had some truly eye-popping years, such as 2023 when it soared in value by 924%, it has also seen some truly horrendous years.

An investment in Solana will not go straight up, and there will be plenty of volatility along the way. But sometime within the next decade, investors could be talking about Solana as the next trillion-dollar cryptocurrency after Bitcoin.

Dominic Basulto has positions in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Bitcoin, Ethereum, Meta Platforms, Solana, and Tesla. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3125. The Evaluation Framework: The Most Underbuilt Part Of An AI System

Hiren is CTO & co-founder of Simform, an AI-native digital engineering services company.

When a production AI system starts to lose quality, spotting the decline is only part of the problem. The harder question is whether the team can explain what changed and judge, with enough confidence, whether the next fix will actually improve the system.

I was brought in to assess a production AI system that had begun to regress after months of stable performance. The production metrics showed the deterioration, but the team could not pinpoint when the behavior had shifted or tell whether the proposed fix would recover the quality they had lost.

My first question was whether we could take the same representative interactions and compare how the last-known-good version and the proposed fix handled them. We could not. The system was being monitored in production, but the measurement infrastructure needed to compare behavior across versions had never been built.

In that situation, engineering could make another change, but it could not show with confidence that the change improved the behavior that mattered. For the business, that meant additional engineering effort without consistent evidence of a better customer outcome, less manual intervention or a lower cost of completing the work.

What the team needed was a repeatable way to judge every proposed change against the same production-relevant expectations before it was released. Evaluation had to become part of the release process rather than a periodic quality check.

A production evaluation framework has three parts: a maintained set of representative examples, a defined way to judge how the system performs on them and clear thresholds for deciding whether a change is ready to release. Together, they answer a practical question: What evidence is enough to say that the next version is better?

It may begin with historical or curated examples, but it should incorporate real production interactions, known failure patterns and situations the team did not anticipate before launch. When a meaningful production failure occurs, that case should become part of the evaluation set so future versions have to prove they do not recreate it. This is especially important for low-frequency failures that carry a disproportionate cost, such as an incorrect action, unnecessary escalation or work that has to be corrected manually.

Some behaviors can be tested automatically, such as whether the system used the correct policy, extracted the expected information or passed the right inputs to another system. Others depend on context and require human review against defined criteria. The scoring method needs to stay consistent enough that changes in performance reflect the system, rather than changes in how it was assessed.

Teams should decide in advance which regressions are serious enough to block a change. A decline in a critical behavior may matter more than an improvement in the overall score, especially when that behavior affects customer experience, manual effort or the cost of completing the work.

Evaluation and observability thus serve different purposes in the release process. Observability helps engineers understand what is happening in the live system and investigate failures as they occur. Evaluation tells them whether the version they are about to release performs better on the behaviors that matter. The two should work together: production failures feed the evaluation set, and that evaluation set informs the next release decision.

The trade-off for CTOs is between investing engineering time in validation before it becomes urgent and prioritizing product work with a more visible near-term payoff. When the system is performing well, the value of stronger evaluation can be difficult to demonstrate compared with the next feature, integration or model improvement.

But deferring evaluation does not remove the work; it pushes it into future releases. Engineers may then have to reconstruct test inputs, inspect outputs manually and rebuild confidence around each significant change. What appeared to save time earlier becomes recurring validation work, slowing delivery when the team is already trying to move quickly.

The cost also shows up in the economics of the system. A change may reduce inference spend while increasing retries, escalations, human review or reopened work elsewhere in the workflow. For outcome-based applications, I care more about the fully loaded cost per resolved outcome than the cost of any one technical component. A cheaper configuration is only an improvement if the organization is also completing the work successfully at a lower overall cost. Evaluation should therefore reflect the outcome the system exists to produce, not only the quality of its output.

An evaluation framework should sit directly in the change process rather than be reviewed occasionally. Before release, the candidate version should run against the maintained evaluation set and be compared with the current version against agreed thresholds. After release, new production failures should feed back into that set, with clear ownership for keeping it current.

And before that work is cut from scope, I would ask one question: If we change this system next month, what evidence will tell us that the change helped?​

Management stated that the acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials has added metallization and alloy making capabilities to its operations, while progress continues toward a final investment decision for the Donald Project. Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you all for joining us for Energy Fuels Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, today's session is being recorded. Kim Casey: Good morning, and thank you for joining our third quarter earnings call. Presenting today are Ross Bhappu, President and Chief Executive Officer; and Nate Bennett, Chief Financial Officer. Ross Bhappu: Well, thank you, Kim. Last quarter, I told you that our story was one of execution. This quarter, I'm very pleased to tell you about several important steps we've taken to advance on that path. On August 28, we closed on the acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials, ASM. During the third quarter, we continued to advance the proposed acquisition of Vacuumschmelze or as I'll refer to it during the presentation, VAC. At the White Mesa Mill, we qualified our heavy rare earth oxide production with a major global permanent magnet manufacturer, and we approved commencement of construction of our Phase 1B and 1C heavy rare earths expansion as well as our MREC processing operations.

Finally, we received conditional government loan commitments for our Donald Project and continued successfully moving this valuable project toward a final investment decision, which we hope to make by the end of the year. There's still a lot of work ahead of us, but quarter-by-quarter, we're putting the pieces of our strategy together and advancing our goal of building a fully integrated rare earth mine to magnet supply chain, which we expect to achieve soon. While we successfully execute on our rare earth strategy, we also continue to drive revenue from uranium sales, and we're readying ourselves for future uranium expansion as we believe the demand for uranium will increase and with the commodity prices.

With respect to our uranium business, we experienced some lower grades in the mined areas of Pinyon Plain Mine, which affected our contained U3O8 yellowcake totals for Q3. However, we've made some adjustments to our operations, and we expect to see improvements in grade and future production, which should get our mined contained U3O8 totals back on track. I'll come back to uranium in just a few minutes. But first, let me start with ASM. ASM, Australian Strategic Materials, we closed on this acquisition in late August, and I'm very pleased to officially welcome the ASM team to Energy Fuels. ASM is an important component because it gives Energy Fuels a capability we simply did not have before.

ASM takes us into metallization and alloy making, one of the critical pinch points in the global rare earth magnet supply chain. Importantly, ASM brings Energy Fuels an operating facility in Ochang, South Korea, just south of Seoul, that's actively producing and selling neodymium and iron-boron rare earth to magnet manufacturers today, including VAC. Furthermore, capacity expansions are currently underway at the Korean plant with new furnaces and a new strip caster being installed as we speak. ASM and now Energy Fuels plans to build a new metal and alloy plant here in the U.S. when the time is right.

The ASM acquisition also brings to us the Dubbo Project in Australia, which could become another near-term source of rare earth feedstock for the White Mesa Mill. I recently visited ASM's operations in Australia and Korea, and I came away more excited about the acquisition than ever. The early integration is going well as the local teams and technical experts have not missed a step with the transition. This is exactly the point of our acquisition strategy. Rather than developing metal and alloy magnet manufacturing capabilities internally, we're adding commercial facilities, technical capabilities and customers at scale and in rapid time.

The Korea metals plant has existing capacity of 1,300 tonnes per year of neodymium-iron-boron alloy along with existing commercial metallization capabilities for neodymium and praseodymium. The plant is currently being expanded to increase neodymium-iron-boron alloy capability to 3,600 tonnes per year, which is expected to be commissioned early in 2027. While I was visiting the plant a few weeks ago, we have just taken delivery of a new strip casting machine that's now in the process of being installed. We continue to produce metals and alloys and sell them to fulfill commitments we inherited from our ASM. This offers direct revenue until we're able to transition to feed our own magnet manufacturing with the planned VAC acquisition.

Our focus now is on execution, scaling operations and capturing additional value across the supply chain. ASM establishes our platform in metals and alloys. VAC will take us the final step downstream into highly sought-after finished rare earth magnets. We continue to work through the appropriate applicable regulatory processes and still anticipate that the VAC transaction will close early in 2027. I also want to directly address another topic regarding VAC and provide some context for investors. A few weeks ago, news came out that there was a dispute with a large customer of VAC Sumter, South Carolina facility. Some inaccurate and incomplete investor narratives have been developed. So please allow me a few minutes to set the record straight.

Energy Fuels knew of the Sumter customer dispute before signing the VAC acquisition agreement. Indeed, the dispute was reflected in the transaction structure, pricing and economics. Purchase price adjustments could be implemented depending on the outcome of the arbitration between VAC and its customer. An arbitration result below the agreed assumptions is expected to reduce the acquisition price, while the result above them benefits VAC and of course, after closing will benefit Energy Fuels. Our internal valuations and projections excluded current and future revenue and EBITDA from this customer and the related offtake. The dispute, therefore, does not change Energy Fuels valuation assumptions and rationale for the acquisition. The Sumter facility has capacity to fulfill the existing agreement.

And if it does not continue on those terms, that capacity can be used to support new customer contracts. While we may need to expend some capital to meet new customer requirements, which is again reflected in our valuation, we firmly believe there is considerable demand for Sumter's rare earth magnets and processing capabilities. In addition, I'd like to stress we have no concerns about VAC's technical abilities, customer base and the ability to produce rare earth permanent magnets to customer qualifications and specifications. The Sumter plant is brand new. It's a state-of-the-art facility, highly robotic, and it's located right here in the United States. I believe it's important to reiterate that VAC has approximately 1,000 existing customers.

They've been making rare earth permanent magnets for over 40 years, and they've delivered over 1 billion rare earth permanent magnets over the past decade. They know what they're doing. They're highly qualified and they're a highly unique company, and they remain the clear Western leader in the production of rare earth permanent magnets. Demand for neodymium-iron-boron magnets across the globe is expected to grow by more than 50% over the next decade with Europe and North America being key demand growth drivers. VAC brings established manufacturing expertise and when combined with ASM, it will give us capabilities spanning metals, alloys and finished magnets.

In addition, we disclosed a bit of housekeeping with an updated $500 million prospectus supplement for our existing ATM program. The program preserves flexibility to issue equity selectively and when market conditions and the stock price warrant. We've used an ATM in the past for many years, and we have a long track record of strong fiscal discipline in using it. We intend to remain disciplined in using this one. That brings us back to our upstream operations. If we're going to build a meaningful downstream magnet business, we need the ability to supply it with a secure source of feed. To that end, we continue to advance the Donald joint venture project in Australia.

A big milestone was reached last week when we announced receipt of a conditional commitment with the Export Finance Australia and the Australian National Reconstruction Fund Corporation for AUD 180 million of a proposed AUD 200 million senior project debt facility. The remaining AUD 20 million commitment will be coming from commercial banks. As we continue to work closely with relevant government financing authorities and we finalize term sheets, those discussions have been constructive, and we remain on track for a final investment decision by year-end. Together with our heavy mineral sands asset, Donald is intended to establish a reliable, long-duration source of feedstock for our rare earth business.

Importantly, the Donald Project is an excellent source of heavy rare earth minerals and is very high in dysprosium and terbium in particular. These are key ingredients for producing high-performance rare earth permanent magnets. As we move forward in developing our raw material feedstock, we're also making preparations to expand our commercial scale of rare earth processing capacity at the White Mesa Mill. During the quarter, we approved commencement of construction on our Phase 1B and 1C heavy rare earth expansion. Once operational, Energy Fuels will have the commercial scale light and heavy rare earth production capacity.

Just as importantly, the expansion will include an MREC, mixed rare earth carbonate, circuit that will allow us to process uranium and rare earth simultaneously, something we can't do today. Today, we have to decide whether to produce rare earths or uranium in campaigning the mill. When the expansion is complete, we expect to have a significantly greater flexibility to produce both rare earths and uranium simultaneously. The White Mesa Mill is ultimately intended to become the bridge between our feedstock assets upstream and our metals, alloys and magnet manufacturing operations downstream. That flexibility matters.

As the downstream business grows, we'll be able to make thoughtful decisions about where our capacity creates the greatest value based on market conditions, economics and the needs of our business. So when you step back and look at what we're putting together, the logic is quite clear, feedstock, processing and separation, metals and alloys, the ultimately -- and ultimately, the finished magnets. We are truly creating a fully integrated minded magnet company. Each piece has an important role, and our job now is to execute and put those pieces -- get those pieces working together. As you can see, we're making tremendous progress. Now let me turn to uranium.

Uranium remains the core business for Energy Fuels and an important operating and financial foundation for the company. We're seeing upward movement in the uranium pricing in both the spot and the term markets as supply and demand fundamentals are taking shape. During the quarter, we mined 385,000 pounds at our operations, but we didn't process any uranium at the mill. That was idled for planned maintenance and rebuilding of our stockpiles and feedstock. Please recall that the mill processes ore and mineralized material faster than we are currently mining it.

As a result, and as a further reminder, we met our planned 2026 finished uranium production guidance by the end of the second quarter, and we're well inventoried to fulfill next year's contract commitments while potentially selling opportunistically on the spot market. We ended the third quarter with approximately 2.4 million pounds of combined ore mineralized material in processed and finished uranium inventory. To be clear, the ore grades at Pinyon Plain came in below our expectations this quarter. In response, we deployed an overnight crew to double our efforts in the quantity mined and are now seeing improvements in total production. You may recall the Pinyon Plain is a small underground breccia pipe mine. These formations are quite unique.

They're very high-grade deposits, which are mined differently than other uranium mines. Due mainly to Pinyon Plain, Energy Fuels remains the largest U.S. producer and one of the lowest cost sources of yellowcake U3O8 in the world. As we look to the future, we continue to progress our domestic uranium production and bring additional assets online as the Pinyon Plain production is expected to decline in coming years. As part of that effort, we've advanced 4 of our pipeline projects, including the Whirlwind, Pandora, Bullfrog and Roca Honda projects.

And of course, Nichols Ranch is still there sitting on care and maintenance and can quickly be called into service when economic environment improves to the point that we can maintain margins for production. The Whirlwind mine has seen activity this quarter, including current dewatering and plans to reopen next year. Bullfrog, Pandora and Roca Honda permitting has progressed, and we continue to move those projects forward. These 4 assets, Nichols Ranch and others in our pipeline can complement our existing uranium operations and give us production capacity as demand for the U.S. uranium market grows. Now let me spend just a minute on our balance sheet and capital. We're executing an ambitious and capital-intensive plan.

We're not shy about this fact. Indeed, it energizes our team every day as we believe we are well down the road towards capturing highly unique and valuable market opportunities. The important point is that we're starting from a position of strength with multiple funding sources already in process, which gives us flexibility in how we fund our growth. We ended the quarter with approximately $932 million in working capital and total revenue of $29.2 million. Our results this quarter also reflect several onetime operational and transactional-related items, which Nate is going to walk you through here in greater detail.

As we finance our growth, we have several sources of capital available to us, including our balance sheet, several government funding sources, our term loan facility, our ATM program and other conventional financing alternatives. We will evaluate those funding options as well as the viability and timing of actual asset development and project -- on a project-by-project basis. We will not progress a project and expansion or a funding source if it's not advantageous or accretive. Our objective is simply not to fund growth, but it's to fund the right growth at the right time and in a way that we believe creates the greatest long-term value.

When I look back at the quarter, I'm encouraged by the progress we've made. ASM is now part of Energy Fuels and operating today. Donald is nearing FID. White Mesa is efficiently processing uranium and the heavy rare earth processing expansion is advancing. We continue to work towards closing on the VAC acquisition. And despite some operational challenges this quarter, our uranium business continues to deliver. There's still a lot of work ahead of us, but the path is clear. Last quarter, I said our story was about execution, and that hasn't changed. Quarter-by-quarter, we're moving the strategy from plants on paper to operating assets.

We're building the capabilities that we believe are necessary to establish a fully integrated Western rare earth supply chain while continuing to grow our uranium business. That's what execution looks like, and that's what remains our key focus. Now I'd like to turn the presentation over to Nate Bennett for our financial results. Nate?

Nathan Bennett: Thanks, Ross. Before I get into the numbers, I encourage everyone to review today's discussion alongside our Form 10-Q and other public filings as those documents provide additional detail and context around our results, risk factors and related disclosures. As we continue to grow and diversify the business, it's important to remember that we manage and evaluate our operations by commodity line. Today, that primarily includes uranium, while our rare earth and heavy mineral sands, metals, alloys and magnet businesses continue to advance through development activities. Turning to our financial results. Energy Fuels continues to have a solid foundation.

As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately $932 million of working capital and $1.7 billion of total assets, which provides us with a strong foundation for our strategic growth initiatives and allows us to be flexible in our projects as we put capital to work. During the third quarter, we reported a net loss of $52.2 million or $0.20 per share. The loss was driven primarily by $35.3 million of noncash unrealized mark-to-market losses on our marketable securities. At the same time, our investment portfolio generated $9.4 million of cash interest income during the quarter, which partially offset the unrealized valuation loss.

The majority of our marketable securities are interest-bearing debt securities, primarily U.S. treasury bills and government agency bonds. During the quarter, higher market interest rates put downward pressure on bond values. And because these securities are carried at fair value, those market movements resulted in unrealized losses. Importantly, these losses did not represent a current cash outflow. We are excited to highlight that our uranium segment remained profitable for the third straight quarter. The weighted average realized price per pound of U3O8 sold also rose for the third consecutive quarter, increasing 10% from Q2 and 27% from Q1, while operating cost per pound and cost of goods sold remained steady. Turning to our operating results.

Performance benefited from improved realized uranium pricing and higher margins on uranium sales. SG&A was $18.3 million during the quarter, with the year-over-year increase primarily reflecting higher personnel costs and the inclusion of approximately 1 month of ASM following the acquisition. We also incurred $9 million of transaction and integration-related costs associated with the ASM acquisition and pending VAC acquisition. Our uranium segment generated $28.7 million of revenue and $17.9 million of gross profit, representing gross margin of approximately 63%. We sold 320,000 pounds at an average realized price of $88.90 per pound, while our weighted average cost applicable to uranium revenues was approximately $34 per pound.

The uranium segment continued to generate positive operating income, helping to support our exploration and development activities and corporate costs. This steady quarter-over-quarter performance highlights the resilience of our uranium business, reinforces our position as the leading U.S. uranium platform and provides a strong foundation for our strategic growth plans across our businesses. In contrast, the losses incurred with our rare earth elements and heavy mineral sand businesses primarily reflect planned developments to advance projects, including Vara Mada, Donald and Bahia toward future production. These investments include drilling, engineering, permitting, infrastructure, development and organizational growth. We closed the ASM acquisition on August 28, and therefore, our third quarter results include only a limited contribution from ASM.

In the near term, we intend to take a disciplined approach to utilization of the Korean Metals Plant as we focus on completing the planned expansion. As such, we expect ASM's contributions to our financials to be limited over the near term. Over time, we expect that contribution to build as the individual components of our mine-to-magnet strategy come online, including ASM, VAC, Donald and additional feedstock sources. As these pieces come together, we expect to be better positioned to realize the Korean Metals Plant's expanded capacity and drive a more meaningful contribution to our operating and financial results. Turning to uranium. The segment generated strong revenue during the quarter.

Pinyon Plain ore grades averaged 1.04% during the third quarter, which improved meaningfully from 0.71% in the second quarter as we continue to progress through the ore body. While the improvement has taken longer than we initially anticipated as mining transitions between higher grade zones, the trend is positive, and we expect grades to continue to improve as we advance through the current mining zones and ultimately into the Juniper Zone. Year-to-date, we have mined approximately 1.1 million pounds of contained U3O8. As Ross mentioned, we have added an overnight crew at Pinyon Plain, effectively doubling the number of operating shifts, and we expect grades to improve as mining progresses through the current mining zones and into the Juniper Zone.

Turning to costs. Our Finish U3O8 inventory carried a weighted average cost of approximately $34 per pound as of September 30, broadly in line with the end of the second quarter and down from approximately $36 per pound at the end of the first quarter. Our finished inventory reflects production and purchases from various sources over time and does not yet fully reflect the recently mined Pinyon Plain ore, which has not been fully processed. The Pinyon Plain ore processed in the most recent mill run had a weighted average cost of approximately $23 per pound. As this lower cost material is processed and moves into finished inventory, we expect it to benefit our overall uranium inventory cost profile.

We believe this low-cost production base provides us with a meaningful competitive advantage as we continue to grow our uranium business. The mill completed planned maintenance during the third quarter, and we currently expect the next uranium processing run to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 or early 2027 as we continue mining and building our ore and mineralized material stockpiles. Our uranium inventory remains a significant strategic asset, providing flexibility to meet customer commitments while supporting our long-term strategy to build a fully integrated critical minerals platform.

With approximately 2.4 million pounds of U3O8 at quarter end, we have the flexibility to fulfill long-term contract deliveries, pursue spot sales when market conditions warrant and manage the timing of production and sales to maximize value. As we move through the remainder of the year, our focus remains on executing our uranium production plan and positioning the business for continued growth. Turning to our 2026 guidance, as shown on this slide, we have already achieved the low end of our full year guidance for processed pounds and remain on track to achieve the low end of our full year guidance ranges for sales.

We remain hopeful that the additional shift in higher grades at Pinyon Plain will help us reach the low end of our mining guidance. Our uranium operations continue to provide a strong economic foundation for the company, supported by attractive market fundamentals and the value generated across our production and sales activities. Overall, we continue to advance our uranium operations, maintain a competitive cost structure and reinforce our position as a leading U.S.-based uranium producer. The progress across our operations, coupled with the significant production potential of our existing asset base provides a solid foundation for expanding our capabilities, capturing future opportunities and strengthening our presence across the nuclear, energy and critical minerals markets.

And with that, I'll turn it back to Ross.

Ross Bhappu: Thank you, Nate, for that summary. With that, I'd like to conclude with a few comments and summarize the milestones we've accomplished and where we are as we head toward the end of 2026. Looking ahead, our priority is to make the pieces of our strategy work together. At the White Mesa Mill, the heavy rare earth expansion and terbium oxide qualification provide a foundation for advancing our production capabilities. With ASM now part of Energy Fuels, our focus is on integrating and scaling our metals and alloys operations. The proposed VAC acquisition, subject to regulatory approvals, will extend Energy Fuels platform into finished rare earth magnets.

Our goal is not simply to own assets across the supply chain, but to build and connect a scalable business from mine to magnets. That means advancing the Donald Project from conditional financing toward a final investment decision while continuing the permitting and government work needed to support a future investment decision at Vara Mada. We're also advancing both the engineering and permitting of the White Mesa Mill Phase 2 expansion. It also means continuing our low-cost uranium production while progressing permitting and development of our uranium pipeline to support future production. We will approach these opportunities with discipline, matching development and capital commitments to the project readiness and economics.

The bigger picture is a company with 2 complementary priorities: first, building an integrated rare earth magnet materials business; and second, sustaining a strong uranium foundation. There is still work ahead and progress continues to depend on execution, government approvals and sound investment decisions. But our direction is clear. We intend to turn the capabilities we're assembling into operating business units that create substantial cash flow and long-term value for our shareholders. With that, I'd like to thank you for joining us today, and thank you for your interest in Energy Fuels.

Day 1, they all had Energy Fuels e-mail addresses. Again, the integration was pretty seamless. So we're very pleased with that. But I think the biggest unappreciated part of this transaction is the new strip caster and the 12 new furnaces we have at the facility for processing oxides.

Heiko Ihle: That's fair. And then just a little bit on the site, the mill maintenance. Can you give some color on the actual cash spend at site from forecast for Q2 and maybe a little bit of color on what exactly -- or you anticipate doing the next mill run, I mean, next week we will be at the midpoint of the quarter?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. So our plan right now, the mill has been shut down. As you recall, the mill will outrun the mines. And so we're producing at, call it, 2 million pounds or thereabouts per year from the mines. But the mill has the capacity to go up to 6 million pounds per year. So the mill, we campaign it as ore is available. We ran the mill all of the first half of the year, and we shut it down on June 30, both for care and maintenance as well as to allow the stockpiles of ore to build again. Those stockpiles are now being built, and we're anticipating restarting the mill probably around the 1st of December.

So we'll get 1 month of operations this year, and then we'll continue to operate the mill probably through Q1 of 2027. And at that time, we would hope that -- and we're sort of anticipating at this stage that we would then transition to processing rare earths after that uranium mill run. So that would be sometime kind of Q2 sort of time frame.

Operator: Your next question comes from Matthew Key with Texas Capital.

Matthew Key: I just had a quick follow-up on kind of like the economics and accounting treatment of the intercompany sales to ASM from White Mesa. Is the plan to sell oxide like production to ASM at market pricing? Basically, what I'm just trying to determine is, obviously, scale improves as feedstock availability improves. But do their cost of feedstock also get enhanced as they get tied into White Mesa?

Ross Bhappu: I'm going to let -- Matthew, good to talk to you. I'm going to let Nathan Bennett -- Nate Bennett, our Chief Financial Officer, respond to that.

Nathan Bennett: Yes. Thanks, Matt, good to talk to you. So we will have transfer pricing studies in between the different locations. So essentially, you'll be selling the goods from White Mesa Mill at market prices to ASM, and they'll treat it like an arm's length transaction. But then in the financial statements, we will eliminate those intercompany transactions and revenue. So you'll be able to see it gross up, but then also the elimination of those transactions. Hopefully, that helps you.

Matthew Key: Got it. Yes. No, very helpful. I appreciate it. And just a quick one on kind of CapEx spending in '27. You have a great slide that highlights the near-term growth CapEx. I think it appears that, that would include spending expectations in 2028 as well. But what would be the spend in '27 specifically and kind of the main buckets that would drive that?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. Sorry about that. We dropped off for some reason for a second, and I apologize. So CapEx spend, look, I think the key there is we have Phase 1B and 1C, which will largely be spent next year. That's roughly $100 million. We do anticipate that Donald FID. And with the Donald FID, there will come a fair bit of CapEx that goes into that. Now part of that will get funded from the debt facilities that we announced with EFA and NRFC, but part of that will be from Energy Fuels. And once we build our position to 49% of the Astron -- with Astron, then we share those expenses with Astron.

Nathan Bennett: Yes. So we have $60 million that's remaining to earn into our 49% to give some context. There's a table in our 10-Q that outlines what we've contributed to date that's pretty helpful.

Ross Bhappu: I hope that helps. And then we'll have ongoing costs at our various other projects for Vara Mada and just our ongoing operating costs and then other work that we're doing at the mill. But I think it's summarized pretty well in the previous...

Operator: The next question comes from [ Thomas Devic ], a private investor.

Unknown Analyst: How does your Brazil mine fit the picture now? Or what's the game plan or some background on how critical it is to your process?

Ross Bhappu: Thomas yes, thanks for the question. So our first priority on the mining side is going to be Donald. We want to get that up and running as just as quickly as we can. I would say when we look at the order that these mines will come in, I think Vara Mada would hopefully come in next. Then what we've -- another -- coming back to Heiko's question earlier, pleasant surprises. One of the pleasant surprises we've had is just the excitement around the Dubbo Project. The Dubbo project came with the ASM acquisition, and we've been doing a tremendous amount of work on that.

And it looks like the economics of that project are going to be very favorable. So we may move Dubbo up in the queue where we thought it would be fourth, if we may move it up in the queue in terms of priorities of which ones we develop next. That being said, Bahia is still an important project. We're continuing to do drilling work out there, but it's a little bit behind in terms of engineering and development work that's required. It's a little bit behind the other 3 projects. So I would kind of rank it moving more towards the fourth in line of our mines that we're developing internally.

Unknown Analyst: [indiscernible] said Brazil may want to get in the processing process, not let everything leave the country. So that was kind of what I was asking.

Ross Bhappu: Yes. We've heard about that as well. And that's not uncommon for a lot of countries where they want to see more downstream processing. And it's just something that we're going to continue to follow, and we'll address at the time we're looking to put these projects into development, but certainly something we're following.

Operator: Your next question is a follow-up from Nick Giles of B. Riley Securities.

Nick Giles: If I saw correctly, it looks like long-term uranium deliveries were largely complete for the year. And Nate, I think I heard you allude to it in your prepared remarks, but can you just kind of walk us through what's realistic in terms of 4Q sales and just as Pinyon Plain remains strong?

Nathan Bennett: Yes. So that's correct. We've essentially completed all our long-term contract sales for the year, but we still anticipate to meet the low end of our guidance of 1.5 million pounds sold in 2026. So that's what we're targeting, and that's what we're on track to meet for the rest of the year.

Nick Giles: Okay. And then just on some of the exploration work to advance the pipeline. Can you just speak to kind of what type of activities went on throughout the quarter? And what you think realistic time lines are for some of those projects just as we think about backfilling Pinyon Plain further down the road?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. Thanks, Nick. Yes, we've been doing a fair bit of work there. We've been doing some drill work drilling at Nichols Ranch to expand that resource. We've had a lot of preparation work at Whirlwind, mostly dewatering that facility and prepping it for production, and we anticipate bringing it online sometime next year. We've got a lot of work going on in New Mexico with our Roca Honda project, and that's more of a permitting process. And so we've been spending a lot of time there on the regulatory side. So yes, look, we're making progress across all fronts. And then we have Bullfrog and the EZ mines that we're advancing as we speak.

So there is quite a full pipeline there of projects that we're focused on.

Operator: That concludes our Q&A session. I'll now turn the call back to Ross Bhappu for closing remarks.

Ross Bhappu: Well, with that, look, I'd like to thank everybody. I'd like to thank our Energy Fuels team. I mean I've been pushing them to the brink. They've been working extremely hard. And I think it's showing in all the successes we're having. I'd like to thank the shareholders for your continued support. These are kind of uncertain times and certainly, our share price has been very volatile. But what we can control, I think we're doing our -- doing a very good job. And I'm excited about the future of Energy Fuels. And I think our results will show for themselves here over the next couple of years.

So again, thank you very much for your support and for participating on the call.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

Mortgage rates jumped after stronger-than-expected jobs data raised expectations for a Fed rate hike next month.

Mortgage rates are higher today on the heels of strong labor market data released yesterday.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points higher than yesterday but 25 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

Mortgage rates are always on the move, so if you're tracking rates day-to-day, you're going to see a lot of volatility.

As for today’s jump: Job openings hit a four-month high of 7.5 million in September, according to the Labor Department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey released yesterday. Hiring picked up, too, while layoffs declined. Friday’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other.

To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

#3120. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.
