#3119. RLJ Lodging (RLJ) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Urban pricing power drove a strong quarter and a raised outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

RLJ Lodging Trust (RLJ -2.44%) reported third-quarter results that exceeded management's expectations across all reported metrics, driven by accelerating business travel demand and a recovery in urban markets. The company raised its full-year guidance for RevPAR growth and Adjusted EBITDA, reflecting the third-quarter performance and preliminary positive trends in October. Management indicated that lodging fundamentals are converging to drive occupancy and pricing power for the first time in several years, particularly in urban-centric portfolios. Strategic capital allocation remained focused on hotel conversions and the opportunistic disposition of non-core assets to enhance shareholder returns.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the RLJ Lodging Trust Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A brief question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. Please note, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your host, John Paul Austin, Director of Investor Relations. Thank you, sir. You may begin.

John Paul Austin: Thank you, operator. Good afternoon, and welcome to RLJ Lodging Trust 2026 Third Quarter Earnings Call. On today's call, Leslie Hale, our President and Chief Executive Officer, will discuss key highlights for the quarter. Nikhil Bhalla, our Chief Financial Officer, will discuss the company's financial results. Tom Bardenett, our Chief Operating Officer, will also be available for Q&A. Forward-looking statements made on this call are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties that may lead the company's actual results to differ materially from what has been communicated. Factors that may impact the results of the company can be found in the company's 10-Q and other reports filed with the SEC. The company undertakes no obligation to update forward-looking statements.

Also, as we discuss certain non-GAAP measures, it may be helpful to review the reconciliations to GAAP located in our press release. Finally, please refer to the schedule of supplemental information, which includes pro forma operating results for our current hotel portfolio. I'll now turn the call over to Leslie.

Leslie Hale: Thanks, John Paul. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. We had a very strong quarter, achieving results that exceeded our expectations across every metric. The strength of the operating momentum we saw was broad-based and accelerated from the second quarter, with business travel leading the way as it continues to benefit from healthy corporate profits and a growing economy. The acceleration we are seeing in business travel reflects a step change in the momentum we have been highlighting since last year, and we are pleased to see this strength persisting into the fourth quarter. Overall, the positive trends across all segments of demand, including sustained strength in leisure and group, continue to disproportionately benefit urban markets.

Our results reflect the favorable positioning of our urban-centric portfolio, which has allowed us to outperform the broader industry all year. During the third quarter, we delivered robust RevPAR growth that outperformed the industry by 260 basis points. We generated another quarter of solid growth in our non-room revenues. We achieved strong bottom-line flow-through, which drove significant margin expansion and our EBITDA to increase at twice the pace of revenues. Our completed conversions and high-impact renovations once again delivered robust RevPAR and EBITDA growth. Additionally, we made progress towards our next phase of conversions, which will further expand our lifestyle orientation and EBITDA growth, and we opportunistically sold a small portfolio of assets at an accretive multiple.

Our year-to-date results demonstrate our portfolio's ability to capture the accelerating resurgence in urban markets, in addition to the strong lift from our conversions and renovations. The combination of our favorable footprint and our embedded growth catalyst gives us confidence in our ability to continue delivering strong bottom-line growth. With respect to our third-quarter operating results, our RevPAR grew by a robust 9.7%, driven by increases in both demand and rate, with each month of the quarter exceeding our expectations. Demand grew within every segment, driving occupancy growth of 230 basis points.

The strong and consistent demand dynamics we have seen throughout this year are giving our operators further confidence to increase rates, allowing us to achieve ADR growth of 6.4% during the quarter. Several of our markets benefited from hosting World Cup matches, and we continue to estimate approximately 45 basis points of overall contribution from the tournament to our full-year RevPAR growth. That said, our outperformance extended well beyond the World Cup, with our non-World Cup markets achieving RevPAR growth of nearly 12%. This positive momentum carried into October, which achieved preliminary RevPAR growth of 6%, even with the shift of Dreamforce into September, further underscoring the sustainability of the trends we saw during the third quarter.

Our urban markets continue to lead our performance, achieving RevPAR growth of 10%, with 11 markets delivering double-digit RevPAR growth. Our largest market, Northern California, grew RevPAR by more than 13%. Year to date, RevPAR for our Northern California market is up by more than 16%. More importantly, our EBITDA in this market is up 63% over the last two years, with meaningful upside remaining. Performance in this market continues to be underpinned by the expansion of the AI industry, which is fueling corporate investment, citywide activity, and business travel against the backdrop of an improving local environment that is attracting more leisure activity.

We continue to believe in the multi-year growth trajectory for Northern California as the epicenter of the broader AI boom that is driving the next phase of economic growth. Other top-performing markets that delivered double-digit growth include Washington, D.C., Pittsburgh, Austin, New York City, Los Angeles, and Tampa. Even with the robust performance of our urban markets year to date, there remains plenty of room to run. As it relates to segmentation, significantly higher transient revenue drove much of this quarter's improvement, and the mix within transient shifted in a way that allowed us to optimize dynamic pricing.

Business transient was once again our strongest segment, with revenues increasing by 15% during the third quarter, driven by a robust 13% increase in ADR along with a 2% increase in demand. We saw double-digit BT revenue growth in each month of the quarter and healthy BT trends across all of our markets. The consistency and the breadth of the growth in business travel is illustrating the sustained momentum we have been seeing build throughout this year, with our 15% revenue growth following the 10% growth we achieved in each of the prior two quarters. This robust business travel demand is being supported by a healthy economy, with elevated levels of business investment.

The nature of this investment is generating demand with a longer average length of stay, which our portfolio is well-positioned to capture, as reflected in our occupancy gains. We continue to see strong activity across a wide array of industries, such as tech, consulting, defense, energy, and healthcare, including both large corporations as well as small and medium-sized businesses. This is reflected in our improving midweek demand, which drove a 15% increase in compression nights during the quarter, creating the backdrop for pricing power. With this dynamic still building, we believe we are in the early phases of a broader BT expansion.

Regarding leisure, our leisure revenues grew 10% during the quarter, driven by an 8% increase in ADR and a 2% increase in demand. While our footprint benefited from the World Cup games during the quarter, leisure revenues grew at an equally strong pace in our non-World Cup markets, underscoring the diversified leisure demand drivers within our urban portfolio. The strength in leisure persisted throughout the quarter, in particular in September, with revenues generating 16% as the timing of Labor Day extended the summer travel season. Our hotels in live, work, play locations continue to capture robust urban leisure demand as travelers increasingly prioritize travel around sports, concerts, dining, and other entertainment experiences found in our vibrant city centers.

Our group segment also achieved strong results, with revenues increasing 10% during the quarter, led by significant growth in room nights. This demand provided us with a strong base of business, allowing us to drive higher rates in our transient segment. While the booking window remains short, in the quarter, for the quarter demand materialized ahead of our expectations, and we were pleased to see our group pace for the fourth quarter improve by 500 basis points during the third quarter. We are also encouraged by the increasing share of corporate group within our overall group mix, which has positive implications for both ADR and out-of-room spend.

The strength across each of our demand segments continues to translate into healthy non-room revenues, which grew nearly 7% during the quarter, reflecting the significant returns generated by our investments through our conversions, renovations, and ROI initiatives. In aggregate, our robust top-line growth, combined with our lean operating model and our disciplined cost control efforts, translated into a nearly 18% increase in our EBITDA and 190 basis points of margin expansion for the quarter. Turning to capital allocation. The investments we have made in our portfolio over the past several years are continuing to drive meaningful incremental growth.

During the third quarter, our eight completed conversions, including our most recent conversion in Pittsburgh, achieved RevPAR growth of 12% and EBITDA growth of 18%. Our high-impact renovations that we completed last year achieved RevPAR growth of 26% and more than doubled EBITDA. We also advanced our conversions in Boston and Key West. Subsequent to quarter end, we commenced the physical renovation at the Fairfield Inn & Suites Key West, which will join the Margaritaville family. We are initiating the physical renovations at the Wyndham Boston Beacon Hill, which is slated to join Hilton's Tapestry Collection, with both projects on track to relaunch in 2027.

The relaunch of these two assets next year will further enhance the lifestyle orientation of our portfolio and provide incremental growth. More broadly, the success we have achieved through our conversion strategy to date gives us conviction to pursue additional conversions as we continue to expand our pipeline, targeting two conversions per year. We also remained active on the disposition front, opportunistically divesting assets on an accretive basis. In mid-October, we sold a portfolio of seven assets near the Chicago Midway Airport for $110 million, representing an attractive multiple 14 times 2026 forecasted EBITDA, or 16 times including required capital expenditures.

This sale allows us to reposition our Chicago exposure to align with our focus on harder demand locations while increasing the lifestyle orientation of our portfolio, which now represents roughly half of our total EBITDA. Overall, our strong liquidity and flexible balance sheet positions us to pursue a range of options to further drive long-term growth, enhancing shareholder returns. Now turning to our outlook for the balance of the year. Demand continues to be supported by a favorable macro backdrop, including healthy corporate earnings and elevated levels of business investment, which is fueling sustained momentum in business travel. We believe our urban-centric portfolio is well-positioned to remain a beneficiary.

As such, we are raising our full-year guidance to reflect our third-quarter outperformance, the strong operating results seen in October, and our expectations that positive trends should carry into the remainder of the year. That said, we acknowledge that a degree of geopolitical uncertainty persists, and we will continue to monitor demand closely. Looking ahead, we believe we are in the early phases of a multi-year cycle, with 2026 marking the first time in many years that lodging fundamentals converge in a way that drives occupancy higher, creates greater compression, and yields true pricing power. As we look beyond 2026, we believe the positive momentum we are seeing is sustainable, supported by durable demand drivers.

All of this is occurring as a backdrop of an extended period of muted supply growth, creating a favorable setup across all demand segments, in particular for business travel, and fueling the continued resurgence in urban markets. While 2026 saw very strong growth, we believe the building blocks are in place for growth to continue in 2027, further supported by a positive holiday calendar. For RLJ, our portfolio will also have strong convention calendars in several of our markets, including D.C., Boston, and San Diego, continuing momentum in Northern California, and the ongoing ramp from our completed conversions and renovations, along with the relaunch of our Boston and Key West conversions.

Additionally, given our concentration in urban locations with strong entertainment demand drivers, we will continue to benefit from the annual rotation of recurring major events within our footprint in 2027, including the Super Bowl in Los Angeles, the NFL Draft in Washington, D.C., the Major League Baseball All-Star Game in Chicago, the NBA All-Star Game in Phoenix, as well as pre-Olympic activities in Southern California, and unique events such as the Star Wars 50th anniversary in L.A. Collectively, this positive setup is reflected in our group pace, which is tracking ahead by mid-single digits for next year.

Overall, with our embedded growth catalysts and a strong balance sheet that provides significant optionality, we believe our portfolio is well-positioned to continue delivering strong relative performance in 2027 and beyond. With that, I will turn the call over to Nikhil.

Nikhil Bhalla: Thanks, Leslie. To start, our comparable numbers include our 91 hotels owned at the end of the third quarter. Our reported corporate adjusted EBITDA and adjusted FFO include operating results from all sold hotels during RLJ's ownership period. Our third quarter results came in well ahead of our expectations and once again meaningfully outperformed the industry. Comparable RevPAR of $153 grew 9.7% versus the prior year, driven by an increase of 6.4% in average daily rate to $203, along with a 230 basis point increase in occupancy to 75.4%. Each month delivered RevPAR growth ahead of our expectations, with July up 13%, August, which we expected to be flat, up 4.2%, and September up 11.5%.

As Leslie mentioned, our urban markets continue to lead our performance, benefiting especially from widespread BT strength, with a number of these markets achieving double-digit BT revenue growth, including D.C. at 53%, Austin at 24%, Northern California at 22%, and New York at 19%. Strong growth in BT was also evident in our weekday RevPAR growth of 9.9% during the quarter, with Tuesday through Thursday seeing double-digit RevPAR growth. In addition to strong BT, our urban markets also benefited from robust urban leisure, with revenues growing by 10.3%. Strengthening urban leisure growth led our weekend RevPAR in urban markets to achieve nearly 10% growth.

Strong demand in both BT and corporate group throughout the quarter also drove healthy non-room revenues, which were up 6.5%, our fourth consecutive quarter of high single-digit growth. This performance reflects the value created from our investments in ROI initiatives, with an emphasis on improving food and beverage margins, maximizing the productivity of underutilized spaces, and adding new ancillary revenue streams through our renovation and conversion initiatives. Turning to operating expenses. Our strong top-line performance, combined with our disciplined approach to controlling expenses, allowed for strong flow of nearly 50% to the bottom line, demonstrating the benefits of our lean operating model. During the third quarter, total cost per occupied room increased by approximately 3%, in line with our expectations.

Drilling down further into hotel operating expenses, variable costs such as commissions and fees increased in line with revenues. And while energy costs remained elevated, they moderated from the second quarter. Partially offsetting these increases, our fixed costs were slightly lower relative to the prior year, benefiting from the successful renewal of our insurance program last year, as well as the success from our property tax appeals. We delivered hotel EBITDA of $93.9 million during the third quarter, representing an increase of $14 million, or 17.5% over the prior year, which is nearly two times the increase in our revenues. Hotel EBITDA margins were 26.5%, expanding by 190 basis points over the prior year.

These results translated to adjusted EBITDA of $85 million and adjusted FFO per diluted share of $0.34, representing increases of 17.3% and 25.9% respectively over the prior year. Turning to our balance sheet. As of the third quarter, we had $2.2 billion of debt and no maturities due until 2029. Overall, our balance sheet remains well-positioned with strong liquidity of over $1 billion as of quarter's end, including $600 million of undrawn capacity on our corporate revolver, 91% of hotels unencumbered by debt, and approximately 70% of our debt either fixed or hedged at the end of the third quarter.

With respect to capital allocation, subsequent to the end of the quarter, we opportunistically sold our Chicago Midway campus of seven hotels for $110 million to an owner-operator. Our strong liquidity provides us with significant optionality with respect to capital allocation opportunities, including continuing to unlock the embedded growth in our portfolio through our transformative conversions. We remain committed to enhancing shareholder returns through our well-covered quarterly dividend of $0.15 per share, and will continue to allocate capital strategically to enhance portfolio growth while maintaining balance sheet strength and financial flexibility. Turning to our full-year outlook.

Our updated guidance reflects our strong third quarter outperformance and our improved outlook for the fourth quarter, which assumes continuation of the positive operating trends we are currently seeing through year-end, as well as the sale of seven Chicago Midway hotels. For 2026, we now expect comparable RevPAR growth to range between 5.75% and 6.25%, an increase of 200 basis points at the midpoint. Comparable hotel EBITDA to range between $377 million and $383 million.

Corporate adjusted EBITDA to range between $352 million and $358 million, a $9 million increase from our prior outlook at the midpoint, which reflects the $6.5 million third quarter beat relative to our implied guidance, and a raise to our fourth quarter outlook by an additional $2.5 million. Adjusted FFO per diluted share to be between $1.47 and $1.51. Our outlook assumes no additional acquisitions, dispositions, or balance sheet activity beyond what has been completed to date. We continue to estimate capital expenditures will be in the range of $80 million-$90 million. Cash G&A will be in the range of $34.5 million-$35.5 million, and expect net interest expense will be in the range of $101 million-$103 million.

Finally, please refer to our press release from last evening for additional details on our outlook, and to our schedule of supplemental information, which will include 2026 and 2025 quarterly operating results for our comparable hotel portfolio. Thank you, and this concludes our prepared remarks. We will now open the line for Q&A. Operator?

Operator: Thank you. We will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. One moment, please, while we poll for questions. Thank you. Our first question comes from the line of Austin Wurschmidt with KeyBanc. Please proceed with your question.

Austin Wurschmidt: Great. Thanks. Just, you guys hit on a lot about the flow through this quarter and how it improved significantly versus recent quarters, despite there being a mix of ADR and occupancy growth driving RevPAR. What really changed this quarter, and do you think you can sustain that flow through to the extent that fundamentals do remain strong?

Leslie Hale: Yeah, I would say, Austin, what changed was really what I talked about in our prepared remarks in terms of this being the first time in a long time where fundamentals have really converged. If you sort of think about the building blocks here, we've had a consistent strength in group demand, which has remained healthy, but it's giving us a base of occupancy. Now we have true compression building, and so we've seen transient demand really accelerate. Leisure demand has remained relatively stable and growing, but BT is seeing meaningful acceleration sequentially. We've seen the pace of growth in business travel and demand. We've seen it in the form of weekday trends, midweek trends as well.

The length of stay has expanded, and all of those things are happening against limited new supply, so it's creating compression on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and we've seen our compression go up 15%. When you have that kind of compression in demand, you're able to have true pricing power. In a post-COVID world, we had already decoupled rate and occupancy, but what we've been able to do is to have less discounting, less promotion, less OTA channel, and we've seen a remix within transient to more dynamic pricing. All of this is happening while you have your highest-rated customer, business traveler, coming back.

That's really allowed us to sort of drive the rate side while still seeing an increase in occupancy, which has clearly helped the flow through to the bottom line. We do believe, as we mentioned in our prepared remarks, this is sustainable, particularly given the economic backdrop that we are seeing from a business investment and corporate profit perspective.

Austin Wurschmidt: I guess you said, I think group pace is up mid-single digit for next year. I mean, does that just set the stage for this to continue, and how much of a mix shift opportunity is there remaining in that kind of midweek business transient segment?

Leslie Hale: Yeah, I think that the building blocks for 2027 are set. We think that the momentum we've seen and the positive fundamentals in terms of how they're converging, we think that will carry forward, and that we can continue to see the compression that we've seen. I'll let Tom talk about what he's seeing on a midweek trend perspective.

Tom Bardenett: Yeah, so if you compare to our occupancy, which is where Leslie started the conversation, we're still about six percentage points off of 2019 on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. So, even with the growth that we're having in BT, which was 10, and 15, if you look at this past quarter, we know that the accounts that are coming back, Austin Wurschmidt, whether it's tech or energy, aerospace, and even the consultants, the fact that we're getting length of stay that Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and growth both on demand and rate, we think there's a lot of room in the tank to continue to have that.

Group kind of sets the pace, to your point, and even in our largest assets that have leading indicators, and Leslie talked about some of the markets where they're either citywide or self-contained, we're in a good position coming out of the gate for 2027 based on those two dynamics. The last thing I would say, because of the channel mix, we're seeing more people book through GDS, which is great because you don't have to pay a commission on that. You have more people going to brand.com, again, less commissions, and we're controlling that Tuesday, Wednesday because of that length of stay and compression dates, less OTA channels midweek.

I think we're in a good spot coming out of 2026, and I'll let Leslie recap one more item.

Leslie Hale: Yeah, I think that, just to put a number on Tom's point about GDS, our GDS is up 10%. I think the other note to add on to the numbers that Tom gave is to look at it from a rate perspective as well. I've said this before, that historically, business travel rate was above group. Historically, it was somewhere between 12%-15% above group. Today, it sits 12%-15% below group. That's a 30 percentage point swing. I'm not suggesting that BT will get back to its historical relationship in terms of being ahead, but what I am saying is that there is room to grow there from that relationship perspective. Remember, your group traveler is your BT traveler.

Our corporate group represents 50% of all of our group, and so they're already paying this rate. It's already in the market, and we're just chasing that. Those are the things that give us confidence in terms of remixing, both from a rate perspective and a demand perspective.

Austin Wurschmidt: Yeah, a lot of good stuff in there. Thank you for the time.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Michael Bellisario with Baird. Please proceed with your question.

Michael Bellisario: Thanks. Good morning, everyone. Good afternoon to you. Leslie, big picture for me, just obviously there's some sort of one-time benefits from last year in today's numbers, so maybe could you just give us your sort of best guess of what you think the underlying or go-forward run rate is for the portfolio and where you maybe think some upside or downside might actualize next year? Thanks.

Leslie Hale: Yeah. Mike, in terms of one-time events, I think clearly, everybody expected World Cup to perform and drive our performance. But when we actually look at our portfolio performance ex-World Cup, our non-World Cup markets were up 12%, and we believe that demonstrates the broad-based nature of the strength that we're seeing that is beyond World one-time events. We've seen it in other metrics as well. Keep in mind that the momentum carried into September, and our leisure, overall September was up 11%. Our leisure in September was up 16%, and that's post-World Cup. We really think that's a function of our footprint, a function of the demand we're seeing, and a number of factors.

Obviously, Labor Day was in there as well. But the general point is that the strength we're seeing across the fundamentals are well beyond one-time special events.

Tom Bardenett: If you think about our footprint, Mike, when you think about the special events, because of our size and our scale and the smile of America where many of these events rotate, Leslie kind of referred to a few of the items that are critical in regards to big events, Super Bowl, NFL Draft, things that are now really becoming entertainment venues. I think because of L.A. having pre-Olympics and some action even before 2028, it gives us confidence that we got a good footprint to be able to take advantage of those special events so they don't become anomalies.

Michael Bellisario: Got it. That is helpful. Just one more for me, sort of on the out-of-room spend. Are you seeing the same demand and pricing lift that you have been seeing on the room side? That is all for me. Thank you.

Leslie Hale: Yeah, on the out-of-room spend, I would say we are very pleased with the fact that we have seen high single-digit out-of-room spend for the last four quarters, and it is really a function of not only the demand side, but also our strategy around F&B being very thoughtful. We continue to see demand from outside the hotel relative to the F&B outlets that we have created. We are excited about what we are doing in Pittsburgh, Boston, and Key West, which are going to continue the themes that we think into next year. Also, just parking continues to be a bright light for us as well.

Tom Bardenett: The only thing I would add to Leslie's comments, we have put a lot of time and energy on the renovations, on enhancing our markets, really appealing to the grab-and-go consumer trends, and that was up 16%. We feel like those are great ROI initiatives where people are taking advantage of that before they depart or upon a late arrival. Then, as Leslie stated on the corporate group side, we are seeing that benefit the banquets department, right? Whether it is banquets, outlets, lounge, because that corporate customer tends to spend a little bit more on their stay versus, let us say, a leisure customer.

Corporate really drives that group side, and that is healthy when we start to see those type of activities, because that typically is your more profitable food and beverage that Leslie referred to.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Sydney Rom with Barclays. Please proceed with your question.

Sydney Rom: Hi. Thank you so much for taking the question. Could you walk us through how the $20 million seller note financing came together in its basic terms, like rate and maturity? Then, with the midway cash proceeds, I think you're at about $500 million of cash on the balance sheet. How are you kind of thinking about the right level of cash for the business, and would paying down some of the higher-cost term loans or buying back some of your preferred be on the table?

Nikhil Bhalla: Hi, Sydney. This is Nikhil. Thanks for the question. On your first question here on the $20 million seller financing, it's a three-year payback period, and obviously, it's structured in a way that there's accelerated payback to us. In terms of rates on the seller financing, it's an attractive rate. It's a high single-digit rate on this financing.

Leslie Hale: Yep. Then I would say, on the capital allocation side, Sydney, in terms of the proceeds, we view the capital that we just raised within the context of our broader framework for capital allocation. Our objective clearly is to maximize value for shareholders, and we measure that primarily with growing FFO and free cash flow per share. Our liquidity position gives us tremendous flexibility and real optionality.

As we intend to use these proceeds, we're going to do it in a very disciplined way, and we're going to evaluate optionality with thinking about every dollar that we use, whether it is to convert a hotel that we already own, to acquire a new hotel, to return capital to shareholders through buybacks, or to strengthen our balance sheet, like you said, in terms of paying down potential debt in a higher rising interest rate environment. All of the use of cash flow must raise FFO per share in order to earn our investment. Yes, you mentioned we do have ample liquidity. We are going to deploy it in a very disciplined way.

We believe that we have tremendous optionality that is provided by our balance sheet, and we have demonstrated the ability to unlock embedded value within our portfolio through our transformative conversions, while at the same time remaining committed to returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. Our conversions have performed exceptionally well. They are up double digit, both on the top line and bottom line this quarter, and we are going to continue to execute on our pipeline. We will also consider acquisitions if they meet our underwriting criteria and return requirements, while at the same time driving value creation.

We will also look at further strengthening our balance sheet by potentially paying down some debt in a rising interest rate environment. I think the key takeaway here is that all of these tools are available to us, and we are going to exercise them under the right conditions. They are not mutually exclusive, and on a relative basis, they have different benefits under different market conditions. We believe that the market is improving, which is providing some potential interesting opportunities, but we are going to stay disciplined and focus on driving free cash flow for our shareholders this year and next year as we deploy the capital.

Sydney Rom: Thanks so much, Leslie. Thanks, Nikhil.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Gregory Miller with Truist. Please proceed with your question.

Gregory Miller: Thanks. Good afternoon. I would like to start asking a question about corporate negotiated rates, and I know we are probably early in the process for 2027, but just curious to get your initial thoughts about whether you think hoteliers may be too aggressive in rate setting or perhaps too timid, just given the improvement in BT this year and ADR growth. Thank you.

Tom Bardenett: Yeah. Hey, Greg. This is Tom. A couple things. First and foremost, if you think about the last few years, we have really taken the stance, and this is brand as well as management companies, to try to move more and more people to dynamic pricing, because then when you are in an upcycle, the ability to drive BAR and retail is pretty significant. As an example of that, our retail segment grew 13.8% this particular quarter, and that is considerably up from a mix standpoint that now is in the low 30s versus high 20s.

That is a big shift in regards to how you think about negotiating rates when it comes down to national corporations and even local accounts in your backyard. The second thing that I would say is, when you look at rates for year-over-year, we typically will listen to the tea leaves in regards to, are you going to have more demand or not? And that kind of sets the stage in regards to if they are going to have more demand and you have compression nights that is increasing significantly. I think Leslie referred to 15%. That is a great opportunity for you to force that Tuesday, Wednesday into a longer period of time, and that is helping us.

Because if we can pick up a Monday or a Thursday on that, or price ourselves appropriately on Tuesday, Wednesday, that helps you on the dynamic pricing as well as your ability to negotiate rates based on demand. I feel that we are going into 2027 in a great position because we are seeing it happen right now, and therefore, we are going to continue to push to try to see increasing average rates. It is early, though.

I mean, this is the beginning of the RFP season, but the fact that at GBTA, people were talking about more demand, and we think that is because of what is happening in AI and many different segments of our corporate business, as I mentioned to you earlier, whether it is tech, energy, aerospace, consultants, all are traveling more, and that is what we need to take advantage of when we go into 2027.

Gregory Miller: Thanks, Tom. This question, my follow-up may also go to you. I am curious if you could provide the latest state of the union as it relates to AI impact to hotel operations, and if you could provide an update on your progress at the hotel level. Maybe as a side question, are you more or less encouraged about the opportunities, just given that there is a lot of hype today and more recently some third-party hoteliers that suggest that AI can lead to perhaps 300 basis points or more of hotel margin upside over the next five years?

Tom Bardenett: Wouldn't that be great? I would say we are looking at all avenues, and let me break it down for you to simplify it. There are brands, there are management companies, and there are owners, and everybody has a different role in this process. The brands are really focused on making sure that search continues to go through brand.com, and that is where they are spending a lot of time and energy talking to that consumer.

Because you have 295 million members and 275 million members between Marriott and Hilton, as you know, we carry a lot of the premium brands, that is where we need to make sure we are protecting distribution and continuing to go to the channels that cost less. So their focus is on that. The management companies and the ownership groups are really focused on the middle of the P&L, to your point about the basis points and the opportunity there. Those are tactics like labor management efficiency, scheduling, hours of operations, taking all these data insights in regards to how to build a better mousetrap to help the field really operate in an environment that is going to enhance productivity.

When we can do that, we also believe that we can provide better service. When you think about things that happen on a regular basis, we can automate those low-value activities so we can allow the teams to really focus on higher revenues and better service, which will ultimately mean you can have a guest that wants to come back and feels good about their stay.

Those are the areas that we are seeing that are really actionable intelligence versus artificial, and I think we are leaning in heavily on beta tests, opportunities to really go after those 300 basis points that you mentioned, because that is going to be the critical part, because we think the revenue picture is in a good spot. Now we just need to make sure we are bringing it to the bottom line.

Gregory Miller: Thank you very much, Tom. Appreciate it.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Jamie Feldman with Wells Fargo. Please proceed with your question.

Jamie Feldman: Hi, thank you. You have Connor on with Jamie here. Maybe returning to the conversions topic, and I think you've spoken to about two to three a year. Maybe beyond Boston and Key West, how are you thinking about the next candidates, and are franchise expirations driving that timing again?

Leslie Hale: Yeah, I mean, we've said that we are targeting two conversions per year, and when we look at our pipeline, we're going to be on that cadence. And we think about it, to your point that you raised, ones that are arising as a result of franchise expiration or other opportunities before the franchise expires, where we can renegotiate early to make adjustments out of those brands. But it's about two per year. We're on that cadence, and we don't see any need to change that at this point in time.

Jamie Feldman: Thank you. Appreciate the color. Last year you mentioned Q4 benefited from a favorable insurance renewal. How is this year's renewal shaping up, and how should we think about taxes and insurance as a piece of 2027 fixed costs?

Nikhil Bhalla: Hi, this is Nikhil, Connor. What I would say is we are in the middle of our negotiations at the moment on the insurance part, so there is not much I can say other than to say that I think the environment is still very, very positive. We will update you when we get to our fourth quarter earnings call. With respect to the real estate tax environment, again, we will have more color at the time when we have our call next quarter.

Jamie Feldman: Got it. Makes sense. Thank you very much.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Logan Epstein with Wolfe Research. Please proceed with your question.

Logan Epstein: Yeah, thanks for taking the question. You mentioned in the prepared remarks that you're seeing an increased corporate group in your demand mix. Just curious if you can talk about any specific industries that you're seeing there drive that across the portfolio.

Tom Bardenett: Yeah, happy to, Logan. What we're finding is because of the way our footprint is set up, we deal with a lot of small groups, somewhere between 10 and 15 nights peak night. The type of corporate groups that are attracted to us are the same type of companies that are traveling on the BT side. So, it's a lot of regional sales meetings, product launches. With AI, we're actually finding that software is getting implemented in healthcare, universities. There's a variety of reasons why people are traveling on the group side that are project-related.

That gives you an idea why we think length of stay is up, because they're going in and they have to be there for a few days. It's your typical groups that we have seen. What we like about those groups on the corporate side is that's where we see the additional F&B spend, AV, room rental, as an example of that. We had some nice lift, which goes back to the non-room revenue, where we had AV up about 20%, room rental up about 12%. Those are good signs that it's healthy corporate group, because they're not afraid that they have to put some money against those initiatives because they're going to be there for two, three days.

It's a variety of things, but I'm very encouraged that corporate continues to grow in our overall category when it comes to group.

Logan Epstein: Thanks, Tom. Maybe a follow-up to prior questions and comments in the prepared remarks. As we sit here today and see the recovery in business transient demand, just curious if you can talk about where that midweek occupancy sits today versus prior peak levels, and maybe what markets you expect are best positioned to grow from here. That's all for me. Thank you.

Tom Bardenett: Yeah. So, a couple things. I will talk about where it sits, but I think even more importantly, as we talked about where we are getting our RevPAR growth, our Tuesday, Wednesdays were in the 12%-13% and 11% on those two nights. So, the growth is happening midweek, in addition to that length of stay that we are getting a nice growth on Sunday, Monday, and in addition to that, Thursday, because of the length of stay. Little bit less growth than we are on Tuesday, Wednesday, but that is where the pricing power that Leslie is referring to.

When we talk about occupancy, I referred to earlier, we are at around 91% of 2019 on Mondays, 92% on Tuesday, Wednesday. So, when you think about pure occupancy for the whole portfolio, we are about six percentage points off, but midweek is where the most room in the tank is. Where weekends, we are closer in the 97%, 96% on the occupancy side, and we all know average rate is significantly up when it comes to leisure and weekends based on entertainment and all the events. Leslie, do you want to add something to that?

Leslie Hale: Yeah, I mean, in addition to just the broader compression we saw across our portfolio, just to support Tom's comments, the compression growth on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday was up 20%. The portfolio was up 15%, but when those three nights, it was up 20%.

Logan Epstein: Got it. Thank you so much.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Floris van Dijkum with Ladenburg Thalmann. Please proceed with your question.

Floris van Dijkum: Hey, thanks. Leslie, you made a comment in the beginning which I found fascinating, and maybe wanted to see if you could expand on that a little bit. You talked about the relationship historically between RevPAR growth and GDP growth, and how you see that now it's starting to reassert itself. Maybe if you could touch on what the historical, particularly in low supply environments, I suppose, this is an environment we're in right now, and it doesn't look like that's going to change anytime soon. Maybe talk about what the historical, or maybe touch on the historical RLJ RevPAR growth relative to GDP growth in two prior low supply environments.

Leslie Hale: No problem. The comment I made was the convergence of fundamentals in terms of having group demand be as strong as it is, while also transient demand was accelerating, with leisure travel continuing to be stable growth and with BT accelerating. Those are the fundamentals that are helping us drive overall pricing power and the overall fundamentals that we've seen this year, which we think can continue. We are starting to see that RevPAR growth and GDP growth continue to converge back to historical trends. I will let our historian give you some data points.

Nikhil Bhalla: Hey, Floris. Thanks for the question. It is a good one, because when you go back in history and you kind of look at GDP and RevPAR correlation, obviously it has been very tight. I think what you saw from 2015 or 2017 through 2019 was that supply growth was so great that it kind of masked the real growth in RevPAR growth that would have taken place along with GDP growth. The current environment is actually a really good one, where now you are starting to see, as Leslie pointed out, sort of demand converge with GDP growth, but no supply.

Clearly that is a good outcome, and that is a good positive environment to be in, and augurs well for RevPAR growth going forward.

Leslie Hale: I think it is that relationship between all the convergence of the fundamentals, pricing power, low supply, that give us comfort and confidence about the trends carrying forward.

Floris van Dijkum: Thanks. Maybe my follow-up question. I like the sale of the Midway portfolio at a, call it a 7.2% EBITDA yield. That gives you presumably significantly more capital that you can reinvest into conversions that are doing 15%+ . I think historically you said in the past it was 40% on some of those conversion returns. Maybe if you talk about one of the things, could you consider accelerating your conversions? I guess it depends a little bit on the timing of some of these brand agreements or franchise agreements as well.

Because it would significantly, it would appear to be deleveraging to do more of these kinds of investments at north of 15% IRRs, particularly when you are funding it with 7% sales. If you can talk about that a little bit.

Leslie Hale: Yeah. Well, first of all, thank you for recognizing the value that we have been able to unlock in our transformative conversions. I would say that, Floris, what we are doing, what we have done is increase our pipeline. I think that we will still stick with the cadence of probably two per year, just given the limitations around the franchise expirations, but also just making sure that we do not become a disruption story. We have been very thoughtful about managing that, and you have seen the compound growth. We are now up to eight conversions. We are going to be adding two more next year.

We think that is the right cadence, and you have seen the quarter-over-quarter growth that the pool of assets have generated. But what we have done is expanded our pipeline, and looking at our own portfolio, there are other optionality that we have that we have now increased the number of assets that we see going forward that are candidates for conversion.

Tom Bardenett: The one last thing I would add is, when you talk about non-room revenue, all those conversions, and even the renovations that we have, we find the nooks and crannies to be able to drive those ROI initiatives, and that helps us to feel confident we can continue to sustain non-room revenue growth, because our footprint is very different when you think about lifestyle and what you are trying to do to appeal to that consumer.

Floris van Dijkum: Have you ever quantified the renovation or conversion for the Wyndham Beacon Hill?

Nikhil Bhalla: We have, and we've given a stat before. We've said that we expect our EBITDA on a stabilized basis to be 40% higher than pre-renovation levels.

Leslie Hale: Does that complete your question?

Floris van Dijkum: Yeah. It actually. But the total conversion cost is that? You haven't given that, presumably, right? We can back into that, assuming a 20% return on investment?

Nikhil Bhalla: The return is actually far greater than that overall, Floris, and we have given the CapEx number to you and all the investments that have been included in that number.

Leslie Hale: We expect high double-digit returns similar on the incremental capital that we have done before, north of 40% returns on this deal as we have done before, which is what is driving the EBITDA number that Nikhil gave you.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chris Woronka with Deutsche Bank. Please proceed with your question.

Chris Woronka: Hey. Good afternoon, everyone. Thanks for taking the questions. A lot of focus on AI in different ways, and my question kind of relates to if there's a way to kind of isolate maybe the upside you've seen year-to-date in specific regions or hotels. The nature of the question is, we're not exactly sure where things are going. We had an election, and the market is a little bit concerned today anyway about less AI and data centers and things. The question is, do you feel like in those markets, in specific hotels, if you look back a couple years ago, is the demand pool big enough to offset if a little bit of the AI demand comes out?

Do you worry that there's enough of a backup to not see a meaningful drop-off? Then I have a follow-up. Thanks.

Tom Bardenett: Yeah. On the demand front, I would say there's a lot of oars in the water outside of just AI. I do appreciate your question, because I think there's a significant amount of demand that's related to AI as well. It really is market by market when you start to get into those conversations, Chris. I feel that when we looked at that broad-base demand, where you see a lot of markets going double digits in Q3, that's a lot more than AI travel, number one. You're going to see a lot of different reasons why people are traveling. It's around those industries that are thriving around corporate profits, not just AI.

So I understand your comment about data centers, but data centers typically don't produce a lot of demand when I have a data center next to my hotel. What I would say is, what people are investing around corporations, there's a race out there to continue, because if you don't invest, you're behind.

Tom Bardenett: And what we are finding is the opportunities for platforms to really try to drive that productivity and efficiencies. #3118. Data Sovereignty Isn't About Where Your Data Lives—It's About Who's In Control

Emma McGrattan is the Chief Technology Officer at Actian.

In June 2025, a French Senate committee asked a Microsoft executive if he could guarantee that data stored on Microsoft Azure in France would never be handed to U.S. authorities without explicit consent. He said he couldn’t. His answer confirmed that controlling where your data is stored is only part of data sovereignty. You also need to control who can access it, under whose authority and for what purpose.

I’ve spent much of my career helping organizations navigate changes in enterprise data architecture, from the days when they ran nearly everything themselves to today’s increasingly complex cloud and AI ecosystems. More recently, my work on data and AI sovereignty has brought a recurring concern into focus: Organizations often have far less control over their technology than they think. Splitting my time between Dublin and New York, I see the same challenge playing out on both sides of the Atlantic, even as the regulatory and political pressures differ.

​Many technology executives I speak with still reach for a map when I ask about their data sovereignty. But location alone doesn’t equal sovereignty.

So, how do you know whether your organization genuinely controls its data or simply complies with the rules governing where it resides? I’ll explore why traditional approaches to sovereignty are falling short, how AI is raising the stakes and what technology leaders should be thinking about as they build more resilient businesses.​​

Twenty years ago, most business-critical applications ran inside environments that organizations largely owned and controlled. Today, enterprise data flows continuously across cloud platforms, SaaS applications, integration services, partner ecosystems, AI models and autonomous agents. Every new integration introduces another dependency that sits outside the organization’s control.

In this environment, knowing where your data is stored tells you surprisingly little. A company may be able to demonstrate full compliance with every residency requirement. Yet, it still depends on cloud infrastructure, foundation models, identity providers, APIs and software platforms that it has little ability to influence.​

As we’ve seen, data residency in France alone can’t prevent U.S. authorities from demanding access to it. So, France is replacing Microsoft with a local provider as a step toward controlling the country’s own health data.​​

Over the past few years, external forces have continually reshaped technology ecosystems. Governments introduce technology restrictions with little warning. Cloud providers change licensing models and commercial terms. AI platforms release new capabilities and retire others at remarkable speed. Constant change is now the normal operating environment.​

That’s why I believe data sovereignty is an architectural property rather than a compliance initiative. Compliance proves that today’s requirements have been met. The architecture determines what an organization controls, what it depends on and how quickly it can respond when circumstances change.

​To build a resilient sovereignty strategy, review the following:

• Technology Landscape: Map every system, platform and integration that touches critical data. Know what the organization controls, depends on and breaks if external services change or become unavailable.

• External Dependencies: Clarify the organization’s reliance on cloud providers, AI services, software vendors and other infrastructure.

• Critical Data: Identify business-critical systems, sensitive information flows and external services involved in decision making to prevent misallocating resources by risk area.

• Alternative Options: Identify alternatives for each critical service or technology. The range of options impacts the degree of resilience.

Successful organizations don’t apply the same level of control to every system. Identity systems, customer data and intellectual property require organizational ownership. Analytics and metrics on non-sensitive data may stay in the cloud. Decide what matters and build accordingly.​​

A 2026 BARC survey showed that a total of 89% of respondents consider data sovereignty either “very important” or “rather important,” but just 10% have budget for it. This tells me sovereignty is on the executive agenda, but the lack of dedicated funding means that they haven’t yet operationalized it.​​​

​AI is one reason why sovereignty has become urgent. In the BARC survey, increased use of data and AI in core business processes was the top-ranked driver of sovereignty initiatives, cited by 62% of respondents. The reason stems from the way AI reasons across data from multiple sources, infers new relationships and makes recommendations that previously required human judgment.​​

As organizations introduce autonomous agents into production, sovereignty extends far beyond where information is stored. It now includes where models execute, what information agents are permitted to access, which external tools they invoke, how their decisions are governed and whether those decisions can be reconstructed months later when someone asks why.

It’s hard to establish trust in the data used by AI. When an AI agent acts, organizations must know which data informed it and be able to explain the decision and how governance policies were applied. Without transparency, organizations can’t deploy AI responsibly at scale.

Organizations that invested in governance before generative AI became fashionable are further along in their AI journey. They know which data can be trusted, who owns it and how those governance policies are enforced. Instead of slowing innovation, their architectures allow new AI technologies to be adopted with confidence because they already have the guardrails in place.​​

The biggest misconception about data sovereignty is that it requires organizations to isolate themselves from the rest of the technology ecosystem. Complete independence has never been the objective. Modern enterprises will always depend on external technologies, partners and cloud providers. What matters most is maintaining meaningful control over critical capabilities and being able to pivot quickly if the need arises.

When data sovereignty comes up in your next board meeting, resist the urge to reach for the map. Instead, ask yourself: If one of our most important technology providers changed its commercial terms, exited a key market or simply disappeared tomorrow, how much of our business would continue to operate as it does today?

I suspect the answer will reveal far more about your organization’s sovereignty than any map of your data ever could.

#3117. Viemed Healthcare (VMD) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Sleep therapy growth and a lower capex outlook drove margin gains this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Viemed Healthcare, Inc. (VMD -10.88%) reported record quarterly revenue and significant growth in net income, driven by expansion in sleep therapy and maternal health services. Management indicated that the company is transitioning to a standardized rollout for its women’s health business while managing increased regulatory audit activity across the home medical equipment industry. Management reported that the company's financial position remains flexible, supporting both debt reduction and organic expansion across its respiratory and sleep care platforms. The company increased its focus on less capital-intensive services, which contributed to sequential margin expansion and influenced the updated full-year guidance.

#3115. Pet Insurance on Your Mind? Buy It Now, Not Later

If your pet is young and healthy, the cost of coverage may not seem worth it. But that math can change fast.

Senior Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

It feels natural to protect your pet’s health with insurance in the same way you protect your loved ones with health insurance. After all, fur babies are part of the family.

But if you’ve shopped for pet insurance recently, you might have cringed at the cost. Should you really pay hundreds of dollars every year for something you might not use? For some pet parents, the answer is yes, even if their pet is young and healthy. And that’s partly because of how pet insurance handles pre-existing conditions.

A pre-existing condition is any illness or injury that shows symptoms before your pet insurance policy takes effect. Pet insurers usually won’t cover these conditions.

Dr. Rebecca Greenstein, chief veterinarian at Kleinburg Veterinary Hospital and veterinary expert for rover.com, says she’s seeing an increase in claim denials based on pre-existing conditions. “The whole point of insurance is you want broad spectrum coverage for a variety of things,” she says. “By the time they're excluding major organ systems and anything related to that, you may be paying monthly for coverage that doesn't actually help you when you need to go make a claim.”

If you’re considering pet insurance, it’s best to buy a policy before your pet needs it.

Your pet’s pre-existing conditions will determine which treatments and procedures insurers cover down the road.

Say your dog has a history of allergies. If you buy a policy after your four-footed friend has shown symptoms, pet insurers typically won’t pay for allergy shots or other treatments. The exclusion might also apply to related problems like itchiness or ear infections, says Dr. Michael Goldstein, medical director at Billerica Veterinary Hospital and Thrive Pet Healthcare.

He offers the example of a dog who goes to the vet for a hotspot one year and an ear infection the next. If you got pet insurance for your dog between those visits, the insurer might deny your claim because both issues could be caused by underlying allergies.

The best way around this type of scenario is to buy coverage when your pet is young, before any symptoms develop.

» MORE: The best pet insurance for pre-existing conditions

It’s tricky to figure out if pet insurance will actually save you money in the long run. The most common type of plan covers accidents and illness. It costs an average of $836 for dogs and $435 for cats each year, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA). You could pay these premiums for years before an emergency surgery or chronic illness makes its way to your financial doorstep.

It’s impossible to know for sure whether your pet will stay healthy or run up sky-high vet bills. But you can assess the potential value of pet insurance by looking at common chronic conditions that pets develop with age and how much it costs to treat them.

For instance, “cats generally, as younger animals, don't have a lot of problems,” Goldstein says. “But as they get older, there are definitely common issues. Older cats in particular get chronic kidney disease.”

In cats over age 10, the Cornell Feline Health Center estimates that as many as 40% have chronic kidney disease. The annual cost to treat this condition can top $1,200.

Another example is atopic dermatitis from skin allergies, a common ailment affecting as many as 15% of dogs, according to the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center. A single vet visit to address these itchy, persistent symptoms can cost $250 or more. And while that’s a fraction of what you might pay for pet insurance, costs of chronic conditions can add up over your pet’s lifetime.

Vet bills can also balloon quickly if chronic conditions require surgery. One example of this is hip dysplasia, a genetic disorder that can cause arthritis and pain in large-breed dogs. Depending on the procedure, you could pay up to $10,000 for hip surgery.

Many pet insurance plans cover treatments for hip dysplasia, including surgical costs, as long as it's not a pre-existing condition. However, some policies have waiting periods of six to 12 months for orthopedic issues like hip dysplasia. If symptoms develop during that waiting period, the condition will be considered pre-existing. That’s another argument for buying your pet’s coverage earlier rather than later.

Most importantly, having insurance means you can choose the best treatment for your pet no matter the cost. “It's really tragic when it's a life and death decision that is needed and it’s based on someone's financial constraints,” Greenstein says. “What is best and what's affordable often are not on the same side of the spectrum.”

One option to keep pet insurance affordable is to buy an accident-only plan. This type of coverage is usually much cheaper, costing about $190 annually for dogs and $112 for cats, according to NAPHIA. These plans cover injuries resulting from accidents, which include not just wounds and broken bones but also objects or toxins your pet might swallow.

However, an accident-only plan won’t help with some of the most common vet expenses. Illnesses, not injuries, are behind most claims submitted to pet insurer Lemonade, the company said in an email. In the past year, more than 60% of Lemonade's pet insurance claims stemmed from illnesses. That’s twice as many as the next-largest claim category, which was preventive care. A similar trend can be found in data from Nationwide, where chronic diseases make up a clear majority of pet insurance claims submitted to the company in 2025.

If you opt for an accident-only plan or no coverage at all, it’s still smart to set aside some savings for those inevitable pet emergencies and illnesses. This pool of funds can keep you from having to make difficult decisions about your pet’s care based solely on the cost of treatment.

#3114. AI Slop Is Turning Bug Bounty Programs Into A Security Liability

Ido Geffen, CEO and Co-founder, Novee Security.

​Bug bounty programs have traditionally relied on human researchers to identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities, with submission volumes that security teams could generally manage.

There were always strong reports and weak ones, but the weaker submissions were often easy to spot. They were thin, poorly written or obviously misunderstood the environment, so an experienced analyst could simply reject them quickly.

AI is changing both the volume of reports and how easily teams can distinguish legitimate findings from noise. A bad report today might look carefully analyzed, technically plausible and full of detail—and still be wrong. The “AI slop” phenomenon is not limited to creative disciplines such as writing and design. It’s all too rampant in cybersecurity as well.

That can make things expensive. Analysts now have to take more time to investigate—reading the report, reproducing the claimed issue, understanding it in the context of the application, assessing whether it’s actually exploitable and deciding where it belongs against other risks—before discovering that there’s nothing there. A researcher can file a report in minutes, while the team receiving it pays in hours.

HackerOne reported in May 2026 that the industry experienced a 100%-plus surge in report volume after more advanced AI models and tools arrived in February. The new volume includes valuable findings alongside duplicates, unverifiable submissions and reports lacking enough depth to act on.

Bug bounty programs were designed around human researcher attention as the scarce resource. AI is changing where that scarcity sits.

In January 2026, Daniel Stenberg, a maintainer of curl, a widely used open-source data-transfer tool, ended the project’s monetary bug bounty after what he described as an explosion of AI-slop reports. The share of submissions that became confirmed vulnerabilities had fallen from above 15% historically to below 5% in 2025. Stenberg specifically cited the time required to debunk bad reports.

By April, curl had returned to HackerOne as its reporting platform while keeping monetary rewards eliminated. Stenberg reported that submission volume was running at roughly double the already elevated 2025 rate, but quality had improved substantially: Roughly 15% to 16% of reports were again becoming confirmed vulnerabilities, and he believed AI was involved in almost every submission to varying degrees.

curl’s experience also shows that AI can improve vulnerability research. The deeper problem is economic. The cost of generating a plausible hypothesis has fallen, while the cost of proving whether it represents real risk remains high.

And the capacity problem didn’t disappear when quality improved. curl subsequently stopped accepting vulnerability reports for the entire month of July to give maintainers relief from the workload. Once discovery runs continuously and automatically, scarcity moves somewhere else.

You might look at a growing queue and see an efficiency problem. I see a security problem.

When teams can’t quickly discern irrelevant findings from important ones, every hour an expert spends disproving plausible noise is time they aren’t spending investigating or remediating real exposure.

That pressure compounds because the people doing the sorting are often the people with the deepest application knowledge. They are the ones who can reproduce a finding, understand whether it conflicts with the system’s intended design, and judge whether it creates a real attack path. As queues grow, their expertise gets pulled into triage instead of remediation.

The polished nature of AI-generated submissions can make the problem worse. A weak report that looks credible takes longer to reject, while a legitimate vulnerability may sit behind it in the same queue.

Triage latency is just dwell time you’ve handed to an adversary.

A finding without a working demonstration is a hypothesis, and hypotheses can be generated by the thousands now.

The evidentiary threshold has to evolve with the cost of producing a report. Programs should put more weight on evidence that a finding can be reproduced and tied to real impact:

• Reproducibility: Can the researcher reliably reproduce the behavior?

• Demonstrated Impact: What can an attacker actually accomplish?

• Context: Does the finding account for how the application actually works, including permissions, architecture and business logic?

Raising the bar too bluntly could discourage legitimate researchers or incentivize people to cause actual damage merely to prove that an exploit works. The goal is to demand better evidence without encouraging researchers to cause harm in order to prove a point.

That could mean clearly defining what constitutes acceptable reproduction, giving researchers safe testing boundaries/environments where appropriate, and distinguishing a serious disclosure that lacks a complete exploit chain from mass-produced speculative findings.

AI has increased the potential to create noise, but it also lets more people examine more software, and capable researchers can potentially work faster. Now the question is whether the incentive structure rewards researchers for producing the kind of evidence defenders can actually use.

Bug bounties historically rewarded discovery because skilled human attention was expensive and limited. As AI-assisted and eventually autonomous discovery becomes more common, discovery itself accounts for less of the scarce value in the process. What remains scarce is proof, context and a verified fix.

That suggests the unit of value may change over time. Bounty structures could place more weight on demonstrated exploitability, useful remediation and confirmation that the risk has actually been closed. The programs that hold up best will be the ones that reward evidence and risk reduction, not just report volume.

#3112. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream company operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

"As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," said Mackay.

Mackay ranks No. 569 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.9%. See Kinetik's Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving to Crescent Energy (CRGY), an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian, and Uinta Basins. With a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share (annualized dividend of $0.48 per share), CRGY's dividend yield stands at 3.56%. Earlier this month, Crescent announced an agreement to acquire Eagle Ford assets from Devon Energy (DVN).

Heading into Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reiterated a buy rating on Crescent stock and slightly lowered the price target to $17 from $18, citing dilution from new shares.

"CRGY's recent acquisition of DVN's Eagle Ford assets marks a strategic, growth-oriented move, potentially enhancing cash flow performance," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst noted that the acquisition of the Eagle Ford assets at a net purchase price of $3.85 billion will add about 68 MBoe/d of net production and over 600 net Tier 1 locations. Richardson added that a solid track record of synergies from past deals in the Eagle Ford region increases confidence about Crescent achieving efficiencies with this deal.

Additionally, Richardson noted that the financial implications of the acquisition seem impressive, with a projected increase in cash flow per share of about 9% for 2027 to 2029.

The analyst believes that Crescent is not just expanding its business through acquisitions but positioning itself as a more durable company, regardless of market conditions.
