#3107. AI's Workforce Gap And The Lessons We Keep Forgetting

Phillip Marangella, Chief Marketing and Product Officer, EdgeConneX.

Every revolution is a story about people, and the race to build digital and AI infrastructure is no different. Behind the headlines about chips and power are human questions: Who benefits, who feels left behind and who will build it?

The AI era is built on concrete and conduit, and there simply aren’t enough skilled hands to make it happen.

According to the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, construction faced a shortage of roughly 439,000 workers as of November 2025. Associated Builders and Contractors estimates the industry needs 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and another 456,000 in 2027, while the National Center for Construction Education and Research projects that about 41% of the workforce will retire by 2031.

Electrical systems alone account for 45% to 70% of a data center build’s cost, according to International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, and McKinsey estimates the country will need 130,000 additional electricians by 2030 to build data centers and new manufacturing facilities.

To meet AI demand, the data center industry has to grow the talent pool. Many potential beneficiaries do not know what data centers are or the careers they offer. The industry needs workers across more than 230 specialist roles, from construction trades and facilities technicians to engineers, controls specialists and network technicians. Some require a degree, but many call for a trade credential or equivalent hands-on experience.

Demand is growing faster than traditional education pipelines can produce skilled workers. In 2025, Google committed $10 million to the Electrical Training Alliance to help train more than 100,000 electricians and 30,000 new apprentices within five years.

The challenge is considerable, but not without precedent. In 1940, as skilled workers were drafted and war production surged, the War Manpower Commission created Training Within Industry, which broke complex jobs into teachable steps. By the end of the war, more than 1.6 million workers in 16,500 plants had been certified.

The lesson: Workforce gaps close when industry and educators treat training as critical infrastructure.

The second half of the people story is opportunity. In Northern Virginia, Northern Virginia Community College offers the state’s first accredited associate degree in data center operations. Microsoft partners with the college on scholarships and internships, and Amazon Web Services has teamed with Virginia’s community college system to expand similar programs statewide.

Virginia’s legislative watchdog, JLARC, found in 2024 that a single data center building puts roughly 1,500 workers on-site at construction peak, but sustains about 50 permanent jobs once running. Goldman Sachs Research reported that construction jobs tied to data center development have grown by 216,000 since 2022, and PwC’s 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer found that workers with AI skills now earn a 62% wage premium.

History suggests that as technologies mature, new opportunities emerge. When ATMs spread across American banking, economist James Bessen documented in the IMF’s Finance & Development that fewer tellers were needed per branch, yet banks opened more branches and teller employment held steady as the role evolved.

AI and other technology shifts are predicted to create a net 78 million new jobs worldwide by 2030, according to the World Economic Forum, and LinkedIn’s 2026 Jobs on the Rise ranked AI engineer as the fastest-growing U.S. role, with tech and AI-related jobs among the top five.

Workers in these roles are key to AI’s benefits, but none of that happens without data centers, and data centers do not happen without skilled workers.

Then there are the people attending town halls to stop data center builds, and their concerns deserve to be understood rather than dismissed. A Gallup survey found seven in 10 Americans oppose constructing an AI data center in their local area. Shawn Patterson of the Annenberg Public Policy Center told Newsweek that opposition jumped from 49% to 61% between surveys. The Brookings Institution reports that local opposition blocked or delayed 75 projects worth $130 billion in early 2026.

Like the workforce challenge, opposition to new ways of working is not without precedent. Luddites protested automation in the 19th century, and Time warned of “The Automation Jobless” in 1961. The anxiety was not irrational; it eased when new livelihoods became visible and attainable.

The way through this fear is not a louder argument. It is a more inclusive, fact-based discussion that treats people closest to the build-out as neighbors, not obstacles. That means transparency, open training programs, verifiable community benefits and local hiring commitments that get kept.

No community ever learned to love infrastructure. People made peace with power lines, highways and factories when those things stopped being built near them and started being built with them. AI and digital infrastructure will earn its place the same way every transformative shift has: one neighbor and one kept promise at a time.

Workforce gaps close when we build fast, practical on-ramps like apprenticeships and community college programs. Creating pathways from classrooms to technology careers has been an EdgeConneX priority for years, including Hello World, which uses AI and VR in project-based computer science classes at the K-12 level. We are on track to reach more than 100,000 students across the U.S. by early 2027, with a goal of 1 million by 2030. That matters because students do not pursue fields they have never seen themselves in.

Positive momentum increases when local people can see benefits today and a brighter future ahead. Opposition softens not through better marketing, but through shared benefit, meaningful jobs locals can get and the promise of more time being human. The AI build-out will be won or lost not only in innovation, but in the meaningful building of human infrastructure.

You’ll also get an in-stay credit when you book a vacation home through The Edit for four nights or more.

Starting in 2027, Chase’s The Edit collection of upscale hotel and resort stays will broaden to include more than 10,000 vacation homes. If you carry the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, that means you’ll soon have more ways to use The Edit credits on those cards.

This addition will significantly expand The Edit’s footprint — currently at more than 1,500 hotels and resorts — although its usefulness will depend on your travel style. The new properties are curated in partnership with Plum Guide, a vacation-rental booking platform.

Plus, when you book a stay of four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use at your vacation home.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming changes to The Edit.

Eligible Chase cardholders can currently book vacation homes through the issuer’s travel portal. However, those bookings are not eligible to receive The Edit benefits. That changes Jan. 1, 2027, with select listings.

If you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, here’s what you can expect when you book a vacation home through The Edit:

Up to $250 in statement credits on prepaid stays of two nights or more. Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardholders are capped at $500 in credits a year, while Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ cardholders get up to $1,000 (starting Jan. 1, 2027).

$150 in-stay credit when booking a stay of at least four nights.

Early check-in and late checkout, when available.

Compared to booking hotels and resorts with The Edit, you’re losing out on perks like a $100 property credit (which doesn’t have a four-night minimum), complimentary breakfast and room upgrades.

While cardholders will be able to redeem points toward vacation-home stays, Chase told NerdWallet that these bookings will not be eligible for Points Boost at launch.

You’ll also need to book vacation homes at least seven days in advance — a requirement that’s currently in place with standard vacation homes available in Chase’s travel portal. Chase said it plans to reduce that requirement in the near future.

Chase’s addition of vacation homes to The Edit follows American Express’ recent move to add Airbnb Luxe properties to its own lodging credit for eligible cardholders.

When you book a vacation home for four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use on services like massages, a private chef, dry cleaning and airport pick-ups.

Options vary by property, but you’ll see a list of available offerings prior to booking your stay. You won’t be able to see pricing, but you can reach out to a Reserve travel designer — a travel concierge who can help plan your trip — to get pricing estimates prior to booking. (You won’t be able to contact the vacation home host until after you’ve booked your stay.)

While it’s nice to get the credit, the four-night minimum could be frustrating for cardholders. When you book hotels through The Edit, there isn’t a stay minimum to get the $100 property credit (although you must stay two nights to use your eligible card’s $250 prepaid stay credit).

By comparison, AmEx offers a $250 Airbnb Experiences credit on the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express each calendar year when you book a prepaid Airbnb Luxe property through its travel portal. Terms apply. That statement credit is good for the rest of the calendar year in which the booking is confirmed. However, you can only unlock one $250 credit a year, even if you make multiple bookings.

Booking a vacation home through The Edit makes the most sense for longer group trips.

One of the best perks of booking a vacation home is that everyone gets to stay together in a shared space — something that’s difficult to do in a traditional hotel. If you’re able to get a larger group, you’ll also have more people to split the booking cost with.

Plus, you’ll want to stay at least four nights to benefit from the $150 in-stay credit.

If you’re traveling by yourself or with a partner on a shorter trip, you might find more value staying at a hotel or resort that’s part of The Edit. You’ll get useful perks like complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of adding vacation homes to The Edit is creating more booking options. If vacation homes fit your travel style, this is a great development to look forward to. If not, you’ll still be able to book hotels through The Edit like before.

#3104. Stock Market Today, Nov. 5: Amazon Shares Slide as Technology Selloff Erases Early Gains

On Nov. 5, 2026, Amazon shares reversed an early rally as rising yields and tech selling took over the session.

Amazon.com (AMZN -2.19%), a global e-commerce, cloud computing, and logistics platform, closed at $260.21, down 2.19%. Thursday's move reflected early election-related gains that faded as technology selling and higher yields took over. Investors are watching the company's AWS cloud computing division's profitability and AI infrastructure spending next.

Trading volume reached 83.5 million shares, coming in about 117% above its three-month average of 38.5 million shares. Amazon.com IPO'd in 1997 and has grown 265,645% since going public.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -4.36%) closed at 7,354, down 4.36%, while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.52%) closed at 24,315, down 5.52%. Among e-commerce, digital advertising, and retail logistics peers, Walmart closed at $127.72, down 1.12%, while Costco Wholesale closed at $1,065.59, up 1.83%.

On Thursday, Nov. 5, Amazon shares gained during early trading after the company announced a partnership with Uber that provides its Prime members with free restaurant-delivery benefits through Uber Eats. However, that didn't last, as a broad sell-off of tech stocks took place today in the wake of U.S. midterm election results.

The Democratic Party gained control of Congress, raising worries that incoming Democratic leadership could demand tighter AI regulations and put a hold on data center construction projects key to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. This could result in a major impact to Amazon's AWS business just as the company is spending substantial sums to expand its AI infrastructure.

At the same time, Wall Street is concerned about the e-commerce giant's AI costs. Last week, Amazon's third-quarter earnings report missed revenue estimates while the company's capital expenditures continued to rise, resulting in negative Q3 free cash flow (FCF) of $42.4 billion compared to positive FCF of $14.8 billion in the previous year.

In a macroeconomic environment of rising interest rates, which makes borrowing to fund an AI buildout more expensive, and persistent inflation likely to impact consumer spending and Amazon's sales, the company is facing a challenging time right now. But over the long run, its AI investments could position it for success. Management forecasted AWS revenue to grow by 40% year over year in 2027 and 2028 as well, thanks to strong demand for its AI offerings.

TL;DR: Rates fell today, but not by enough to change your mortgage math.

Mortgage rates fell today, possibly helped by post-midterm election clarity and a drop in oil prices.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.01% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is six basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Tomorrow, the Nerds will be watching the release of the October jobs report. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.51% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3100. From Pilots To Payoff: The Top IT Priorities Every Executive Should Accomplish Before Year-End

Scott Francis is Technology Evangelist at PFU America, Inc. and Ricoh Document Scanners.

​As the end of 2026 draws near, the central question for business leaders has shifted from asking whether their organization is adopting and deploying AI fast enough to assessing whether AI is performing as expected. With IT budget planning for 2027 well underway, organizations should use the waning months of this year as a reality check that will serve to separate organizations positioned to scale in 2027 from those still catching up.​

There’s no question that the demand for AI is skyrocketing. What is unclear is whether organizations are meeting the projected return on investment thus far. Gartner predicts AI spend will reach $2.59 trillion globally this year, a substantial 47% increase over 2025.​​

With the end of the year quickly approaching, there is an opportunity to take stock and refocus on overcoming challenges to achieving ROI and readjust where necessary. Rather than taking a scattershot approach to AI deployments, organizations should take a measured, strategic approach on where to apply AI; for example, using one workflow, establishing KPIs and then tracking those quarter-over-quarter before expanding to more departments or enterprise-wide.​

As the saying goes, “life moves fast.” And we’ve seen from technological advancements over the last few years that AI moves just as fast. Many companies are already in the planning phase of employing agentic AI, according to McKinsey’s report, with 40% of companies surveyed already scaling agents, up from 27% in 2025.

Despite the positive uptick in deployments, organizations should prioritize getting current AI deployments right, determining what’s hindering ROI and preparing for the next phase of digital transformation.

AI systems are only as trustworthy as the data foundation, which is a major reason why prioritizing data quality is imperative. Flawed data takes on a new meaning in the AI era because it has the potential to undermine the models built on it.

The “2026 State of Data Integrity and AI Readiness” survey of data and analytics leaders puts a spotlight on data quality challenges: 43% of respondents cite data readiness as the most significant barrier to AI alignment with business objectives. Creating proactive strategies to fix bad data, including data errors, redundancy and more, is still one of the most inexpensive approaches to protecting against downstream damage. This imperative step provides organizations with the confidence that their AI deployments will meet performance expectations and transform data into the dependable foundation that reliable, high-performing AI requires.

Before expanding AI deployments and introducing agents, executives should audit whether the underlying systems can actually support agentic workflows, including clean data pipelines, defined APIs and integration between the systems agents need to touch.

Preparing teams well before AI is rolled out across the organization is critical. Skipping this step can breed employee resentment and pushback and result in lowering morale.

Workplace tension is already a challenge, and for good reason. A WRITER study found that “92% of the C-suite are actively cultivating ‘AI elite’ employees, while 60% plan layoffs for non-adopters.” Business leaders should not view AI as a replacement for skilled personnel; it should be used to surface insights and recommendations, while consequential decisions, especially those affecting employees or customers, remain in human hands.

Training, communication and genuine feedback loops are what separate adoption from chaos, making change management well worth the investment. Reskilling and preserving the human element build trust and catch the blind spots LLMs can’t.

IT leaders should be aware that AI is not immune from volatility, and a backup plan is mandatory. One well-publicized example of AI disruption is Anthropic’s suspension of global access to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 following a U.S. government export control directive. Access was later restored under a modified compliance structure; however, business leaders should take this incident seriously and acknowledge that government-initiated suspension or access restriction can occur without advance notice. Business leaders can address regulatory instability by identifying which models and vendors they rely on and identifying fallback options before a suspension forces an unplanned migration.

There is also a growing regulatory divide between jurisdictions. The U.S. export rule’s workforce application means enterprises with frontier AI API integrations and global engineering teams may be exposed to compliance risk regardless of where their servers are located. Gartner projects more than a third of enterprises will run localized AI platforms by 2027, up from just 5% in 2025. For multinational firms, this means agentic AI strategy can no longer be a single global architecture; it will need to incorporate jurisdiction-based contingency planning.

​The gap between AI pilots and AI payoff won’t close on its own. The executives who make real progress before year-end will be the ones connecting these three priorities to long-term success to achieve business goals and ROI goals. I believe it’s imperative for business leaders to focus on the fundamentals this year before expanding AI projects and incorporating agents, treating their data quality, teams, economics and risk as interconnected.​

#3099. Genesis Energy (GEL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Deepwater shortfalls and Shenandoah updates shaped the quarter's results.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Genesis Energy, L.P. (GEL -5.81%) reported third-quarter results and addressed operational delays in the Gulf of Mexico. Management stated that results were impacted by lower-than-expected volumes from certain deepwater production facilities and a planned turnaround at Salamanca moved into the third quarter. The company continued its capital allocation strategy by reducing high-cost preferred units and maintaining no borrowings on its senior secured credit facility. Management indicated that while some production has shifted to later periods, the long-term outlook for offshore infrastructure remains supported by active drilling on dedicated leases.

The marine transportation segment is engaged in the maritime transportation of primarily refined petroleum products. The onshore transportation and services segment is engaged in the transportation, handling, blending, storage, and supply of energy products, including crude oil and refined products, primarily around refining centers, as well as the processing of sour gas streams to remove sulfur at refining operations.

Genesis' operations are primarily located in the Gulf Coast states and the Gulf of Mexico. At this time, I would like to introduce Grant Sims, CEO of Genesis Energy L.P. Mr. Sims is joined by Kristen Jesulaitis, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Legal Officer, Ryan Sims, President and Chief Commercial Officer, and Louie Nicol, Chief Accounting Officer. With that, I will now turn the call over to Grant.

Grant Sims: Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining us today. As noted in our earnings release this morning, our third quarter results came in modestly ahead of where we thought we would be internally. In broad terms, the third quarter played out consistent with what we described in August, with the back half of the year being shaped by two things largely outside of our control: hurricane season and the timing of producer activity in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico. The weather cooperated in the third quarter, as we had no weather-related disruptions during what is typically the most active part of hurricane season.

Unfortunately, the benefit we would have otherwise expected to see was partially offset by lower-than-anticipated volumes from certain production facilities which flow exclusively through our pipelines. While volumes from a couple of these deepwater facilities are expected to be lower than originally anticipated in the fourth quarter, and in all likelihood, last through the early part of 2027, it is important to remember we have visibility to at least four new high-impact wells that are scheduled to be completed and turned to production over the coming quarters.

Ultimately, none of these temporary impacts change the amount of oil in the ground, the acreage that is dedicated to our pipelines, or the fact that none of this incremental production requires any additional capital from Genesis. It simply becomes a discussion around timing and when, not if, we will move the volumes through our offshore infrastructure. In the Gulf, things can slide to the right, but rarely is there a total geophysical bust. If there is, lost volumes are virtually certain to be replaced by new discoveries that are developed in the same geographic neighborhood.

Elsewhere, our onshore transportation and services segments once again performed ahead of our expectations, and our marine transportation segment was generally in line with our expectations, despite our final blue water dry docking of the year unexpectedly extending into the third quarter. Both of these businesses are being supported by the same set of macro fundamentals: strong Gulf Coast refinery runs, shifting crude and product flows into and around the Gulf Coast, and in marine, a Jones Act market that is, if anything, getting [audio distortion] level of activity around our irreplaceable midstream infrastructure in the Gulf of America, as well as the macro fundamentals driving our other businesses. With that, let me turn quickly to the balance sheet.

Following the significant financing activities we completed in the first half of the year, there is very little new to report this quarter. We ended the quarter with no borrowings outstanding under our $900 million senior secured credit facility, approximately $41.5 million of unrestricted cash on hand, no debt maturities until 2029, and a bank-calculated leverage ratio of approximately 5.03x. In February, we issued $750 million of 6.75% senior unsecured notes due 2034 and used the proceeds to take out, in full, the higher-cost 7.75% notes due 2028, which pushed our nearest senior note maturity out to 2029. We also upsized and extended our revolving senior secured credit facility with our extremely supportive bank group.

Additionally, as a reminder, we entered this year with approximately $529 million of our Series A cumulative preferred outstanding, paying a current cash rate of 11.24%, clearly the most expensive current pay paper anywhere in our capital structure. In nine months, we have retired roughly 40% of it, taking the remaining face amount down to approximately $311 million. I would point out, had we paid down debt rather than retiring this very expensive security, our bank-calculated leverage ratio would have been closer to 4.7x. We think running a little higher leverage ratio in the near term to get rid of such high-cost security is in the best interest of everyone else in the capital structure.

We will continue to focus on right-sizing and optimizing our capital structure, and we expect to be able to drive future cash savings over the next several years from three places. We will focus on reducing debt in absolute terms, opportunistically refinancing our higher coupon senior unsecured notes with lower coupons and extended maturities as they become callable at more attractive premiums beginning in the first half of 2027, and redeeming the remaining approximately $311 million of the 11.24% Series A cumulative preferred still outstanding, all as we work towards our ultimate long-term leverage target of around 4x.

Consistent with the all-of-the-above approach to capital allocation that we have discussed, both prior to and since turning cash flow positive, our board of directors declared a quarterly distribution of $0.20 per common unit. That is unchanged from last quarter, but represents an increase of approximately 21% as compared to the third quarter of last year. We would otherwise expect to thoughtfully and prudently grow distributions to our common unit holders over time, all while preserving our financial flexibility to pursue attractive organic and inorganic opportunities as they may emerge in the future. With that, I will go into a little more detail on each of our business segments. Let me start with the offshore.

As I mentioned earlier, our offshore pipeline transportation segment operated without any weather-related downtime during the quarter. The offset was lower-than-anticipated volumes. Specifically, that included unplanned curtailments at a couple of our legacy connected fields, the continuing challenges from two of the initial wells at Shenandoah, and a planned turnaround at Salamanca that the operator moved forward from the fourth quarter into the third quarter. As we said last quarter, we do not believe any of these items have long-term negative implications for the ultimate recovery reserves already discovered and being developed.

In the operator's view, and we would concur, these impacts are transitory and simply result in timing differences for when those reserves are produced and when those barrels enter our pipeline for transportation to shore. In this pricing environment, the producers are clearly incented to figure it out. They do, however, tend to play the long game, accepting lower current production in order to maximize total ultimate recoveries from these world-class hydrocarbon reservoirs. Things can indeed shift to the right, but that's precisely why we have minimum volume commitments, or MVCs, in most of our new contracts. We are protected to the downside, even if it takes longer than expected for them to execute.

Owing to certain things, about which we are not in position to go into a lot of detail, Shenandoah operated at or slightly below the MVC level in the third quarter and is expected to do so until several new wells come on. It is now projected that production from the first well has slipped into early next year, but we would expect additional throughput from these two Monument wells to be in the range of 20-25 KBD, or thousand barrels a day of oil, reaching that level sometime in the first quarter of 2027. Excuse me. The rig will then return to Shenandoah and drill a fifth producing well, with initial production from it expected to be ±20 KBD. A subsea pumping system is scheduled to be installed in 2028, improving well performance and, most importantly, maximizing the ultimate reserves to be recovered from Shenandoah.

Beyond 2028, there are at least four, and possibly as many as eight additional locations at Shenandoah proper, possibly another location at Monument, two, maybe three locations at the Shenandoah South field, and as we understand it, there are already four additional exploratory prospects that have been identified within a 30 mi radius of the Shenandoah production facility. Suffice it to say, regardless of near-term challenges, we expect significant volumes to flow across the Shenandoah production facility and exclusively into our 100% owned SYNC pipeline and onto shore through our 64% owned CHOPS pipeline for decades and decades to come without requiring any additional capital from us.

At Salamanca, there are currently two rigs on location drilling wells to be completed and tied into the Salamanca facility, the production from which will flow through our 100% owned SEKCO lateral and onto shore through our 64% owned Poseidon pipeline. We expect both of these wells at Salamanca to come online early in 2027, which should move total production closer to the facility's design capacity of 60 KBD-70 KBD.

Harbour Energy, doing business in the U.S. as Louisiana Land Oil and Gas, has added a second rig to their Gulf of America program, and this activity at Salamanca, as well as expected additional activity there and at Buckskin, which also is transported exclusively through our facilities, is consistent with their stated goal of doubling their production out of the Gulf by the end of 2028. Elsewhere across our connected fields, the expansion of BP's Atlantis facility, which I mentioned last quarter, came online in July.

A new development well at one of our legacy connected hubs is expected to be turned to production during the fourth quarter, and multiple well intervention and remediation projects are scheduled before year-end that, if successful, could add meaningfully to the volumes moving across our infrastructure. Stepping back from the individual fields for a moment and focusing rather on the macro, there are 16 deepwater drilling units currently active in the Gulf of America, and nine of them are working on leases contractually dedicated to flow through our existing pipelines, even though we move just a third of the current production out of the Gulf.

Our pipelines are in the sweet spot for future activity, especially the rapidly developing Deep Wilcox or high-pressure, high-temperature geologic play, and yet we believe there is a lot of runway left in the more mature Miocene play in the central Gulf. There is no doubt the deepwater Gulf is a world-class basin. Our infrastructure is in the right place at the right time and is already paid for. Producer interest remains robust. Interestingly, every single one of the new nine-square-mile blocks leased by the federal government in the central Gulf in its most recent sale sits within tieback range or within a 30 mi radius of an existing production facility connected exclusively to our existing pipelines.

The resource underneath and around our dedicated acreage, both discovered and yet to be found, is vast. The pace at which it gets developed will be set by our producer customers, not by us. But whenever those barrels are produced, they will move to shore through our pipelines under existing or new life-of-lease dedications and without the need for any growth capital from us. This is exactly what has supported our offshore business for the last three decades, and we will continue to support it for decades and decades to come.

Turning to marine, our marine transportation segment performed in line with our expectations during the quarter, despite the dry docking of one of our larger offshore units that began in the second quarter and extended further into the third quarter than originally planned. There are no dry dockings for offshore vessels expected for the rest of this year, so the fleet is back at full capacity in the fourth quarter. We're experiencing, in essence, 100% utilization of available capacity, and negotiated spot rates for all classes of vessels are extremely robust, which we believe will ultimately allow term contracts to follow higher.

Demand continues to be supported by strong Gulf Coast refinery runs, and in particular, we are beginning to see the impact of increased volumes of Venezuelan crude being run at Gulf Coast refineries and the derivative effect that heavy crude is having on demand to move intermediate refined products from one location to another along the Gulf Coast and connected inland waterways. Our fleet of inland heater barges is specifically designed to transport exactly these heavy intermediate refined products, and we are well-positioned to benefit as that demand continues to develop. On the supply side, nothing has changed.

There is essentially no net new construction of comp tonnage, and we see very little on the horizon that could significantly affect this tight supply and demand balance for marine tonnage. Our onshore transportation services segment once again performed ahead of our expectations. We continue to see strong volumes through our Texas City terminal and associated pipeline systems, as well as through Raceland and South Louisiana, supported by increasing volumes offshore moving onshore. In addition, certain of the opportunistic marketing opportunities that arose last quarter continued into the third quarter.

We believe that we could possibly benefit from such opportunities in 2027 and perhaps beyond, as some of the dislocations caused by the Iranian situation, the required reinjection of barrels previously withdrawn from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, as well as the resumption of significant crude imports from Venezuela, take years to fully return to historic norms. We are not building a business plan around it, nor are we budgeting for it in future periods, but we will capture such opportunities as they present themselves. Our legacy sulfur services business performed slightly below our expectations as operational issues at our largest host refinery reduced the supply of sour gas available for our sodium hydrosulfide, or NaHS, production.

Much of that seems to be behind us, and we are currently seeing higher operating rates as well as additional sulfur removal requirements as our two largest host refineries start running more sour crudes. We also remain in active dialogue with multiple parties to diversify our host refinery locations and restore our supply flexibility to historical levels. Looking ahead, we believe the market opportunity for NaHS will increase in future periods. In a post-COVID world, we lost market share in South America to low-cost flake NaHS coming out of China.

More and more of our historical copper mining customers are starting to realize the apparent short-term cost savings simply are not worth the operational headaches they have encountered from their trials of the inferior Chinese flake product. Taken together, we are hopeful we will be able to recapture a meaningful portion of the NaHS segment margin that we have lost in prior years, but that we know is there, given our historical level of activity and financial performance from this market-leading business. As we look towards the remainder of the year, we will likely be near or even possibly below the low end of our original guidance for adjusted EBITDA for the year.

Having said that, I would reiterate that coming in at or below the low end of 2026 guidance has little to do with the underlying fundamentals and the ultimate cash flow generating capabilities of our businesses, especially in our largest segment. In any event, we will remain disciplined and focused on what we can control. Stepping back and keeping everything important in focus, 2026 has indeed turned out to be a transformational year for Genesis, just as we anticipated.

Our businesses, while not without third-party operational challenges relative to our and our producer customers' expectations at the beginning of the year, have performed well enough to allow us to make meaningful progress on right-sizing our balance sheet and reducing the ongoing cash cost to run our business. This has been a very solid year under almost any objective metric, and we are proud to have delivered it. The operational side has simply taken a little longer than we and our producer customers had reasonably expected. We believe in the long-term value of our franchises, and we intend to execute the next phase of right-sizing our balance sheet and go after those additional cash savings available to us.

Rather than focusing on what could have been this year, our attention is squarely on executing that plan, and we believe it represents a compelling setup to continue creating value for everyone in the capital structure. Finally, I would like to say that the management team and the board of directors remain steadfast in our commitment to building long-term value for all our stakeholders, regardless of where you are in the capital structure. We believe the decisions we are making reflect this commitment and our confidence in Genesis moving forward. I would once again like to recognize our entire workforce for their individual efforts and unwavering commitment to safe, reliable, and responsible operations.

I am extremely proud to be associated with each and every one of you. With that, I will turn it back to the moderator for any questions.

#3098. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

#3093. Your Monitoring Stack Isn’t The Problem. The Detection-To-Ownership Gap Is

Judit Sharon is the founder and CEO of OnPage Corporation, an advanced, secure critical communication and collaboration platform provider.

​At 2:07 a.m., a monitoring platform detects that a customer-facing application is failing. It creates a ticket, sends an email and posts to an operations channel. At 2:19 a.m., no engineer has taken ownership of the incident.

The monitoring system did its job. The response process did not.

Detection-to-ownership time is the elapsed time between detecting a critical incident and a qualified responder acknowledging and accepting responsibility for it. Unlike mean time to detect (MTTD), detection-to-ownership time measures the human-response gap after monitoring has already identified the problem.

For CIOs, IT operations leaders and site reliability teams, those 12 minutes represent a distinct failure: The organization knew something was wrong, but no one was responsible for acting on it.

Alert delivery does not guarantee incident ownership because delivery confirms that a notification reached a destination, not that a qualified responder saw it, accepted responsibility or began acting on it.

An alert may reach a shared inbox nobody is watching. A Slack or Microsoft Teams notification can disappear into routine conversation. Email-to-text gateways provide another notification path, but they may still fail to get attention. An answering service can also delay ownership while it determines urgency and locates the on-call responder.

The mistake is assuming that, because a notification went out, the right responder has taken charge. To see where the handoff breaks down, distinguish five states:

• Detected: A system identified the problem.

• Delivered: The alert reached its intended destination.

• Read: The responder has seen the critical alert.

• Owned: A qualified responder has acknowledged the incident and accepted responsibility for the next action.

• Resolved: The issue was addressed, with the alert status synced back to the originating system where supported.

Delivery is not ownership. For a critical incident, “someone received it” is not enough; the team needs to know who read the alert and took ownership, when and what happened next.

An event should trigger an immediate page when it has meaningful business or customer impact, requires timely human intervention and the responder can act on it.

IT and digital operations teams need telemetry, warnings and diagnostic information, but not every event warrants immediate interruption. When routine conditions and genuine failures arrive with the same urgency, responders discount the signal and alert noise becomes alert fatigue.

Set stricter paging criteria. A customer-facing outage, a failed payment workflow or a major security event may require immediate response. A transient warning that clears without intervention may belong in a dashboard or ticket queue.

The distinction should depend on business impact, service criticality and whether the responder can take useful action. A page-worthy alert should clearly state what service is affected, what failed and where the responder should go next. It should also stand out, override silent mode when required and persist until someone responds.

On-call schedules and escalation policies reduce response time by automatically routing critical alerts to the person currently responsible and escalating when that responder does not acknowledge the incident within a defined period.

Static contact lists and manual routing can slow response when people change roles, take leave or rotate through on-call shifts. Schedule-based routing directs the alert to whoever is currently responsible. Round-robin routing can distribute incidents across several qualified responders while preserving individual ownership.

To keep critical pages meaningful, teams can use deduplication, suppression or brief delays for conditions likely to clear on their own. A workflow might begin with SMS, email or a phone call, followed by a persistent mobile page if no one responds. More urgent incidents may warrant immediate paging and automatic escalation.

Consider a database supporting a customer-facing application that becomes unavailable. Monitoring detects the failure and pages the assigned on-call engineer. If that engineer does not read the incident within the defined interval, the alert escalates to the next responder. The notification path continues until someone qualified assumes responsibility.

Automation does not make the technical decisions needed to resolve the incident. Engineers still diagnose and resolve the problem. Automation removes avoidable delay in getting the right person involved.

Slack and Microsoft Teams help coordinate incidents. A channel notification alone, however, does not establish who must respond.

Posting to a channel tells a group something happened. Paging assigns responsibility to a specific responder and creates an escalation path if that person doesn’t respond.

Integrations into on-call management and alerting workflows can reduce context switching by allowing teams to initiate a paging workflow from the Slack or Teams conversation where an incident is already being discussed.

Whether these practices work should be visible in the data. Detection-to-ownership time starts when the system identifies the incident and ends when a qualified person accepts responsibility. Teams can break that interval into delivery time, acknowledgment time and confirmed ownership.

Those measures reveal different problems. Fast delivery but slow acknowledgment may point to alert noise, alert fatigue or ineffective notification methods. Quick acknowledgment without clear ownership suggests unclear responsibilities. Frequent escalation may expose gaps in staffing or on-call coverage.

Testing matters, too. Test the workflow during shift changes, after hours and when the primary responder is unavailable. Test what happens when the first page goes unanswered.

Monitoring tells you what happened. An effective incident alert management process determines who needs to act, whether they received the alert, whether they responded and who owns the incident now.

If the organization already knows a critical service is failing but still cannot say who owns the response, faster monitoring will not close that gap.​

NorthWestern Energy Group, Inc. (NWE +0.02%) focused the third quarter on finalizing its merger with Black Hills Corporation while managing the financial integration of expanded ownership in the Colstrip generation facility. Management affirmed its standalone 2026 earnings guidance but cautioned that results are trending toward the lower end of the range due to unfavorable market power prices and mild weather patterns in the Pacific Northwest. The company is advancing a multiyear capital plan centered on regional transmission development and new natural gas generation in South Dakota to meet updated resource adequacy requirements. Strategic efforts also include the development of a large new load tariff in Montana to facilitate the integration of energy-intensive data center customers into the regulated rate base.

#3090. What Does a ‘Blue Wave’ Mean for Mortgage Rates?

Democrats won big in the midterms, but mortgage rates have bigger forces to reckon with.

Mortgage rates fell again this week, extending a gradual slide that began well before Election Day.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell 13 basis points to 7.05% APR in the week ending Nov. 5, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Homebuyers’ budgets are feeling the pinch from high mortgage rates, steep home prices and a shortage of listings. On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties promised to make homeownership more affordable. But solving that problem is like untangling 20 years’ worth of Christmas lights from your attic. Yank on one strand, and three more tighten.

“Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run and more housing supply plus a more dynamic labor market in the long run,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist for Realtor.com, said in an email.

A shift in political power won’t erase those challenges overnight. Here's what's driving mortgage rates right now — and where a Democratic Congress might have some pull.

How that affects mortgage rates: The relief of one less uncertainty is giving rates some breathing room.

Election results have cleared up one big unknown for investors. With Democrats controlling Congress and Republicans holding the White House, markets are bracing for the reality that any major spending bills could face roadblocks.

Political gridlock isn't always popular, but weirdly, investors sometimes welcome it. When a divided government limits new spending, the government may need to borrow less than expected — which could turn down the heat on mortgage rates.

But there’s a catch. That same gridlock could make it harder to pass laws to help bring down housing costs.

How that affects mortgage rates: Heavy borrowing from the government and tech companies adds upward pressure to the bond market, where mortgage rates take their cues.

When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows the difference by selling Treasury bonds. When there's lots of debt for sale, investors may demand higher returns, called yields. Mortgage rates tend to follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.

The new Congress still faces a mountain of government debt. What they choose to do about it can ripple through the economy to affect your monthly mortgage payment.

“Sound fiscal policy, rather than deficit-financed spending and standoffs over budgets and the debt limit, can help keep rates in check,” Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email.

Meanwhile, Big Tech companies are borrowing a boatload of money to build AI data centers. To get the cash, they issue corporate bonds, giving investors another place to put their money. More bonds flooding the market can push Treasury yields higher, taking mortgage rates along for the ride.

But how long can the AI building boom last? Voters across party lines pushed back against data centers in the midterms. Even if lawmakers pump the brakes on new construction, a slowdown in tech spending doesn't guarantee cheaper mortgages.

How that affects mortgage rates: Wartime disruptions to global oil supplies can fuel inflation, pushing borrowing costs higher.

The unpopular war in Iran likely added to the voter frustration that helped fuel Democrats' midterm victories. Higher energy costs can hit household budgets in multiple ways: at the pump, through pricier goods that need to be shipped, and through higher interest rates on loans (including mortgages) as inflation heats up.

“A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates,” Krimmel said.

A Democratic Congress could push for a different approach to ending the war, but it can't make Iran agree to a deal.

Meanwhile, stubborn inflation from the Iran war has raised the prospect of another Federal Reserve rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Futures traders now put the odds of a quarter-point increase at more than 80%, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but investors anticipate its decisions — so mortgage rates often move before the Fed does.

If buying a home makes sense for your budget now, there's little reason to wait just because Congress changed hands. Buyers can sometimes score lower prices in winter, when sellers are more willing to negotiate. But with today’s mortgage rates hovering above 7%, higher borrowing costs can eat into those savings, so it’s important to compare mortgage lenders to get the best rate.

For longer-term hope, look to the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law this summer. This legislation shows lawmakers can, in fact, work together to make meaningful progress on housing affordability.

“Even with divided government, lawmakers and the administration can build on that common ground to further boost housing production, preserve existing affordable homes, and help families struggling with high housing and utility costs,” Winkler said.

But new homes take time to build, and your house hunt doesn't have to follow Congress's calendar. Your homebuying budget and local market conditions matter more than the next political headline.
