#3088. ArcelorMittal (MT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Tariff quotas and Ukraine charges shaped a quarter of sharp EBITDA gains.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

ArcelorMittal S.A. (MT -3.31%) focused on the structural improvement of its earnings capacity through the implementation of enhanced European trade measures and strategic growth investments in key markets. Management reported that the new tariff rate quota framework has successfully reduced import penetration, allowing the company to restart all its European blast furnaces and strengthen its domestic order book. The company is navigating temporary headwinds from elevated energy costs in Europe and weather-related disruptions in its mining operations while maintaining its 2026 capital expenditure guidance. ArcelorMittal stated that its strategic projects in India, Brazil, and Liberia are progressing to support higher earnings and cash generation as they reach full capacity in 2027.

Daniel Fairclough: Good afternoon, everyone. This is Daniel Fairclough from the ArcelorMittal Investor Relations team. Thank you for joining this call to discuss ArcelorMittal's performance and progress in the third quarter of 2026. Leading today's call will be our CFO, Mr. Genuino Christino. Before we begin, I would like to mention a few housekeeping items. As usual, we will not be going through the results presentation, which was published this morning on our website. However, I do want to draw your attention to the disclaimers on slide 24 of that presentation. Following some opening remarks from Genuino, we will move directly to the Q&A session.

If you'd like to ask a question, then please do press star one on your keypad to join the queue. With that, I will hand the call over to Genuino.

Genuino Christino: Thanks, Daniel. Welcome, everyone, and thanks for joining today's call. As usual, I will keep my remarks brief. Let me begin with safety, which remains our highest priority. We are now approaching the end of the second year of our safety transformation. Through disciplined execution of our safety roadmaps, we are seeing more consistent performance across the group. This is encouraging, and we remain firmly focused on our ambition of achieving zero fatalities and zero serious injuries as quickly as possible. Turning now to the business, I would like to focus on three key points. First, our results continue to demonstrate the structural improvements in margins. Third quarter EBITDA was $2 billion, up 34% year-on-year.

EBITDA per ton increased to $155, which is $44 higher than a year ago and well above historical averages. This demonstrates that our portfolio optimization and strategic execution are delivering results, and I believe there is significantly more to come. Importantly, these results do not yet reflect the full benefit of the new European trade framework, which is restoring sustainability to the European steel industry. Given the length of our order book, the increases in steel prices flow through to earnings with a lag. In addition, around 25% of our European flat product volumes remain under annual contracts that have yet to reset. This brings me to my second point.

As imports normalize, customers are increasingly looking to domestic supply, and we are responding. The TRQ framework provides the opportunity for recently idled capacity to restart, restoring employment and providing direct benefits to the local and regional economy. During the quarter, imports of flat steel products were approximately 50% lower than a year ago. As expected, our European flat product shipments were higher in the third quarter against the second quarter, which is counter to the normal seasonal pattern. As inventories normalize, we expect more of this reduction in imports to translate into higher domestic shipments. Our order book continues to strengthen, and we expect shipments growth to accelerate in the fourth quarter and show a double-digit year-on-year improvement.

This momentum is expected to continue to build into 2027. As customers shift back towards domestic steel supply, we will see higher, more sustainable capacity utilization. With Dąbrowa, Asturias, and Fos back in operation, all of our European blast furnaces are now running, and we are well-placed to serve our customers reliably and efficiently. Higher utilization should support a return to healthy and sustainable levels of profitability and returns on capital across the industry. My third and final point is that ArcelorMittal is exceptionally well-positioned to deliver higher earnings, stronger returns on capital, and continued value creation for shareholders. An increasingly regionalized steel market provides a stronger foundation for sustainable profitability throughout the cycle.

I have already talked about the significantly improved outlook for our business in Europe. Our business in India continues to perform well. We are ramping up our higher added value capacity, and the year to September represented a new shipment record. In North America, we are seeing positive momentum across our franchise. Better import protections are a common theme, and lean inventories alongside growing demand from data centers, energy, infrastructure investment creates a positive outlook for 2027. Against this improved backdrop, ArcelorMittal is well-positioned to succeed. Our scale, our leadership positions in key markets, and our strong track record of product and process innovation will continue to set us apart from the competition.

We are proud of the entrepreneurial culture, which promotes accountability and a relentless focus on continuous improvement. A more supportive industry structure gives us an even greater opportunity to convert these advantages into higher earnings and stronger returns. Over the past four years, we have invested consistently in high-return strategic growth projects that are increasing our earnings capacity. Importantly, many of these projects have not yet reached their full potential, providing a further source of earnings growth as we move into 2027 and beyond. The value created through these investments is further enhanced by our buyback program. This has been a powerful driver of shareholder value.

Given the positive outlook for free cash flow this year and beyond, I expect this to continue. With that, Daniel, I believe we can start the Q&A.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thank you, Genuino. We have quite a long list of questions to get through, but we will start with a question from Alain at Morgan Stanley. Hi, Alain. Please go ahead.

Speaker 2: Hi. Thank you for taking my question. Hi. Two questions from my side. I will start with the first one, which is the usual one, if you do not mind discussing the profit bridge into Q4, and specifically around Europe, where we are seeing many moving parts, including shipment growth, spot prices moving higher, but also elevated or sticky energy costs. Perhaps the same question applies to the other divisions as well, so if you do not mind starting with the bridge. Thank you.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah, sure. Thank you, Genuino. Thanks, Alain. Looking at the major components, the building blocks, the major themes into the fourth quarter, I think it is clear from Genuino's comments and the release that we expect higher volumes in the fourth quarter. That is a common theme, but in particular, we would expect that from Europe, where we have guided to flat volumes being accelerating in the fourth quarter and increasing year-on-year at a double-digit rate. Second component would be generally higher steel prices across the segments. Brazil, perhaps a slight exception to that, just given mix effects, so that is probably going to be a little bit more stable quarter-to-quarter. The third bucket or theme would be higher costs.

You talk about that in your question, the way you posed it, but I think everybody can appreciate the evolving cost dynamics, particularly in Europe, as energy prices have continued to evolve through the quarter. We will have to see how energy prices continue over the next six weeks or so. It is difficult to be specific there on the guidance, but that will clearly be a theme. The last component would be mining. We have guided to a stronger quarter to end the year from our mining segment, given the continued progress at Liberia and our expectation that should be operating at capacity in the fourth quarter. It should be a good quarter from a shipment standpoint.

Then, it is difficult to be specific on the iron ore and freight factors, but I am sure you can accommodate that in your expectations as they become apparent. Then I think just my final comment would be on free cash flow. If you look at our release, if you look at the presentation, we are expecting a good free cash flow performance in the fourth quarter, and that will be in substantial part driven by an expected seasonal release of working capital.

Speaker 2: Thank you, Daniel. Thank you. My second question is, if we stay with Europe into 2027, you talked about the annual contract resets. Do you mind reminding us how many tons will be up for repricing on 1st of January and how quickly this will feed through your ASP? In Europe as well, in your presentation, you talk quite extensively about the benefits of the TRQ framework, which hasn't fully yet fed through your profit and margins. What do you expect to see as we head into early 2027 that will drive the margin upside for your European division? Thank you.

Genuino Christino: Okay. Thank you, Alain. Let me take your second question. First of all, I think it's important to say that TRQ, Q3, of course, was the first quarter in which we could see the benefits of the new framework. We are, of course, very happy with what we have seen. As we were guiding at the time of quarter two, we see higher shipments and flat despite the seasonality, and despite the fact that we were going through a destock during the quarter. It's really working as initially designed, which should then allow us to bring back the capacity that I also talked about at the beginning in my opening remarks.

We will really see the full benefits of the new framework, of course, in 2027, Alain. Also what it does, and we believe it should really be extremely helpful, it allows the industry now to pass on higher costs, right? We are seeing now, we were in a positive trend in terms of recovering our margins. Of course, we were hit by higher energy costs. We are in the process of recovering that. When I look at the pricing guidelines that we have already for January, I'm sure you have seen it's already significantly higher than what you see at the moment coming from index. That's all very positive. We're going to be working through the destocking.

Our expectation is that destocking should largely end in Q4. When I look at the business and the moving parts, I think we can be very optimistic for 2027.

Daniel Fairclough: Thanks, Genuino. Then just coming to your question on contracts, Alain. I think in our release in the presentation, you can see, and you already know it, that 25%, or approximately 25% of our flat volumes in Europe are annual contract. That is predominantly with the automotive customers, and the significant majority of those contracts follow the calendar year. So, a significant majority of that 25% of our flat volumes is set to reprice as we start 2027, which is another significant component of your positive bridge, I think, into the first quarter and for 2027 as a whole.

Speaker 2: Thank you. Thank you very much.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Alain. We will move now to take a question from Reinhardt at Bank of America. Hi, Reinhardt.

Reinhardt: Afternoon, Genuino and Daniel. Thank you very much for the time. Just want to ask about the European furnace restart so far. Can you give us an update on where exactly they are in their ramp-up process and when you think they are going to hit steady state production? I guess related to that, it would be good to get your thoughts on when you think there will be enough demand in Europe for you to actually start bringing some slabs in, perhaps.

Genuino Christino: Yeah, Reinhardt. Sure. First of all, we are bringing capacity as we see demand, right? I think that's number one, I would say. We are not bringing capacity unless, of course, we can see that in our order books. That's why we feel confident to bring back the capacity, because we are seeing order books strengthening. In terms of the ramp-ups, as you know, I mean, it's not easy to bring back capacity, especially when the furnaces have been idle for some time, which was clearly the case here. Poland, we are now up and running since the end of September. We have basically completed the ramp-up. The furnace is running well.

Fos, we are still going through the ramp-up phase. Not yet where we want it to be, but progressing there. In Spain, we are up and running. Two out of three furnaces are running well, and Fos is still in the process of ramp-up.

Reinhardt: Got it. That's clear. A comment on slabs, if you can?

Genuino Christino: Sorry, what was your question on the slabs, Reinhardt?

Reinhardt: When you expect demand to be sufficient in Europe for it to make sense for you to bring in slabs into the continent?

Genuino Christino: Well, I mean, look, I mean, this is something that, of course, remains a possibility for us. Our focus right now, Reinhardt, is to ramp up our capacity domestically, right? So that we can utilize our existing furnaces and tools that we have here. But of course, we have that flexibility. We know already what is the potential for higher volumes next year, just because of the TRQ and low imports that we expect to materialize. We're going to see the full benefits in 2027, right? But of course, we believe that we will have the capacity domestically to take care of that. But as a group, we have optionality, we have flexibility.

Reinhardt: That's very clear. Thank you. Maybe just one more question on developments into Q4. So, I mean, you've previously called out that some of this new capacity does have higher carbon costs associated with it. So, as you're building volumes into the fourth quarter, how should we think about improved fixed cost absorption and EBITDA per ton from that volume increase?

Genuino Christino: Yeah. Our message is the same, Reinhardt. Yes, as we bring back capacity, there will be more CO2 costs. But fixed costs, we shouldn't be really adding much in terms of fixed costs. So, profitability of this volume should be at least as par with the existing business, if not a little bit better.

Reinhardt: Very clear. Thank you very much, Genuino and Daniel.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Reinhardt. We'll move now to take a question from Tristan at BNP Paribas. Hi, Tristan. How are you?

Tristan: Yes. Hi. Thank you for taking my questions. I have two. First one is on Europe. One of your peer said that the shutdown of Ilva would be a game changer for the market. Do you share that view? Do you see a scenario where Southern European prices would trade at a premium to Northern prices? Does that mean ultimately that it could be upside risk to the market share gains you initially contemplated? That would be my first question.

Genuino Christino: Yeah, Tristan. Look, I mean, we all know in which levels ADI was running at, right? We all know. It was not running at very high levels. As a company, we feel we are in a good position here to service that market. As you know, we started Fos, the second furnace in Fos in the south, and we started also our furnace in Spain. It places us in a very good position to supply the market in south. Where prices finally settle in south, I mean, historically, as we know, south has always traded prices were always at a discount to north because of the more exposed to imports, which, as we know now, is being corrected by TRQ.

We'll see where prices finally settle. I wouldn't expect that to trade at a significant premium, but it will depend on trade and other aspects. But again, I think for us, it's a good opportunity to service that market from our facilities in the south.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah. To round up that comment, I think as we look out there, I wouldn't say Ilva is going to have a significant impact. Just reinforcing Genuino's comment that they've been operating at very, very low levels. So the fact, if they drop down a little bit further, I don't think it's really going to change that supply-demand balance notably. So I wouldn't expect any significant or material impact on the market.

Tristan: All right. That's very clear. My second question is on North America. Could you discuss a little bit the strike impact in Canada and also what happened in Mexico? Is there anything structural at play, given it's been a couple quarters with some hiccups? How much of those, I mean, if you could quantify those one-offs and how much you expect to get back into Q4, that'd be great. Thank you.

Genuino Christino: Sure, Tristan. We had two events in North America. One was the strike in our longs division in Canada. That has been addressed. The facilities have been running since beginning of the quarter, so there shouldn't be any further impact from the strike. Back to normal levels. In Mexico, we had reliability issues with our DRI facility, which has also been resolved, addressed. I would expect us to be running at a normal capacity in quarter four, Tristan.

Tristan: And the negative impact, could you quantify it?

Genuino Christino: We are talking about in Q3, I mean, the losses, I would say in the range of 150kt.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Tristan. We'll move now to take a question from Ephrem at Citi. Hi, Ephrem. Please go ahead.

Ephrem: Thanks, Daniel. Two questions. I'll just take them in turn. First, I'm just trying to gauge how conservative your guidance for double-digit year-on-year growth in flat products, volume shipments in Europe is for Q4. Very rough math. I mean, you did about 6.5 million tons in total last year in Europe. 70% assume that is flat. A 10% implies somewhere around a 450,000 tons increase year on year for Q4 2026. If imports are coming down by 2.5 million-3 million tons per quarter, and you maintain your market share of about 30%, I mean, you should be expecting about 700,000 to 800,000 or 900,000 tons increase.

It's almost a 20% increase in shipments, unless volumes have gone down or you're losing market share. Would that be a right math, or please point me where I'm wrong on terms of the amount of volume increase in flats you could expect?

Genuino Christino: Well, I think you've got all the moving parts right. I think the only one that I would also point to you, as we discussed before as well, is we are still going through what we believe is the destock in Europe, which, as I said, should normalize now during the quarter in Q4, which then should, of course, help us as we start 2027. I think that's the only missing piece that I would point to you. Daniel, anything else here you want to highlight?

Daniel Fairclough: No, Genuino. Yeah, it's a good question, Ephrem, and thanks for putting it forward, because as Genuino says, you're picking up the moving parts there. Because inventories are really providing a cushion over the second half period as we transition into this new mechanism. We saw the reduction in imports in Q3. We're going to see, or we expect to see that similar reduction in imports in Q4. But because inventories are being consumed through that period, it's not fully translating yet into our shipments, into our volumes.

But as soon as those inventories are consumed, as soon as they're at normal levels, and as Genuino said in an earlier response, we expect that by the end of the year, then all of that will be translating into our shipments and our production. We're ready for that. We're primed for that. We're going to see progress and evidence of it in Q4, but that then, that momentum is going to continue. It's going to provide a good foundation for the bridge into Q1 and 2027 as a whole as well.

Ephrem: Thank you. Sorry, my second question is on India and Hazira. Obviously, now you're saying ramp up in, or start in 2027, which was obviously flagged a little bit earlier. But should we kind of realistically expect any shipments from the incremental, any new capacity in 2027, or is it really a 2028 story in terms of more volumes? Could you kind of give us a sense as to where we are in the completion of construction process and ramp-up process in terms of the incremental 6 million capacity there?

Genuino Christino: Yeah, sure. I can maybe comment on that. As you know, we have already commissioned the downstream, so the new cold mill, automotive lines for the finishing. We are testing now the new coke oven batteries. We are making good progress with now with the upstream, the furnaces. We do expect to see already in 2027 higher volumes coming from the project. Our expectation is that in the first half of 2027, we will start to see already some action there. We will, of course, provide you guys with some more guidance on that as part of our Q4 results. But we should definitely see already some improvements in 2027, especially in the second half.

Daniel Fairclough: Thanks, Ephrem. We are going to move now to take a question from Timna at Wells Fargo. Hi, Timna.

Timna: Yeah. Hey, good afternoon. I wanted to switch gears to the Americas, if I could, and beginning with Brazil. The investments you are making there are pretty notable. How do you get comfortable with the outlook there given smaller trade protections, the recent election, and at least one of your other competitors there was sounding a bit more cautious than you are? If you could elaborate on the Brazil strategy, please.

Genuino Christino: Daniel, to be honest, I could not hear well the question. Have you heard it?

Daniel Fairclough: Yes, I have. Perhaps I can start, Genuino, and I am sure you will complement. But it was basically, Timna was asking around the outlook for Brazil given the election results, what our plans are for investments there. Would we reconsider them given the election outcome, given the relative lack of trade protection, and noting that one of the competitors, I think, on the long side of things was giving a more somber outlook for the market.

Genuino Christino: Yeah. Okay. No, thank you. Great. Look, I mean, I think we have to differentiate now between longs and flat in Brazil. I mean, when we look at the flat business, we do believe that at least for steel, I mean, we have already good levels of trade protection. We have recently anti-dumping on cold roll, galvanized, painted, which is of course a significant part of what we produce locally. We have seen imports coming down to normal levels. They were quite high in 2025, coming down now to more normalized levels. We have more to come. We have anti-dumping now also coming on HRC against China.

We feel that the government has taken steps to support the business on the flat side. In longs, we also have some protection, maybe not as much as we would like to see, and we continue to engage with the government. And where you see us investing right now in Brazil is in the flat side of the business, with more downstream, which is because it is short. It is important exactly there. So, and we feel that it will make a lot of sense for us to convert exports into more domestic volumes. And that is exactly what we are trying to do.

Timna: Okay, thanks. Sorry if it was not clear. I was referring to a flat roll producer, but your results in Brazil were quite strong, so maybe a different perspective. Switching gears, if I could, to the North America market. You also have some repricing, I would assume there, so would like to hear on the repricing and the perhaps benefit from any lower CRU discounts we have been hearing about. And then on the Calvert performance, been hearing some challenges maybe on the ramp-up there. What could that look like when fully optimized, I guess?

Genuino Christino: Yeah. We continue to make progress with the ramp-up in Calvert, Timna. I mean, of course, to be honest, it's moving a little bit slower than what we were expecting. But our expectation is to exit the year at a very good run rate. As you know, I mean, with this furnace, we expect to produce very demanding high steel for many applications, exposed, automotives. But it's progressing. It should provide good support for 2027 because, of course, each ton that we can produce locally, it's one ton of slab that we're not going to need to pay tariffs. So that should really support the business and profitability in North America in 2027.

I'm sorry, your line for me at least is not great. I think the first part of the question was linked to auto contracts, when it resets. Daniel, was?

Daniel Fairclough: Just to pricing dynamics and whether[crosstalk].

Genuino Christino: So pricing dynamics, yeah.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah, and discounts to index, et cetera, whether that's evolving.

Genuino Christino: Yeah. Look, I mean, as we know, prices in North America, they are strong. The supply-demand is strong. We are seeing tightness in the market. What is also very positive for us specifically is the fact that we are also seeing similar dynamics in Canada and in Mexico as well. We should not forget that we are a North American operations business, which, at the beginning of the year, we were seeing larger discounts in Canada and in Mexico to CRU, and now we are kind of back to the normal levels of normal parity that we were used to see before the new Section 232 and tariffs against Canada and Mexico. Daniel, please?

Genuino Christino: Yeah, go ahead, Timna.

Timna: Oh, I was going to say, if I could sneak one last in, of course, on Dofasco. Any thoughts on a potential benefit from carve-out or any insights you might have there on the trade negotiations?

Genuino Christino: Yeah, I think we are going to need to wait and see what finally what is agreed. I cannot really comment much on that. We will have to wait for the final outcome of the negotiations. What I can say, though, is that we are doing well in Canada. Our business is doing well. I mean, we adapted as much as we could, of course, supported also by trade measures from the Canadian government. We see lower levels of imports, as I said, supporting then prices and demand for our facilities. Yeah, we are doing well. Given where prices are right now, we give us also a good level of confidence that 2027, again, should be significantly better.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Timna. We will take the next question from Boris, Kepler Cheuvreux. Hi, Boris. Please go ahead.

Speaker 7: Hi. Thank you for taking my question. I have two ones. The first, let's stay in the U.S., but now that the Trump administration has been defeated in the midterms, do you see a potential impact on Section 232 tariffs, or do you believe things will stay exactly the same? That is the first question. The second, on slide 22, you mentioned the increasingly supportive regulation in Europe for the industry. What is the main support you see among those measures that would come on top of the TRQ, and when do you expect them to have their first impact? Thank you.

Genuino Christino: Daniel, do you want to take that one?

Daniel Fairclough: Yes. Thanks, Genuino. Thanks, Boris, for picking this one out from the appendix. It is an important slide, and what we're showing on slide 22 is that the trade and policy environment in Europe does continue to evolve. We're all very pleased to be seeing the impact of CBAM from the beginning of the year. We've talked a lot about the new tariff rate quota mechanism kicking in 1st of July and starting to see the effects of this building as we're moving through the second half of the year. We do believe there's more to come. The policy is evolving. It's now moving downstream. I think CBAM and the TRQ is going to be important there.

In terms of CBAM moving downstream to capture sensitive goods, that's going to be very important, and that's something that we're expecting. We're expecting to hear that relatively soon, what the outcome of the trilogue discussions there. Maybe end of this year, early next year, we should see some news on that. I think moving downstream, capturing the derivative products, that's very, very important. Then in terms of the evolution of the tariff rate quota tool, we've had a question earlier around slab.

Slab imports on a near-term basis, not necessarily something to be concerned about, but on a medium-term basis, that is certainly something that we would be concerned about, the scenario where primary steel-making capacity in Europe gets replaced by imported slab. That's clearly very counter to the intentions of the tariff rate quota. The intentions of the tariff rate quota mechanism are to restore the industry to health, to bring idle capacity back into operation, to have all of the jobs and local economy support that then will sustain. Slabs, on a medium-term basis, could put that at risk.

It's very natural that the tariff rate quota should also capture those slabs, and that's something that we're expecting to hear about at the next opportunity, which would be actually the middle of next year, the review then. Hopefully that's clear.

Genuino Christino: Yeah. So maybe let it there. I think there was also a question on Section 232 in the U.S., so let me take this one, Boris. So maybe a few comments from us. I believe we have to acknowledge, right, that Section 232 has been a very effective policy addressing the impacts of global excess capacity and unfair trade, and we believe that it remains pretty much the direction of travel, not only in U.S., but in all core markets, in all core markets. I mean, steel is strategic, it is vital to resilient domestic supply chains, and needs appropriate protection, we believe.

We have seen U.S. policy work well in reducing imports from what investments we have seen, of course, a number of investments in place. We know that Section 232 was also supported by the Democrats before, and our expectation is that Section 232 will remain. We will, of course, see, but our expectation is that it remains.

Daniel Fairclough: Super. Thanks, Boris. We will move now to take a question from Max at ODDO. Hi, Max.

Max: Yeah. Good afternoon, Ben. First question is on Europe, and really zooming in on the long product segment. It seems to be considerably weighing on your operations there. It's working on EAF, so I guess it's very much concerned by the higher electricity costs. It doesn't seem to be as impacted by a TRQ system as the flat products. Construction is the main end market, so also there depressed. Do you see some prospects for this business to earn its cost of capital? If not, what is the future of this business within ArcelorMittal?

Genuino Christino: Yeah, sure, Max. Let me take this one. First of all, we like our long business. It's a franchise business, and we have high-quality products that are very important. Just an example, rails, heavy beams that we are exporting to different parts of the world at very good levels of price. It's, as you know, over the years, we have disposed parts of the business that we felt we would not be competitive, the pure commodity business. The business that we retain is a high-quality business. What you see really in Q3, and I think the dynamics that we are seeing are very much similar to what we talked about for flat.

We saw also in quarter three for longs a significant reduction of imports, but at the same time, that was offset by the destocking that we also talked about in the case of flat. That should also normalize, right? The same dynamics in terms of prices moving up to cover for the high energy costs is happening. I would expect the same dynamics that we talked about to impact our long business as well.

Max: Okay. Yeah. The second and last question is on Ukraine. Can you perhaps quantify the residual cost associated with these operations? Not that they were run under cold idle format. More generally, production has come to a halt in Ukraine. All other facilities have also stopped. Do you see any impact on the European market? Also perhaps on the world iron ore market, given that Ukraine was a significant producer?

Genuino Christino: Yeah. This is all, of course, we're very sad with the developments in Ukraine. I mean, as we speak, we are in the process, so we are idling the facility. As we have guided, going forward, from a cash flow point of view, our expectation is that it will be very limited needs to supply cash. We're going to be liquidating, of course, the existing inventories that we have, so that we will take care of the needs of the facility for an extended period of time. After that, our expectation is that we are talking about a minimal amount just to keep the security of the site.

It should be a low number just to keep the optionality here for the future.

Max: Okay. In terms of wider impact on the European market, is positive or negative?

Genuino Christino: I don't think. Look, as we know, the capacity in Ukraine was already significantly impacted, right? They have also quota. I wouldn't expect, to be honest, to see a significant impact in European market because of. We were, ourselves, we were not really exporting into Europe. I don't expect any significant impact.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Okay, thanks, Max. We'll take the next question from Andy at UBS. Hi, Andy.

Andy: Hi, Daniel. Thanks, Genuino. I just want to ask about the demand [audio distortion] support factors in your outlook with regards to the Oh, hello? Can you hear me?

Daniel Fairclough: You're breaking up quite a bit there, actually, Andy. Can you start your question again?

Andy: Cool. I just want to ask about the demand situation. What are you seeing in terms of your end markets, in terms of demand evolution after the summer lull? Has demand recovered as you would have expected? Has it been softer? Any impact from the, obviously, the higher interest rate environment and energy costs? Are you seeing that in your order book, or are we making too much of that given the headlines we see?

Genuino Christino: Andy, the real demand in Europe of what we see is relatively stable. To be honest, I don't see change to what we were seeing before. What is clear, what the dynamics that we see, so real demand relatively flat. We see automotive resilient. What we are seeing really is the destock, right, that we talked about. That, of course, had an impact on the apparent steel consumption in Europe in quarter three. It should continue to be the case in Q4, not to the same extent, less. After that, our expectation is that it normalize, inventory normalize, which again leave us in a good place to start 2027.

As we know, I mean, I'm sure you have seen PMIs in Europe at expansionary levels. Clearly, the energy story doesn't help, right? But so far, I cannot really say that it has had a significant impact in the order book. Order book size strong. We are fully booked for quarter four. We're taking orders now really for next year.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah. Just to make sure, Andy, you're appropriately noting the specific comments that we've given this quarter and also for the fourth quarter that we did see counter seasonal progress in Q3. There's good potential beyond that as the inventories normalize, and then all of that reduction in imports will be seen in our production and shipments.

Andy: That's clear. Just on, I guess, a follow-up to Ephrem's question. I mean, if you take Fos plus Poland and the Spanish blast furnace, I mean, between all of those, it should probably be about 5 million tons of pig iron or more. Genuino Christino: Well, I think, Andy, we all know the math, right? We talked about what we expect in terms of decline in imports. That number is not changing, right? I think what is to be seen is how the real demand in 2027, right? To the extent that we are destocking now, I mean, you could also imagine that at some point in 2027, we may also see some restocking, right? Then we will have to see and wait. We are not yet providing guidance in terms of apparent consumption for 2027, but if you just look at the World Steel Association, they came out with their forecast.

Daniel Fairclough: Thanks, Andy. We will move now to take a question from Bastian at Deutsche Bank. Hi, Bastian.

Bastian: Yeah, thanks, Dan. All of my questions have been answered.

Daniel Fairclough: No problem. Thanks, Bastian. We will move now to take a question from Cole at Jefferies. Hi, Cole.

Cole: Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. Just some clarifications on this side. Genuino Christino: Yeah. So maybe first on segment Others, Cole. Typically, what we guide for segment Others is an expense of about $200 million for the year, right? So about $50 million a quarter. This quarter in particular, it's positive, slightly positive, because we have a significant release of intercompany profits. And also an improvement in the results in South Africa, right? So that's why it's positive this quarter, slightly positive.

But everything being normal, it should be about $50 million or so negative. In North America, specifically for Calvert, as you know, our contract with Cliffs has already expired, so we have replaced that proportionally with another contract with US Steel that is in place and will continue to be in place for some more years. Then the opportunity for us there, as I said at the beginning, is the ramp-up of the electric arc furnace so that we can reduce the amount of the slabs that we import. And that's the focus. That's what everybody's trying to achieve, to get the furnace up and running as per nameplate capacity as soon as possible.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Cole. I think we are going to take a question now from Matt at Goldman Sachs. Hi, Matt.

Our expectation is for shipments to be flat. Coming now to the two other questions.

Working capital, I mean, as we have been guiding, we do expect the large majority of the investment up to now to reverse, following normal seasonality of our working capital. That, of course, will provide strong support to free cash flow generation. We will allow the debt to come down. When it comes to capital allocation, we will continue to apply the policy. What I would say, though, is that based on everything that we just talked about, the good prospects for the business going forward in 2027, we believe that there is, of course, it's an opportunity for us to perhaps deploy more than the 50% that the policy would call for, right?

It is something that we will definitely be discussing very seriously.

Dom: Is that something that you can do outside of Well, do you need an EGM approval to do that type of distribution, or could you do it within your existing authorization?

Genuino Christino: Yeah, we have the authorizations, enough authorizations to do it. As always, when we have the AGMs in May, to the extent that we need, we will get extra approval. But so far, we have enough in our authorization to We have plenty of flexibility.

Daniel Fairclough: Thanks, Dominic. We do have maybe one more minute to take a follow-up question from Tristan at BNP Paribas, and then I am going to hand back to you, Genuino, for closing remarks. Tristan, last question.

Tristan: Yeah, thank you. Just a quick one on Liberia. If we can calibrate a bit better the volume uptick in Q4, if you can tell us how much volume you shipped in the nine months from Liberia, and any comment on the cost outlook, if you think it is going to be relatively steady or on course.

Genuino Christino: Yeah. Up to now, nine months, we shipped about 10.5 million tons. As you know, we are guiding now for 16. What I would say is important here just to keep in mind is that in Q4, our expectation is to be, for the first quarter, to be able to run at capacity, right? As you know, it is a 20 million tons project. We are ramping up the concentrator lines. We are going to be We see already the capacity in rail and at port to get to the 20 million in 2027, which is good.

We are also taking steps to prevent issues as we face in quarter three in future, by basically covering the stockyards at the port so that we can continue to ship even under more severe rain conditions. This is also something that we have been doing. Of course, there is still room as we ramp up the project lines to not only improve the mix. We will have a richer product. As we increase capacity also, then costs should come down. It again places well for next year.

Tristan: All right. That is clear. Maybe if I squeeze one little more. Just on the two projects you plan to confirm in Q4 in Brazil, the strategic growth project. Is that still going to be within the CapEx framework you discussed now for a number of years, $4.5 billion-$5 billion, or could that change a bit, the CapEx framework?

Genuino Christino: Yeah. Thank you for that. Look, I mean, as you know, the project in Tubarão, the cold rolling mill and coated, it is a project that has been approved. It is been executed as we speak. Orders are being placed, so that one is progressing. It is not yet part of the $1.8 billion in terms of EBITDA that we expect to get from the projects. We will be updating that in Q4 together with our guidance for CapEx. At this point, I can tell you that the $4.5 billion-$5 billion remains a good reference for the CapEx envelope for the group going forward.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah. Perhaps, Genuino, I can just add a couple of points to your response. Because I think you're saying there, no change to our CapEx spending, our rate of spend still in that $4.5 billion-$5 billion range. I think we've spoken on this call about the positive outlook for EBITDA in 2027 and various elements that we can look forward to in that bridge. If the other components of the cash flow statement are not changing, that does bode well for free cash flow in 2027. Going back to the previous question around capital allocation, what are we going to do with that cash?

Using that for our share buybacks, given our positive outlook for the business, our view on our share price, with buying back more stock with that free cash flow going beyond the minimum 50% would seem very appropriate.

Daniel Fairclough: I think that's our last question, or certainly the last we have time for, Genuino, I'm going to hand back to you for any closing remarks.

Genuino Christino: Thank you, everyone. Before we close, let me briefly reflect on the key message from today's discussion. First, our third quarter results again demonstrate the improved earnings power of the business. Margins remain well above historical levels, and importantly, the full benefits of the new European trade framework are still to come through. Second, we have evidence that the new TRQ mechanism is working as intended. Imports are materially lower, our shipments are increasing, and momentum is building as inventories normalize. Third, ArcelorMittal is exceptionally well-positioned as we move into 2027. We have positive momentum across our business.

On top of the improving market backdrop, our strategic growth investments provide a further source of earnings growth as projects continue to ramp up. I leave you with the final message. I'm even more optimistic about the outlook for our business than I was three months ago. We have a strong portfolio, improving market conditions in our key regions, meaningful embedded growth, and a disciplined capital allocation framework. Together, I am confident in our ability to deliver high earnings, stronger returns on capital, and continued value creation for our shareholders. With that, I will close today's call, and if you have any follow-up questions, please reach out to Daniel and his team. Thank you again for joining us.

#3086. Open-Source Dependencies: 19 Trust Signals Worth Checking

Open-source libraries power much of today’s software, allowing developers to build on existing code rather than start from scratch. But every dependency a team adds also brings potential risks tied to its maintainers, the software it relies on, and how security issues are handled. Popularity and download counts can create a false sense of safety, and even a widely used package may be neglected or slow to receive security fixes.

Knowing what to look for before adding or retaining a dependency can mean the difference between a solid foundation and an inherited liability. Here, members of Forbes Technology Council share the trust signals teams should evaluate when choosing open-source dependencies or reviewing those already in use.

Check the transitive dependency footprint. A tiny package that pulls in dozens of libraries, install scripts or native binaries expands your attack surface far beyond the code you chose. Trust is not only about the package itself; it is about the chain of code and maintainers you inherit with it. Prefer the smallest dependency graph that solves the problem. - Alexandro Picolini, COMM

I’d evaluate how safely the project development is going. A reliable dependency should have planned releases, proper migration procedures and no surprises with breaking changes. While security is very important, stability is equally vital. When every update is an engineering challenge, the dependency will silently turn into tech debt despite its popularity. - Ajay Pandey

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

One critical trust signal is verifiable software provenance. Teams should know who maintains a dependency, how releases are built and signed, and whether artifacts can be traced to trusted source code. Popularity and download counts are not security guarantees. Provenance verification, combined with continuous vulnerability monitoring, strengthens software supply chain resilience. - Sai Krishna Manohar Cheemakurthi, U.S. Bank

First, run it through OpenSSF Scorecard. It’s a useful, free and automated check of practices that covers branch protection, code review, pinned dependencies and signed releases. A low score isn’t automatically disqualifying, but it can tell you what risk you’re inheriting and give every team the same repeatable bar instead of a gut feel based on GitHub stars. It’s one tool you can use to evaluate and get consistent results for open-source software. - Dan Sorensen, Nexus Security Advisors

Check when the maintainer last responded to a reported vulnerability, not when they last pushed code. Commit frequency tells you the project is alive. Response behavior tells you whether someone is actually watching the door. A repository with 10,000 stars and an 18-month-old unresolved security issue is not a dependency—it is a liability with good documentation. - Mukul Arora, Persistent Systems Limited

Examine who gets to become a maintainer. Attackers have learned it is easier to earn a tired maintainer’s trust over months than to find a flaw in the code. Check whether new maintainers are vetted by more than one person and whether handoffs happen in public. A project’s process for trusting people matters as much as its code. - Flavius Plesu, OutThink

One trust signal I’ve observed is how maintainers respond to reported security issues. It’s critical to look for clear updates and evidence that they fix problems rather than relying on download counts. A popular dependency can still leave your team waiting for a fix. - Mark Vena, SmartTech Research

The most useful trust signal is the patch track record. With AI now finding vulnerabilities in open source faster than ever, the question is no longer whether a flaw will be found but how quickly it can be fixed once it is found. Teams should look at the dependency’s current vulnerability history and update cadence and determine whether maintainers respond rapidly to security issues. A modern software project that is popular but patches slowly should be avoided in the AI era. - Anuj Goel, Cyware

Check who is actually maintaining it. A popular library with millions of downloads can still rest on one unpaid volunteer who hasn’t merged a fix in a year. Look at recent commit activity, how quickly security issues get patched, and how many active maintainers there are. Download counts measure popularity, not durability, and you’re inheriting the support risk. - Steven Singer, Arbill

Open source runs on shared ingenuity. Give that ingenuity a security check: look for a current assessment of the exact package version you’ll deploy, inspecting its contents for malware, tampering and suspicious behavior alongside known vulnerabilities. Check each update and reassess existing dependencies as threats emerge. Trust the community, and give it the backup it deserves. - Mario Vuksan, ReversingLabs

Look at support and usage. Open source is great in terms of lesser cost and general support, but with general support, there is more risk. An open-source project can have security flaws or problematic issues that are not easily spotted by even the most advanced professionals. Look for something that serves one purpose and has been proven before by use in other high-profile projects or companies. Then go for it—with contingencies in place. - WaiJe Coler, InfoTracer

A useful signal is whether another party can rebuild the published release from the tagged source and get the same artifact. Signed provenance says who claims to have built it; reproducibility lets an independent team check that claim without trusting the maintainer’s pipeline. Before adoption, try this on one release and see whether the project documents the toolchain, inputs and steps needed to repeat the build. This makes artifact integrity independently testable. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech

A trustworthy project actively updates its own upstream dependencies, maintains clear semantic versioning, and demonstrates steady commit velocity. If a library has millions of downloads but hasn’t shipped a patch or addressed security pull requests in six months, its technical debt becomes yours the moment you import it. - Japjeev Kohli, Transurban

Look for active community adoption and scrutiny. Widely used, actively maintained packages benefit from more people reviewing, testing and finding problems. I would also avoid automatically adopting a new release on day one. Give the community time to validate it before bringing it into a critical environment. - Alex Spokoiny, Check Point Software

Ask who chose it. More dependencies now arrive because a model suggested them, not because an engineer compared options. At Google, adding a dependency meant someone had to argue for it and own it afterward. That argument is the trust signal. If nobody on the team can say why this package is better than the alternatives, you have not evaluated a dependency. You have accepted a recommendation. - Prashant Jalan, Guickly

I’d look at whether the project has an active, healthy maintainer community. Not all open-source projects are resilient. A dependency can be technically excellent yet still introduce risk if it’s maintained by only one or two individuals, receives infrequent updates, or lacks clear governance. Healthy open-source projects tend to show consistent releases, responsive issue management, transparent security practices and a diverse contributor base. - Ciaran Cosgrave, Nearform

Read the license on the model weights, not only on the code. Teams now pull open-weight AI models into products the way they pull in libraries, and some of those licenses ban commercial use, cap the number of users, or restrict whole categories of use. The code around a model can carry an MIT license, while the weights you ship come with different terms. - Jerry Tang, Atlas Cloud

One key trust signal is whether an open-source dependency creates accurate and consistent results. Libraries used in calculations, data conversion or scientific computing can cause errors that affect major decisions. Test key functions against trusted reference results and check for rounding errors or erratic outputs. A package may meet security standards but still produce wrong results. Trust must include functional accuracy, not just security and maintenance. - Salice Thomas, Wipro Limited

Essentially, I look for good governance signals. How large and spread out is the group of top maintainers—the more coherent, the better—and what’s their relationship with the project? How fast do they fix issues, especially security issues? Are security tests embedded in the build and release pipelines? Are there external security validations like OpenSSF? Regarding general health, how many stars and how many forks? What’s the recent commit and release cadence? - Julien Vantyghem, Quintess AI

#3085. Marriott Bonvoy Boundless vs. Bevy: Which One Comes Out On Top?

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

» Learn more: Hilton versus Marriott — Which one is right for you?

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

» Learn more: Marriott elite status: what you need to know

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, please visit American Express' rates and fees page.
