#3084. Strategic Education (STRA) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Visa curbs in Australia triggered a $134.1 million impairment charge.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Strategic Education, Inc. (STRA -21.33%) reported third quarter results characterized by growth in its Education Technology Services and U.S. healthcare portfolios, offset by regulatory challenges in its Australian segment. Management announced a plan to increase growth investments by $50 million in 2027 to accelerate product development in high-demand areas. The company recorded a $134.1 million non-cash impairment in the Australia/New Zealand segment as international student visa restrictions proved more severe than expected. Despite these headwinds, the company maintained a debt-free balance sheet and reported that productivity savings would limit operating expense growth to 2% in the coming year.

Operator: Welcome to Strategic Education's Third Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call. I will now turn the call over to Terese Wilke, Senior Director of Investor Relations for Strategic Education. Mrs. Wilke, please go ahead.

Terese Wilke: Thank you. Hello, everyone, and welcome to Strategic Education's conference call, in which we will discuss Third Quarter 2026 results. With us today are Karl McDonnell, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Daniel Jackson, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. Following today's remarks, we will open the call for questions. Please note that this call may include forward-looking statements made pursuant to the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. The statements are based on current expectations and are subject to a number of assumptions, uncertainties, and risks that Strategic Education has identified in today's press release that could cause actual results to differ materially.

Further information about these and other relevant uncertainties may be found in Strategic Education's most recent annual report on Form 10-K, the 10-Q to be filed, and other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, as well as Strategic Education's future eight-Ks, 10-Qs, and 10-Ks. Copies of these filings and the full press release are available for viewing on our website at strategiceducation.com. Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Karl. Karl, please go ahead.

Karl McDonnell: Thank you, Terese, and good morning, everyone. Our third quarter results reflect continued strength in the parts of SEI where we have been investing for growth: Education Technology Services, our broad employer strategy, and our U.S. healthcare portfolio. The strength in these areas, however, was mostly offset in the third quarter by our Australia segment, where the environment has proved more challenging than we expected. This morning, I'll briefly review the quarter, then I'll walk through each of our segments. As I do, I'll discuss the opportunities behind our intent to make 2027 a year of increased growth investments.

As always, unless I note otherwise, my comments refer to adjusted results on a constant currency basis, and those results exclude the $134 million non-cash impairment of goodwill and intangible assets in Australia that we recorded this quarter, and which I will discuss with that segment. Third quarter revenue was $320 million, essentially flat with the prior year. We did hold operating expense growth to less than 1%, resulting in operating income of $50 million, a 2% decrease, and an operating margin of 15.7%, 30 basis points below the prior year. Earnings per share increased 4% to $1.69, reflecting a lower share count from share repurchases.

Given the strong demand across ETS, and given our desire to accelerate our product roadmap to serve that demand, our intent is to increase our growth investments in ETS in 2027. These investments will slightly reduce the ETS segment-level operating margin next year, but will also result in higher revenue growth in our current five-year plan, defend Sophia's market leadership position, and strengthen Workforce Edge's ability to sign new corporate clients. Turning now to U.S. Higher Education. Total U.S. Higher Education enrollment declined 1% to approximately 84,700 students, as growth in employer-affiliated enrollment was offset by lower unaffiliated enrollment. Revenue was essentially flat at $214 million, as higher revenue per student offset the enrollment decline.

Our productivity initiatives continued to hold operating expense growth to less than 1%, including continued investments in growth. Operating income was $22 million, a 4% decline, and an operating margin of approximately 10%. Student retention reached 89.2%, a new all-time high for U.S. Higher Education. Our healthcare portfolio continues to be the strongest source of growth in U.S. Higher Education. Healthcare enrollment grew 9% in the quarter and now represents 54% of total U.S. Higher Education enrollment, up from 49% a year ago, an increase of 500 basis points over the last year. Healthcare is also central to our broad employer strategy. Roughly 38% of our healthcare enrollment comes from employer partners, and employer-affiliated enrollment overall reached 35% of U.S.

Higher Education total enrollment, up 200 basis points from the prior year. We are now extending that portfolio into licensure track programs. Earlier this year, Capella enrolled the first cohort in its pre-licensure Bachelor of Science in Nursing program, and Strayer enrolled its first students in the new Associate of Applied Science in Radiologic Technology. Early demand for both programs has exceeded our initial assumptions. These two programs join Strayer's Licensed Practical Nurse diploma and Capella's expanded nurse practitioner portfolio, all aimed at the healthcare talent our employer partners increasingly need. To support that demand, we intend to also increase our growth investments in U.S. healthcare in 2027 with funding for new programs, clinical faculty, expanded clinical and instructional capacity.

This will allow programs like pre-licensure nursing and radiologic technology to grow at the pace their demand supports. Turning to Australia. Total enrollment declined 9% to approximately 17,100 students, and revenue declined 7% to AUD 64 million. The Australian team continued to manage costs well, with operating expenses down 4%, and operating income was AUD 10 million compared with AUD 12.5 million in the prior year, and an operating margin of approximately 16%. The decline is entirely a function of international enrollment. Over the course of this year, the Australian government restrictions on international students have become materially more severe than we anticipated.

New visa approvals for prospective students have slowed sharply, and in some months declining as much as 80% versus the prior year. In addition, the government has effectively closed the onshore transfer market by requiring international students already in Australia to obtain a new visa in order to change institutions. Given this environment, we have lowered our near-term growth expectations for the ANZ segment, which resulted in this quarter's $134 million non-cash impairment. Notwithstanding the headwinds on international enrollment, our domestic enrollment continues to fare well. Domestic new enrollment has grown every quarter this year, including 9% in each of the second and third quarters, and domestic students now represent close to 70% of new enrollment in Australia.

The quality of Torrens' academic experience remains strong and has shown significant improvement over the past year. We were pleased to see Torrens University's performance in the 2025 Quality Indicators for Learning and Teaching Student Experience Survey, the most comprehensive national survey of current higher education students in Australia. Torrens achieved widespread momentum across all undergraduate indicators, including a rise to sixth nationally for undergraduate teaching quality, up significantly from 19th the year before. At the postgraduate level, Torrens continues to lead at the top tier of Australian higher education, ranking in the top four nationwide for both skills development and peer engagement, alongside a seventh place ranking in postgraduate teaching quality.

This performance against national sector benchmarks reinforces Torrens' value proposition and supports student retention and long-term brand equity in industry-aligned education. The quality of Torrens' academic programs, combined with our own success in growing domestic enrollment, gives us confidence to increase our growth investments in Australia's domestic market in 2027. We are expanding our existing Adelaide campus and will launch several new health science programs, and we also plan to open a new campus in Perth in late 2027. Western Australia is the fastest-growing state in the country, with population growth 50% higher than the national average.

Greater Perth is projected to add more than a half a million residents over the next decade, and its economy is concentrated in the sectors where our new programs are focused, namely healthcare, engineering, construction, and defense. Perth will also position Torrens well for international recruitment from Asia when those constraints ease. Turning now to an update on our outlook versus our notional model. Given our current forecast for the balance of this year and the fact that the international enrollment environment in Australia deteriorated since the first half of the year, it appears unlikely our full-year results will fall inside of our notional outlook.

In terms of 2027, given that our forward revenue growth is mostly a product of current-year enrollment, we think the most likely outcome for consolidated revenue next year is to be flat with this year. We expect the cost of the growth investments that I have described this morning to be approximately $50 million in 2027. However, the productivity savings achieved this year will offset nearly half of that, such that year-over-year increase in operating expenses will be limited to just 2%.

Given that these incremental investments are targeted to support areas of proven strength at SEI, that is, our two high-growth, high-margin platform businesses, our U.S. healthcare portfolio, and our domestic market growth in Australia, we have a high degree of confidence in their ability to return the company to its notional growth rates in 2028 and beyond. Regarding capital allocation, in addition to our regular quarterly dividend, we repurchased approximately 347,000 shares during the quarter for a total of $28.5 million. We ended the quarter with $139 million of cash and marketable securities and no debt.

Finally, as always, I'd like to take this opportunity to thank all of my colleagues here at SEI for their ongoing commitment and support to our students and our corporate partners. With that, Victor, we'd be happy to take questions.

Operator: Thank you. To ask a question, you will need to press star 11 on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star 11 again. Please stand by. We'll compile the Q&A roster. One moment for our first question. Our first question will come from the line of Jeff Silber from BMO Capital Markets. Your line is open.

Jeff Silber: Thanks so much. Karl, really appreciate you giving us some insight into 2027. I was hoping I could just double-click on that a little bit. Is it possible to talk about the different segments? I say, overall, you think revenue most likely flat, but could we see growth in ETS offset by declines in the other two? From a margin perspective, where do you think you'd have the most impact in terms of declining margins potentially next year?

Karl McDonnell: I think we're absolutely going to have growth in ETS, Jeff. I suspect we'll have lower growth in U.S. Higher Education, driven by the strength of the healthcare portfolio that I just described. Overall, that'll be offset by the continuation of the restrictions in Australia, although we do expect that with the addition of the Perth campus, the expanded programs in Adelaide, launching several asynchronous online programs throughout Australia, we do expect that new student growth in Australia will be growing year-over-year in the back half of 2027.

Just given the headwinds that we've had, it's going to take a few quarters for that to translate into total enrollment growth, so I would expect that probably in the first part of 2028. From a margin standpoint, I would estimate that it could be in the range of 300 to 400 basis points at ETS, and a little less than that in U.S. Higher Education and Australia.

Jeff Silber: Okay, that's really helpful. I really appreciate that. Moving back to, I guess, the U.S., we had an elections earlier this week. I'm not asking you for your crystal ball, but given, guys, where you're located, you're probably closer to most in terms of what's going on and what potentially could go on. Any changes you're expecting with the changeover in Congress towards Democratic control?

Karl McDonnell: Well, I'd say that in the U.S., we have a high degree of confidence in sort of the regulatory and quality posture of both Strayer and Capella. We try to work constructively with any regulators or members of Congress or the administration, regardless of party affiliation, and we look forward to engaging with them once the new Congress is inaugurated in January.

Jeff Silber: Okay, fair enough. Thanks so much.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question will come from the line of Alex Paris from Barrington Research. Your line is open.

Alex Paris: Hi, guys. Thanks for taking my question. I too appreciate the granular detail by segment and the look at 2027. I just had a question on unaffiliated enrollment. Obviously, it was down 4%. That is actually an improvement from the second quarter by my math, when it was down 5.5%. But it has been down for eight consecutive quarters now, and you have consistently said you do anticipate returning to mid-single digits at some point, but it is not an area of focus. I get it. I am wondering, has there been an impact on the funnel from LLM, AI search, and so on? Could that be a contributing factor?

Karl McDonnell: Good morning, Alex. First of all, on unaffiliated enrollment, that's predominantly undergraduate business. It's an area that's important to us, but it's not one of our main strategic priorities in the way that healthcare is. You're right that the rate of decline moderated in the third quarter. We expect it to continue to moderate throughout 2027, perhaps even reaching break-even or growth by the end of 2027. In terms of LLM, it's certainly something that we're watching, but we've been focused on a quality of demand over quantity of demand for going on two years now. We don't peg rate of increase or decrease in any inquiry volume that we're getting as being most important.

We're looking at admission yield and sort of the acquisition cost to lifetime value, and both of those are near all-time highs. Obviously, we want to be relevant and favorably represented in any search medium that people are using, including LLMs, so we have a lot of people that are focused on it. But I can't say that we've really seen any adverse impact from it yet.

Alex Paris: What are you specifically doing to respond to the changes in the way students look at colleges and universities?

Karl McDonnell: It's a multi-function, multidisciplinary set of initiatives that we have. I don't really want to go into details on this call, but we do have a robust set of things that we're doing that we have a pretty high level of confidence will help position us well, not just in LLMs, but frankly, in any search medium that people may use.

Alex Paris: Obviously, it's important, but again, just to be clear, you've not really seen any material impact from the AEO as opposed to SEO on unaffiliated enrollment?

Karl McDonnell: Yeah, because, I mean, put yourself in our position, Alex. It would be next to impossible to ascribe any rate of change to LLM or any other single variable. We're happy with the demand that we're getting. In healthcare in particular, it's much stronger than what we expected. The growth of those new programs is far ahead of where we expected them to be, by as much as a year perhaps. But we're not ignoring it. We have people that are focused on it. We expect that over time, the evolution will become more apparent. I just would say it's very early, and we haven't been able to ascribe any changes to that specifically.

Alex Paris: Got you. My last question, quickly on ANZ. I appreciate you are controlling the controllables, campus expansions, new campuses, a focus on domestic. Is there any light at the end of the tunnel with regulatory? Obviously, this has been going on for a couple years now, and we thought that there'd be an improvement this year because of a lifting of the caps, but by slow rolling the visas, it's had an even more dramatic effect on international enrollment. Any additional color there would be great.

Karl McDonnell: I was a little surprised, frankly, that the transfer requirement to get a new visa was implemented. That was not something that we anticipated. It is what it is. Eventually, we're going to get to a new normal, a normalized rate of international enrollment. I think we're much closer to that as opposed to being further away from it.

If we continue to grow domestic growth in the high single digits as we're doing, or frankly, even in the low double digits when we add the additional capacity in Adelaide and Perth, eventually that's going to result in new student growth, which, as I said in my prepared remarks, I think could be in the latter half of next year, leading to total enrollment growth in the first part of 2028. Then if we get an easing of these restrictions, which some people in Australia think will happen over the coming several years, that will just be added sort of enrollment that we will get. We are not building a strategy around it.

We are accepting it for what it is and building all of our growth capital around the domestic market. Given, as I said, the strong performance of Torrens academically in the federal QILT survey, we think we are well-positioned to grow our domestic market share.

Alex Paris: Great. Appreciate the color. Thank you. I will get back in the queue.

Operator: Thank you. Once again, that is star 11 for questions, star 11. Our next question will come from the line of Jasper Bibb from Truist Securities. Your line is open.

Jasper Bibb: Hey. Good morning, everyone. Apologies if I missed it, but I guess I just wanted to understand how you're thinking about EBIT margin expansions with 2026 at this point. I guess, for me, it would be helpful if you could kind of frame 4Q expectations so we have the right jumping off point for all the kind of helpful points that you probably gave us all.

Daniel Jackson: Hey, Jasper. Yeah, it might be a bad connection. I am not sure I got the full question. I think it was 2026 EBIT margin. Was that your question?

Jasper Bibb: Yeah. I apologize. I am switching to speakerphone now. Hopefully, you can hear me better, but

Daniel Jackson: Yeah, that is much better.

Jasper Bibb: I just wanted to understand kind of 4Q expectations so we have the right jumping off point for kind of all the 2027 comments you gave earlier on the call.

Daniel Jackson: Hey, Jasper, you're talking about margin, right?

Jasper Bibb: Yeah, margin or, I mean, revenue if you have it.

Daniel Jackson: Well, we don't give revenue, forward-looking revenue input. We have commented on margin, as you know, relative to the notional model of 200 basis points of expansion. Karl just mentioned that we're well off of that at this point. However, as we said last quarter, when you adjust for the FWO reserve we took in the second quarter, we're actually not too far off of the 200 basis points.

Jasper Bibb: Okay. I just maybe wanted to, if we could spend a little bit more time on just kind of what you are seeing in U.S. Higher Education right now and kind of how that is informing your expectations for 2027. Enrollment is down a little bit, but I think retention is going up, so I would assume new starts in the U.S. might be down more than enrollment right now. I guess, could you just kind of frame what you are seeing in new starts in the U.S. and how that informs your expectations for next year?

Karl McDonnell: Sure. Well, as I said, healthcare is very strong, growing almost double digits, 9% in the last quarter. That is well over half of our enrollments now, so we are confident that is going to continue to grow, and I suspect the growth rate will increase given the strength of the new pre-licensure programs. The undergraduate unaffiliated has been declining. Part of that is just a function that we have been deploying more of our growth capital into healthcare and not into undergraduate business. As Alex Paris noted, and I confirmed, the decline is moderating. We think it will continue to moderate.

So, net of everything that we are seeing, I suspect that we are going to have net positive new student enrollment growth in 2027, and the division as a whole will sort of mean revert toward mid-single digits as we work our way through the year.

Jasper Bibb: Okay. No, that makes sense. Maybe last one for me, the subscriptions at Sophia Learning just slowed a little bit from the second quarter. Is that kind of harder comps, or have you seen any impact on subs growth or retention from kind of the recent changes you made to the platform over the summer?

Karl McDonnell: It is almost entirely a function of anniversarying that large corporate client that we have. If you excluded that corporate client, direct-to-consumer subscription growth is still close to 20% and growing, holding that growth rate. So it is really a function of the anniversarying of that one client that is quite large.

Jasper Bibb: Okay. Understood. Thanks for taking the questions.

Operator: Thank you. I'm not showing any further questions at this time. I'd like to turn back over to Karl McDonnell, CEO, for closing remarks.

Karl McDonnell: Thank you, everybody. We look forward to discussing our fourth quarter results with you in February.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect. Everyone, have a great day.

#3081. GEO Group (GEO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Adelanto sale proceeds funded a major debt cut and a bigger buyback program.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

The GEO Group, Inc. (GEO -8.57%) reported record-breaking quarterly financial performance, achieving its highest-ever levels of quarterly revenue and Adjusted EBITDA. Management stated that the results were driven by the activation of new facility contracts signed in 2025 and an expanded scope of services for federal agencies. The company completed the $950 million sale of the Adelanto complex to the federal government while retaining a multiyear contract to provide support services at the site. This divestiture enabled the redemption of $650 million in senior secured notes, significantly reducing corporate debt and lowering net leverage to approximately 1.0 times Adjusted EBITDA. Management also increased its share repurchase authorization to $1.25 billion, signaling a shift in capital allocation toward shareholder returns as the company transitions toward a support services-focused business model.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the GEO Group Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in a listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then 1 on a touch tone phone. To withdraw your question, please press star then 2. Please note this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Pablo Paez, Executive Vice President of Corporate Relations. Please go ahead.

Pablo Paez: Thank you, operator. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us for today's discussion of The GEO Group's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results With us today are George C. Zoley, Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and Founder and Shayn March, senior vice president and chief financial officer. This afternoon, we will discuss our third quarter results as well as our outlook. We will conclude the call with a question-and-answer session. This conference call is also being webcast live on our Investor website at investors.geogroup.com. Today, we will discuss non GAAP basis information. A reconciliation from non GAAP basis information to GAAP basis results is included in the press release and the supplemental disclosure we issued this morning.

Additionally, much of the information we will discuss today including the answers we give in response to your questions, may include forward looking statements. Regarding our beliefs and current expectations with respect to various matters. These forward looking statements are intended to fall within the safe harbor provisions of the securities laws. Our actual results may differ materially from those in the forward looking statements, as a result of various factors, contained in our Securities and Exchange Commission filings including the Form 10-Ks, 10-Q, and 8-K reports. With that, please allow me to turn this call over to our Chairman, CEO and Founder, George C. Zoley. George?

George C. Zoley: Thank you, Pablo, and good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Our diversified business units have continued to deliver strong financial and operational performance through 2026. And our third quarter 2026 results marked a record breaking quarter for GEO. Compared to the same period in 2026, our third quarter 2020 revenues increased 12% to approximately $761.1 million. While our third quarter 2026 net income attributable to GEO operations was approximately $49.2 million. Compared to the same period in 2025 our third quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA increased 21% to approximately $145.3 million. And our adjusted net income increased 48% to approximately $51.8 million.

These results represent the highest level of quarterly revenues and adjusted EBITDA ever reported in our company's history. Even better than expected performance in 2026 has been driven by the significant revenue growth from the new contracts that we entered into throughout 2025. They included the activation of 4 facilities to house ICE detainees totaling 6 thousand beds. Valued at approximately $280 million in annual revenues. So far in 2026, we have had an even more successful year for the new expanded services entering into new contracts for the activation of 4 additional facilities to house ICE detainees totaling approximately 4.8 thousand beds.

These contracts, along with the expanded scope of services at existing facilities created an overall value of approximately $500 million in incremental annual revenues. First, we entered into a 5 year support services contract with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center at the 1.19 thousand-bed Bighorn facility in Hudson, Colorado while also entering into a lease agreement with the facility owner. The Bighorn support services contract is expected to generate approximately $85 million in annual revenues in the first full year of operations. Starting in the first quarter of 2027.

We then entered into a 5 year support services contract with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center in the geo owned 1.32 thousand-bed Rivers facility in Winton North Carolina. The Rivers support services contract is expected to generate approximately $80 million in annual revenues in the first full year of operations, also starting in the first quarter of 2027. More recently, we announced earlier this week the city of Big Spring in Texas has entered into a 10 year intergovernmental service agreement with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center at the 2.33 thousand-bed Big Spring complex comprised of 1.4 thousand-bed flight line facility and the 925-bed Cedar Hills facility.

GEO will provide support services at the Big Spring complex which is expected to generate approximately $200 million in annual revenues for GEO in the first full year of operations. Starting in the second quarter of 2027. Under all 3 of these contracts, ICE will reimburse GEO for the capital expenditures needed to reactivate these 4 facilities as well as providing funding for start up expenses during the activation period. Following the activation of these 4 facilities, our total ICE beds under contract will increase to approximately 33 thousand beds at 29 facilities. The current census across our active ICE facilities is approximately 24 thousand representing approximately 1/3 of the current national ICE population of approximately 73 thousand.

Over the past 2 quarters, we have also entered into new or modified contracts for the continued provision of support services at existing ICE processing centers. First, during the third quarter, we entered into a contract modification to increase staffing levels at the 1.94 thousand-bed Adelanto ICE processing center to support the increase in the scope of services at the facility adding $60 million in incremental annual revenues. More recently, last week, we announced that we have entered into a new 10 year management contract with expanded support services at incremental annual revenue value of $50 million at the GEO owned 1.64 thousand-bed Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington.

The new 10-year contract is expected to generate approximately $140 million in total annual revenues for GEO and continue through 10/27/2036, making it the first contract we have entered into ICE with a full base term of 10 years. This new contract was awarded under ongoing procurement that involves 3 other geo owned facilities, the Aurora facility, the Moshannon Valley facility, and Broward ICE Processing Center. Which are also expected to receive new 10-year contract awards. ICE enforcement initiatives nationwide are supported by significant funding that has already been approved by the United States Congress. ICE was allocated $45 billion for the detention under the 1 big beautiful bill which is available through 9/30/2029.

We believe that less than $10 billion of $45 billion has been spent so far. Under the Secure America Act, ICE also received $38.5 billion in baseline appropriations funding as well as an additional $30 billion for other priorities under the 1 Big Beautiful bill all of which is also available through 9/30/2029. As ICE continues to pursue these enforcement initiatives, we expect GEO to continue to be part of the solution as a 40-year partner to the agency. Following our recent contract announcements, we now have approximately 2.9 thousand idle beds that remain available at 4 company owned facilities, which are well suited for the needs of the federal government.

At full capacity, these 2.9 thousand idle beds could generate approximately $170 million in combined incremental revenues. Additionally, we have expansion capacity of several thousands of beds at existing geo managed ICE facilities. Our third quarter 2026 results also reflect a significant expansion in our secure transportation services on behalf of ICE, and the US Marshals Service. As a result of new or amended contracts we entered into in 2025. The support services that we provide under ICE Air transportation subcontract have continued To Steadily Grow Driven By The Increase In The Number Of Removable Flights.

Additionally, Our New Bighorn Rivers and Big Spring contracts with ICE are expected to generate approximately $28 million in combined additional annual transportation services revenues once normalized in 2027. Importantly, during the third quarter of 2 thousand 26, our ISAP contract continued to experience a steady technology shift to more intensive and higher price monitoring devices such as ankle monitors. ISAP is the only ICE program currently in place to provide electronic monitoring and case management services for individuals on the non-detained docket.

The program relies on several forms of monitoring including GPS ankle bracelets, or wrist worn devices that provide real time tracking as well as the SmartLink phone app, which relies on facial recognition voice ID, and GPS to confirm a person's location during the predetermined check-in. The current overall ISAP count is approximately 190 thousand participants up from 184 thousand participants 3 months ago. The number is 58 thousand currently, from 17 thousand early in 2025. We also continue to experience a steady increase in the number of ISAP participants assigned to case management services, which involves staff interaction and monitoring for approximately 121 thousand individuals currently.

As a result of these trends, revenue and net operating income for our electronic monitoring and supervision services increased during the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same period a year ago, reversing a multiyear trend of revenue and net operating income declines. Additionally, during the third quarter of 2 thousand 26, we generated revenues of approximately $3 million from our skip tracing contract. Moving to our outlook, we have increased our net income and adjusted EBITDA guidance for 2026 to reflect the strength of our results in the first 3 quarters of the year. Our fourth quarter 2020 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance exceeds our third quarter 2 thousand and 26 results.

Positioning GEO to set another record breaking quarter. Looking forward to 2027, there are several sources of future upside compared to our 2026 guidance. Additional growth in our additional secure services segment from the reactivation of additional idle facilities and or higher overall populations across our active facilities. The expected transition of our previously announced managed only contracts for the 1.88 thousand-bed Graceville facility and the 985-bed Bay facility in the state of Florida, which are expected to occur on 07/01/2027.

Additional volume increases and/or accelerated technology service mix in our ISAP contract, additional growth in our secured transportation services business, and additional revenue from higher utilization of our skip tracing contracts. Before I turn the call over to our CFO, Shayn March for a more detailed review of our third quarter results and guidance I would like to provide you with an update regarding the plan by ICE and DHS to purchase existing privately owned turnkey ICE processing centers. As we announced last month, we completed the sales of our 1.28 thousand-bed Adelanto West ICE processing center 660-bed Adelanto East, 704-bed Desert View Annex to DHS.

For an aggregate gross sales price of $950 million and net proceeds after taxes and transaction fees and expenses of approximately $705 million. We expect to continue providing support services at the Adelanto complex under our existing contract with ICE, which has a full effective term through 12/19/2034. We used proceeds from the sales of the Adelanto complex for the redemption of our $650 million 2029 senior secured notes and we also entered into an amended and restated credit agreement extending the maturity of our $550 million revolving credit facility to July 2031. And also increasing our restricted pay payment capacity, including share repurchases.

Following the redemption of the 2029 senior secured notes, our total outstanding corporate debt consists of our 2031 senior unsecured notes totaling $625 million. As we previously announced, our Board of Directors has increased our share repurchase authorization, which is effective through 12/31/2029 by $750 million to $1.25 billion. Based on our current leverage and so long as we remain below specified leverage levels, GEO is permitted to make unlimited restricted payments, including share repurchases under both the amended credit facility agreement and the senior unsecured note indenture.

#3080. Tokens Built The Digital AI Business. Physical AI Needs A Different Unit

Brandon Barbello is co-founder and COO of Archetype AI, with over 10 years of product leadership across Fortune 500 and startups.

​Almost every industrial AI deployment I’ve seen lately eventually reaches the same meeting. The pilot worked, the operations team wants to expand to more machines and finance asks what the numbers look like at 300 assets instead of three.

Increasingly, that question comes with another: Will you charge us by the token?​

Enterprises have spent the past few years learning a new vocabulary around AI economics: tokens, inference, context windows, consumption-based pricing and discovering how hard those costs are to predict. Accenture recently reported that one in three organizations exhausts its AI token budget before year’s end.​

For digital AI, token economics are justifiable. Jensen Huang has said he’d be “deeply alarmed” if a $500,000 engineer didn’t consume at least $250,000 of tokens a year, because the spend buys output. For knowledge work, he’s right.​

But a compressor is not a $500,000 engineer. It produces signal every second it runs, regardless of whether anyone asks it a question. It makes more sense to analyze that signal locally, on hardware the customer already owns, than to ship every second of it to the cloud.​

We have an opportunity to build business models that reflect those differences instead of importing LLM economics into the physical world.​

Most LLM interactions are episodic: A person asks a question or gives an agent a task, and the model produces an output.

In the physical world, cameras, vibration monitors, pressure gauges and other sensors generate data continuously, and applications are inherently always-on. Meter by the token, and the bill grows with every hour the equipment runs.

The underlying data is different, too. Language models are trained on text and images. They don’t understand what a bearing sounds like at 4,000 RPM. That takes a model built to interpret physical signals directly.​

Industrial data is also often too proprietary to leave the facility. Streaming that data to the cloud puts the company’s core IP at risk. This affects how physical AI gets deployed, scaled and priced.​

The practical answer is to run intelligence where the data originates. Smaller, general-purpose models can increasingly run on customers’ own hardware, keeping sensitive information on-site and letting decisions happen where the data is produced.

One municipal customer of Archetype AI, for example, uses cameras across hundreds of intersections to improve pedestrian safety. Based on internal analysis, each intersection produces roughly 43 gigabytes of camera data daily. Moving that data to the cloud would cost an estimated $850,000 to $1 million annually before any AI processing. Distilling a larger model into a smaller one let physical AI run on hardware the customer already owns, using its existing cameras.​​

Running at the edge, the system can determine if a pedestrian is still in the crosswalk without sending data to a remote data center and waiting for a response. That round trip could take longer than the window to act.

Training, fine-tuning and fleet-level analysis can continue to happen in the cloud, while time-sensitive decisions happen closer to the edge. Use the cloud where scale is valuable and the edge where speed, cost and responsiveness matter most.​

When AI runs primarily as a metered cloud service, consumption-based pricing makes sense: Someone has to pay for the compute.

But once physical AI runs on the customer’s infrastructure, compute is already paid for, so pricing doesn’t have to correspond to every unit of inference. It can follow from the unit where the customer actually receives value.​ Industrial businesses already think this way, and it’s how they buy software.

This points to a different model: licensing per asset, machine, facility or application, rather than charging when the system processes data. That brings predictability. Finance teams can count machines more easily than forecast tokens; a company expanding from 10 machines to 1,000 knows the cost before deployment.​​

The operational value becomes clearer at scale. In one Archetype AI customer deployment, analysis of data from more than 40 sensors across 63 wind turbines identified nine previously unknown failure modes, revealing critical problems before they cause downtime.​

The trade-off is that per-asset licensing can be less economical for equipment that needs only occasional analysis. Companies should consider how often the system will be used and the operational value it delivers.​

Inference is getting cheaper. Gartner predicts inference on a one-trillion-parameter model will cost providers over 90% less by 2030 than in 2025. Elsewhere, however, Gartner expects inference spend per agentic workflow to climb more than fivefold through 2028, since agentic systems use five to 30 times more tokens per task than chatbots.

In other words, falling unit costs don’t guarantee savings. Every new sensor adds volume, regardless of operational value.

NVIDIA researchers argue that smaller LLMs are already powerful and economical enough for many agentic tasks. Physical AI takes that further, with models built from the start to understand physical signals and run where signals originate.​

Physical AI is still in early days. We shouldn’t assume what worked for digital AI is right for physical. Pricing per asset means vendors grow as customers expand, and customers expand as the system proves its value.

Before expanding a pilot, businesses can bring operations, IT and finance together to compare the total cost at three assets, 30 and 300, including licensing, hardware, integration and ongoing support. Weigh those costs against measurable outcomes such as reduced downtime or maintenance hours, and agree on what would justify expansion.

When finance understands what 300 assets will cost and operations can demonstrate the value, the conversation can move from how usage will be billed to whether—and how quickly—to scale.​​​

#3078. 2027 Tax Brackets and Federal Income Tax Rates

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

#3076. Graham Corp (GHM) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Record backlog and margin gains came as defense and space demand stayed strong.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Graham Corporation (GHM +3.71%) reported significant margin expansion and record backlog levels during the second quarter, driven by sustained demand in the defense and space sectors and the successful integration of FlackTek. Management reported that the company's defense segment now accounts for two thirds of total revenue, supported by multi-decade shipbuilding cycles and strong bipartisan support for naval programs. The company stated that it is executing a three-year strategic framework intended to achieve 8% to 10% annual organic revenue growth and adjusted EBITDA margins of 14% to 16% by fiscal 2029. Management indicated that financial flexibility remains high with zero debt, allowing for continued organic investments in testing facilities and selective pursuit of strategic acquisitions.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Graham Corporation fiscal second quarter 2027 earnings call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. #3073. Cathie Wood Just Sold AMD Stock and Bought This AI Chip Stock Instead

Should investors follow Cathie Wood's recent AI stock play?

Cathie Wood founded Ark Invest in 2014, and the CEO has made a name for herself as an investor to watch when it comes to growth stocks. Ark provides exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that are heavily built around innovative new technologies with explosive growth potential, and the company takes a very active approach to portfolio management. In other words, Ark's investment teams tend to buy and sell stocks frequently for the funds that they manage.

Notably, Ark offers investors a huge degree of transparency and regularly catalogs all of its trades even when it is not required to do so for regulatory purposes. Due to Wood's status as a high-profile growth investor and the high visibility of her company's trading activities, the investment firm's buying and selling moves tend to attract a significant amount of attention -- and Ark just sold Advanced Micro Devices and bought Nvidia (NVDA -9.26%).

Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood. Image source: Getty Images.

At the end of September, Ark made a notable move for its flagship Ark Innovation ETF. It sold shares of AMD valued at roughly $111.1 million and effectively used the proceeds from the sale to buy $81 million worth of Nvidia stock. The transactions seem to send a clear message: Ark believed that Nvidia was the more attractively valued of the two artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor stocks.

As of this writing, Nvidia is trading at roughly 22 times this year's expected earnings. Meanwhile, AMD is valued at roughly 63.5 times expected forward profits. The valuation disparity reflects expectations that AMD will be able to grow earnings significantly faster going forward.

While Nvidia continues to dominate the market for advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) used for AI computing, investors have been betting that AMD will score market share wins in the GPU space and take advantage of huge opportunities as the central processing units (CPUs) become increasingly integrated in the broader artificial intelligence compute stack. CPUs are a category that AMD currently leads Nvidia in, and growing demand for CPUs for AI inference applications could be a powerful demand catalyst for the company.

On the other hand, Nvidia is making a big play for the future of the CPU space -- and its moves in the category could help explain why Wood's company is buying the AI hardware leader's stock while also reducing its exposure to AMD. Nvidia's new Vera Rubin server platform combines the company's next-generation GPUs with its next CPU offerings, and the tech pairing could threaten AMD's growth opportunities.

Here's a rundown of changes to some well-known tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

Each year, the IRS updates common tax provisions, such as income tax brackets and the standard deduction, to ensure the tax code is keeping pace with the rising cost of living.

These tweaks — formally known as inflation adjustments — help prevent “bracket creep,” where taxpayers who received a cost-of-living raise can pay more in taxes even though their purchasing power remains unchanged.

Inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year were set at 3.2% — larger than the previous two years as inflation heated up. This could mean lower tax bills for some people when they file in 2028.

In the U.S., there are seven marginal rates — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37% — which will remain unchanged for 2027.

Contrary to a popular myth, it’s uncommon for people to pay a single flat federal tax rate on their taxable income. Instead, portions of a person’s income can be taxed at different rates depending on which tax brackets they fall into. For example, some of a person’s income could be taxed at 10%, another chunk at 12%, and so on.

For 2027, the IRS is adjusting those tax brackets — the windows of income that dictate where a tax rate ends and begins — for each filing status. The adjustments mean that some people may be able to keep some of their income in lower tax brackets, and those who received a cost-of-living raise may avoid getting a portion of their income pushed into a higher bracket.

Married filers, for example, can make up to $104,050 to remain with a top tax rate of 12%, compared with $100,800 in 2026. This increase could allow some couples to shelter an additional $3,250 from a higher tax rate in 2027.

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Single filers

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Heads of household

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Married filing separately

» MORE: See the full 2027 tax brackets for each filing status

The IRS lets most filers lower their taxable income by taking the standard deduction or itemizing their returns. The standard deduction, a flat amount based on filing status and age, is popular, as it requires less work to claim and is often more beneficial for those who might not have deductible expenses.

For 2027, the standard deduction will be $16,600 for single filers and those married filing separately, a $500 increase from 2026. Joint filers will be eligible to take $33,200 and heads of household can take $24,925, a $1,000 and $775 increase over 2026, respectively.

» Need help deciding whether to itemize or take the standard deduction? Learn about the differences

Also included in the IRS' 32-page inflation release are various updates to several tax provisions beyond the federal tax brackets. Plus, a brand-new tax credit will go into effect in 2027.

Starting in 2027, taxpayers who contribute to a health flexible spending account (FSA) can contribute up to $3,500 and, if their plan permits, carry over up to $700 into the next tax year.

For those with health savings accounts, the 2027 limit for contributions will rise to $4,500 for self-only coverage and $9,000 for family coverage.

The annual exclusion for gifts, which limits how much taxpayers can give an individual without filing a gift tax return on certain gifts, will be $20,000 per person in 2027, an increase of $1,000 compared with 2026.

The lifetime estate tax exclusion establishes a threshold for the taxation of estates upon a person's death. In 2027, estates valued at or below $15.48 million will not be subject to estate tax, up from $15 million in 2026.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit will launch on Jan. 1. According to the IRS, it aims to support private contributions for K-12 scholarships. Taxpayers who donate to a "scholarship granting organization" in one of the 30 participating states can receive a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $1,700 ($3,400 for couples filing jointly).

#3067. Himax Blames 'Abrupt and Significant Correction' in Auto Chip Demand as Stock Crashes Nearly 30%. Is Now the Time to Buy?

Himax sees fourth-quarter revenue falling 22% to 26% after a sudden pullback in auto chips. Is the slump temporary?

Himax (HIMX -26.44%), the fabless chip designer behind display driver chips for TVs, phones and car screens, expects a steep revenue drop in the final quarter of the year, and investors are punishing the stock amid an already bruising day for the market.

On the company's earnings call Thursday, President and CEO Jordan Wu blamed "an abrupt and significant correction" in automotive display driver chip orders for the new guidance. Shares had plunged nearly 28% to $7.55 by about 2:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, a steep decline exacerbated by a broader market sell-off targeting AI-linked names.

Wu told the call that the year began soft in the first quarter. Panel makers then bought heavily in the second and third quarters to keep up with surging orders from Chinese automakers expanding overseas. "Right after China's National Day holidays in early October," he said, the company saw a "sudden and sizable decline in demand among the customers that had purchased aggressively in prior quarters."Wu also said the forecast cut partly reflects Chinese automakers' "earlier, overly aggressive export expectations, along with their growing concerns over inventory levels across distribution channels." He added that panel makers mostly serving customers outside China have held their forecasts steady, and some have nudged fourth-quarter orders higher.The damage is concentrated in automotive display drivers. Wu said automotive timing-controller sales should keep growing from quarter to quarter.That earlier buying spree already showed up in the third quarter. Automotive driver sales rose in solid double digits from the prior quarter, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth, as some panel makers accelerated purchases.

Third-quarter revenue rose 8.5% to $246.8 million from the prior quarter, and gross margin improved to 34.2% from 33.1%. Profit came to $18.6 million, or 10.7 cents per diluted ADS (American depositary share), topping the company's 8 to 10-cent guidance, which Himax attributed to lower-than-expected operating expenses.For the fourth quarter, management expects gross margin flat to slightly up and profit of 4.5 to 6.5 cents per diluted ADS. That range leaves out an expected after-tax gain of about $19 to $20 million from selling its stake in an equity-method investment, a sale Himax expects to close this quarter.

Wu said on the call that automotive chip sales rose a "decent" 16% year over year in the first nine months of 2026, and he still expects about 10% growth for the full year, even with worldwide vehicle production expected to decline. The company also expects automotive timing-controller sales to grow more than 40% this year. Non-driver sales, which include timing controllers, reached $51.0 million in the third quarter, up 11.2% from the prior quarter.The chief executive framed the slump as "abrupt, short-term order adjustments by certain customers, while our market leader position remains firmly intact."Supply is the other theme. Wu said foundries and packaging and testing providers have announced significant price increases for 2027 and that capacity is the company's top priority because automotive customers demand stricter supply assurance. He added that Himax has secured capacity commitments from key suppliers and is working with customers to share rising costs. However, higher foundry prices will remain a cost to watch, with Himax and across tech stocks that rely on outside chipmakers.

It depends on how you read October. If customers simply over-ordered and are now working through inventory, the full-year automotive growth target suggests the business is intact, and that's how management describes it. If end demand for Chinese car exports is weaker than implied by those orders, the correction could run longer than a quarter.With the stock down so steeply in Thursday trading, a lot of bad news may already be priced in, particularly since it appears investors are fearing the worst when it comes to how a newly elected government could interfere with the AI build-out. Even so, a sudden guidance cut does warrant caution. Many long-term investors would likely wait for evidence that the fourth-quarter outlook holds, and anyone interested in these semiconductor stocks might keep a position small.The next checkpoints are whether fourth-quarter profit lands in the guided 4.5 to 6.5 cent range and whether the stake sale closes as expected.

#3066. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

#3061. Why Ecovyst Stock Topped the Market Today

The specialty chemicals company had a beat-and-raise third quarter.

Investors considered specialty chemical manufacturer Ecovyst (ECVT +2.11%) to be a special stock on Wednesday. They traded it up after the company published its third-quarter results that morning, and it closed the day more than 2% higher. That trounced the under 0.4% gain of the bellwether S&P 500 index.

For the period, Ecovyst's sales were just under $309 million, which bettered the year-ago quarter by 51%. However, that total includes sales from Calabrian, a business the company acquired at the end of June.

Getty Images. Image source: Getty Images.

In terms of profitability, net income not under generally accepted accounting principles (non-GAAP, or adjusted) increased by 18% to over $25 million, or $0.23 per share.

With those results, Ecovyst notched a pair of beats on the consensus analyst estimates. The more convincing one was revenue, as those pundits collectively modeled for under $282 million. Their adjusted earnings per share (EPS) estimate was $0.21, meanwhile.

In its earnings release, Ecovyst attributed its organic growth largely to increased export demand, which boosted sales of both regenerated and virgin sulfuric acid.

As for the proximate future, Ecovyst quoted CEO Kurt Bitting as saying, "Given current refining economics, we anticipate high refinery utilization through year-end, and we expect demand across our portfolio to remain healthy for the rest of the year."

In line with that bullish forecast, the company raised its guidance for full-year adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) to a range of $208 million to $212 million. That's well above both the previous estimate ($195 million to $207 million) and the pre-Calabrian 2025 result of $172 million.

It isn't easy to find a thriving company in the specialty chemicals space these days, and it looks as if Ecovyst has hit the sweet spot with its in-demand products. It also seems to be integrating Calabrian smoothly and quickly. With all that, its rosy forecast is fully believable, making it a stock to watch in its sector.
